name: Skill Builder Set
source: Original LR and RC questions written for LSAT Trainer to fill the mastery path, difficulty 1–5, in the style of PrepTests 150–159. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus:
Marguerite: Carrow should replace its annual fireworks display with a laser show. The explosions terrify many residents' dogs, and the smoke drifts over the marsh where herons are nesting at that time of year.

Teodor: A laser show would spare the dogs and the herons, but far fewer people would come to see it. The fireworks draw thousands downtown each summer, and the downtown shops depend on that evening's sales. Carrow should keep the fireworks.
questions.stem: Marguerite and Teodor disagree over whether
choices: the fireworks display frightens many of the dogs that belong to residents of Carrow
the downtown shops in Carrow depend heavily on the sales they make on the evening of the display
Carrow should stop holding its annual fireworks display and hold a laser show in its place
a laser show would draw far fewer people downtown than the fireworks display now draws
the herons nesting in the marsh are harmed more by the smoke than by the noise of the explosions
questions.explanation: Marguerite says Carrow should replace the fireworks with a laser show; Teodor says Carrow should keep the fireworks, so they disagree over (C). (D) is the trap: Teodor claims a laser show would draw fewer people, but Marguerite never addresses attendance, so she isn't committed either way. (A) is common ground, since Teodor concedes a laser show would spare the dogs, and (B) is Teodor's claim alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Marguerite: Replace the fireworks with a laser show; the explosions terrify dogs and the smoke drifts over nesting herons.; Teodor: A laser show would spare the animals, but far fewer people would come, and downtown shops depend on that night's sales; keep the fireworks.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Marguerite's bottom line: swap the fireworks for lasers. Teodor's bottom line: keep the fireworks. That's a clean yes versus no. Notice what Teodor gives away: he admits a laser show "would spare the dogs and the herons." So the animal facts are common ground. The fight is over the swap itself.

choices.note: Common ground, not a dispute. Marguerite says the explosions terrify dogs, and Teodor grants that a laser show "would spare the dogs." When the second speaker concedes a point, it can't be the point at issue.
Teodor's claim only. Marguerite never mentions the shops or their sales, so we can't say she rejects this.
CORRECT. Marguerite: "Carrow should replace its annual fireworks display with a laser show." Teodor: "Carrow should keep the fireworks." One says yes, the other says no.

Tempting, because it's the heart of Teodor's case and it sounds like something Marguerite must dispute. But she never says a word about how many people would come. Maybe she agrees attendance would drop and just thinks the animals matter more. Silence isn't disagreement.
Neither speaker compares the harm from smoke with the harm from noise. Marguerite mentions smoke drifting over the herons, but she doesn't rank the two harms.

questions.stimulus:
Editor: More and more of the Ledger's readers now read it online, and the printed crossword fills a page that could carry local news. We should drop the crossword from the printed paper and run it only on our website.

Publisher: Many of our oldest subscribers tell us the crossword is the main reason they still pay for the printed paper. If we drop it from print, we will lose those subscriptions. The crossword should stay in print.
questions.stem: The editor and the publisher disagree over whether
choices: a growing share of the Ledger's readers now read the paper online rather than in print
some of the Ledger's oldest subscribers would cancel their subscriptions if the crossword were dropped from print
local news is more valuable to the Ledger's readers than the crossword is
the Ledger should stop printing its crossword and offer it only on its website
the Ledger's website should offer a crossword to readers who read the paper online
questions.explanation: The editor wants the crossword dropped from print and run only online; the publisher says it should stay in print, so they disagree over (D). (E) is the trap: the editor wants an online crossword, but the publisher never objects to one; he only wants it kept in print as well. (A) is the editor's claim alone, (B) the publisher's alone, and neither ranks local news against the crossword, as (C) requires.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Editor: Readers are moving online and the crossword's page could carry local news; drop it from print and run it only online.; Publisher: Many old subscribers pay for print mainly because of the crossword; dropping it would lose them; keep it in print.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. The editor's plan has two parts: take the crossword out of print, and put it online. The publisher objects only to the first part: "The crossword should stay in print." He says nothing against an online version. So the dispute is about print, not about the website. Watch for answers that grab the half of the editor's plan the publisher never touches.

choices.note: The editor's premise. The publisher doesn't deny that readers are moving online; he just thinks the old print subscribers matter.
The publisher's claim only. The editor never discusses what the oldest subscribers would do.
Neither speaker makes this comparison. The editor says the page "could carry local news," which is a use for the space, not a ranking of local news over the crossword.
CORRECT. Editor: drop it from print, run it only online. Publisher: "The crossword should stay in print." Yes versus no on the plan itself.

Tempting, because it's part of the editor's plan. But the publisher never says the website shouldn't have a crossword. He could happily run it in both places. Only one speaker takes a side, so it isn't the point at issue.

questions.stimulus:
Arvid: The cargo of the Selkie, the schooner that sank off Cullis Point in 1871, should be raised and placed in the county museum. Divers have already pried off several of the ship's brass fittings, and more will vanish if the wreck is left alone.

Leonie: Raising the cargo would strip away the context that shows historians how the ship was loaded. The cargo should stay on the seabed, and the county should patrol the site to deter looters.
questions.stem: Arvid and Leonie disagree over whether
choices: the Selkie's cargo should be removed from the wreck and placed in the county museum
divers have already taken some of the brass fittings from the wreck of the Selkie
patrolling the site would be enough to keep looters from taking items from the wreck
the way a ship's cargo was loaded can tell historians something about the ship
items taken from the wreck by divers would be of little value to historians
questions.explanation: Arvid says the cargo should be raised and put in the museum; Leonie says it should stay on the seabed, so they disagree over (A). (C) is the trap: Leonie proposes patrols, but she never claims they would be enough, and Arvid never discusses patrols at all. (B) is Arvid's claim, which Leonie implicitly accepts by worrying about looters, and (D) is Leonie's claim alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Arvid: Raise the cargo and put it in the museum; divers are already stripping the wreck.; Leonie: Raising it destroys the context that shows how the ship was loaded; leave it on the seabed and patrol the site.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Arvid: raise it. Leonie: "The cargo should stay on the seabed." That's the clash. Leonie doesn't dispute the looting. Her patrol idea assumes it's a real threat. She just thinks the cure is guards, not removal.

choices.note: CORRECT. Arvid says the cargo "should be raised and placed in the county museum." Leonie says it "should stay on the seabed." Direct yes versus no.
Arvid says this, and Leonie doesn't deny it. If anything, her call for patrols to "deter looters" suggests she accepts that looting is happening. Not a disagreement.

Tempting, because it looks like the obvious rebuttal Arvid would make. But Arvid never mentions patrols, and Leonie never says patrols would be "enough." She only proposes them. Neither speaker is committed on whether they'd suffice.
Leonie's point only. Arvid never discusses what loading patterns tell historians.
Neither speaker says this. Arvid worries that fittings will "vanish," which suggests he thinks they matter, but nobody rates the value of looted items to historians.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Many observers take last year's sharp drop in sales of new bicycles in Dellmont as a sign that residents are losing interest in cycling. In fact, interest in cycling there is almost certainly as strong as ever. Sales of used bicycles in Dellmont rose by nearly a third last year, and membership in the city's cycling clubs reached a record high. Moreover, the drop coincided with a steep rise in the price of new bicycles.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the economist's argument?
choices: Observers are mistaken in thinking that sales of new bicycles in Dellmont fell sharply over the course of last year.
The residents of Dellmont are almost certainly no less interested in cycling now than they have been in the past.
Sales of used bicycles in Dellmont rose by nearly a third last year even as sales of new bicycles fell.
The drop in sales of new bicycles in Dellmont last year was caused by a steep rise in their price.
Membership in cycling clubs is a more reliable measure of a city's interest in cycling than bicycle sales are.
questions.explanation: The economist rejects the observers' reading of the sales drop and claims instead that interest in cycling is as strong as ever; the used-bicycle sales, the club membership and the price rise all support that claim, so (B) is the conclusion. (D) is the most tempting wrong answer, but the economist says only that the drop coincided with the price rise, offering it as an alternative account of the drop, not as the main point. (A) misstates the observers, who are right that sales fell, and (C) is a premise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Interest in cycling in Dellmont is almost certainly as strong as ever.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Used-bicycle sales rose by nearly a third; cycling-club membership hit a record; the drop in new-bicycle sales coincided with a steep price rise.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is the view being rejected: falling sales mean falling interest. "In fact" flags the economist's own position: interest is as strong as ever. Then three reasons. People are buying used bikes, joining clubs, and new bikes just got pricier. It's like a restaurant owner saying: "Fewer people ordered the steak, but they still love it; they're ordering the cheaper steak sandwich, and steak night is packed. Oh, and the steak price doubled." The point is that people still love steak.

choices.note: Distorts the observers. They're right that sales fell; the economist accepts the drop and disputes only what it means.
CORRECT. "No less interested than in the past" is a fair paraphrase of "as strong as ever." Every other sentence is there to support it.
A premise, and the first piece of evidence. It supports the claim about interest; it isn't that claim.

Tempting, because it explains the drop and comes last with "Moreover." But the economist says only that the drop "coincided" with the price rise, and the point of mentioning it is to show the drop needn't reflect lost interest. Also too strong: coincided isn't caused.
The economist never ranks measures of interest. Club membership is one piece of evidence among three.

questions.stimulus: Zoologist: Some researchers propose that octopuses match the colors of their surroundings by seeing those colors. But an octopus's eyes contain only one kind of light-sensitive pigment, and an animal with only one such pigment cannot tell colors apart. Since octopuses nonetheless match background colors closely, they must be detecting color by some means other than sight.
questions.stem: The zoologist's argument proceeds by
choices: presenting evidence that octopuses match the colors of their surroundings less closely than some researchers have claimed
concluding that a hypothesis is false merely because it has not yet been confirmed by experiment
drawing a conclusion about the abilities of all animals from a feature observed in a single kind of animal
describing an alternative mechanism and showing that it explains a phenomenon better than the proposed mechanism does
using a fact about an animal's anatomy to rule out a proposed explanation of an ability the animal has
questions.explanation: The zoologist rejects the seeing-color explanation because the octopus's eyes have only one pigment, which makes color vision impossible, and then concludes that some other means must be at work; (E) describes this. (D) is the trap: the zoologist concludes that some non-visual means exists but never says what it is, let alone shows it explains the matching better. (A) contradicts the stimulus, which says octopuses match colors closely.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Octopuses must detect color by some means other than sight.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Their eyes have only one kind of light-sensitive pigment; an animal with one pigment can't tell colors apart; yet octopuses match background colors closely.

breakdown.analysis: Describe the moves, not the content. Move 1: here's a proposed explanation (they see the colors). Move 2: an anatomical fact (one pigment) makes that impossible. Move 3: so it must be something else. Notice what's missing: the zoologist never says what the something else is. Any answer that has the zoologist describing or testing a rival mechanism has added a step. Prephrase: uses anatomy to knock out one explanation.

choices.note: Opposite. The zoologist says octopuses match colors "closely" and treats that as a fact to be explained.
choices.example: Example of method: Researchers say octopuses match their backgrounds precisely, but photographs show their colors are often off by several shades.

choices.note: The zoologist doesn't reject the hypothesis for lack of confirmation. The rejection rests on a positive fact: one pigment can't distinguish colors.
choices.example: Example of method: No experiment has ever confirmed that octopuses see color, so the claim that they do must be false.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about octopuses. The general rule about one-pigment animals is a premise, not something inferred from octopuses.
choices.example: Example of method: Octopuses can't see color, so no sea creature can.

choices.note: Tempting. The zoologist does point to "some means other than sight," so it feels like an alternative is on the table. But no mechanism is ever described, and nothing is compared. The argument eliminates; it doesn't build a rival.
choices.example: Example of method: Rather than eyes, the octopus's skin may contain light-sensitive cells; this better explains why color matching works even in blinded octopuses.

choices.note: CORRECT. The anatomical fact is the single pigment; the proposed explanation is that octopuses see the colors; the ability is color matching. The fact rules the explanation out.

questions.stimulus:
Okonkwo: Hallam University should stop naming buildings after living donors. A donor honored while still alive may later be disgraced, and the university would then have to choose between keeping an embarrassing name and removing it publicly.

Svetlana: That risk is real, but people honored after their deaths are sometimes disgraced by later revelations too. Naming rights attract large gifts, and the university can simply reserve the right to remove a name. There is no reason to end the practice.
questions.stem: Okonkwo and Svetlana disagree over whether
choices: Hallam University should end its practice of naming buildings after donors who are still living
a donor whose name has been given to a university building might later be disgraced
people honored after their deaths are as likely to be disgraced as living donors are
reserving the right to remove a name would spare the university any embarrassment over a disgraced donor
large gifts matter more to the university than the reputations of the people its buildings are named after
questions.explanation: Okonkwo says Hallam should stop naming buildings after living donors; Svetlana says there is no reason to end the practice, so they disagree over (A). (C) is a tempting overstatement: Svetlana says posthumous honorees are 'sometimes' disgraced too, not that they are equally likely to be. (D) also overreaches, since Svetlana says only that the university can reserve the right to remove a name, and (B) is a risk both accept.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Okonkwo: Stop naming buildings after living donors; they may be disgraced, leaving an embarrassing name or a public removal.; Svetlana: The risk is real but applies to the dead too; naming brings big gifts and names can be removed; no reason to end the practice.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Okonkwo: stop the practice. Svetlana: "There is no reason to end the practice." That's the clash. Two traps stretch Svetlana's words. She says the dead are "sometimes" disgraced too, not equally often. And she says the university "can simply reserve the right" to remove a name, not that doing so avoids all embarrassment. Read the exact strength of each claim.

choices.note: CORRECT. Okonkwo: the university "should stop." Svetlana: "no reason to end the practice." A direct yes and no.
Agreement. Okonkwo raises the risk, and Svetlana says, "That risk is real."
Too strong. Svetlana says posthumous honorees are "sometimes" disgraced; she never says it's equally likely. And Okonkwo says nothing about the dead at all.

Tempting, because Okonkwo plainly thinks public removal is embarrassing, and Svetlana offers removal as a fix. But Svetlana never says removal would spare "any" embarrassment. She might grant that a removal is awkward and still think the gifts are worth it. Only one speaker is committed.
Neither speaker ranks gifts against reputations. Svetlana mentions large gifts as a benefit, but that's not a claim that they matter more.

questions.stimulus:
Hollis: Reintroducing beavers to the upper Wend valley would restore wetlands that once kept the river's water clean. Some farmers fear that dams will flood their fields, but a pipe set through a dam can keep its pond from rising past a fixed level.

Ingrid: Beaver ponds do filter water, and the river would be cleaner for it. But the pipes clog and need frequent clearing, and no agency has agreed to pay for that. Until one does, beavers should not be released.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Hollis and Ingrid agree that
choices: beavers should be released in the upper Wend valley as soon as an agency agrees to pay for clearing the pipes
pipes set through beaver dams can keep the farmers' fields in the upper Wend valley from flooding
beaver ponds in the upper Wend valley would make the river's water cleaner than it is now
no agency is currently willing to pay for keeping the pipes in beaver dams clear
the farmers' fears that beaver dams will flood their fields have been greatly exaggerated
questions.explanation: Hollis says beavers would restore wetlands that kept the river clean, and Ingrid grants that the river would be cleaner for the beaver ponds, so both are committed to (C). (A) is the trap: Ingrid's 'until one does' makes funding necessary for release, not sufficient, so she isn't committed to releasing beavers as soon as funding appears. (B) is Hollis's claim; Ingrid says only that the pipes need clearing, and (D) is Ingrid's claim alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Hollis: Beavers would restore wetlands that kept the river clean; pipes through dams can prevent flooding.; Ingrid: Beaver ponds do filter water and would clean the river; but the pipes clog, no agency will pay to clear them, and until one does, no release.

breakdown.analysis: For agreement, both speakers must be committed to the claim. Silence doesn't count. Ingrid opens with a concession: "Beaver ponds do filter water, and the river would be cleaner for it." That matches Hollis's opening point. Now watch the conditional in Ingrid's last line. "Until an agency pays, don't release" means: release → agency pays. Payment is necessary, not sufficient. Ingrid might have other objections once the money is found. So she hasn't promised a release the moment funding appears.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It reads Ingrid's "until" backwards. "Until X, not Y" makes X a requirement for Y, not a guarantee of it. Ingrid hasn't said funding would settle the matter, and Hollis never mentions funding.
Hollis says this. Ingrid doesn't deny it, but she doesn't affirm it either; she says only that the pipes clog and need clearing. Agreement needs both on the record.
CORRECT. Hollis: the wetlands "once kept the river's water clean." Ingrid: "the river would be cleaner for it." Both say beaver ponds would clean the water.
Ingrid's claim only. Hollis never discusses who would pay.
Hollis hints that the fears can be handled, not that they're exaggerated, and Ingrid takes the flooding problem seriously. Neither commits to this.

questions.stimulus:
Rafaela: Professors at Quarry College should be required to record their lectures and post them online. Students who miss a lecture because of illness or work could then catch up, and every student could review hard material before exams.

Desmond: Recordings would certainly help students who are ill. But attendance falls sharply in courses that post recordings, and students who skip lectures learn less even if they watch the recordings. Recordings should be provided only to students with a documented reason for missing class.
questions.stem: Rafaela and Desmond disagree over whether
choices: students who miss a lecture because of illness would benefit from having a recording of it
attendance at lectures tends to fall when recordings of those lectures are posted online
students who skip lectures learn less than those who attend, even if they watch the recordings
professors at Quarry College should be free to decide for themselves whether to record their lectures
recordings of lectures at Quarry College should be made available to all of the college's students
questions.explanation: Rafaela wants recordings posted online so every student can review; Desmond wants them given only to students with a documented reason for missing class, so they disagree over (E). (B) and (C) are Desmond's reasons, but Rafaela never addresses attendance or learning, so she isn't committed to denying either. (A) is common ground: Desmond says recordings 'would certainly help students who are ill.'

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Rafaela: Require professors to post recordings online; absent students catch up, everyone can review.; Desmond: They help sick students, but attendance falls and skippers learn less; give recordings only to students with documented absences.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Rafaela's plan is recordings for everyone ("every student could review"). Desmond's is recordings for a few ("only to students with a documented reason"). The clash is over who gets them. Desmond backs his view with two facts about attendance and learning, and those are the trap answers: Rafaela never responds to them, so we don't know whether she'd deny them.

choices.note: Agreement. Rafaela says absent students could catch up, and Desmond says recordings "would certainly help students who are ill."
Desmond's premise. Rafaela never mentions attendance, so she isn't on record either way.

Tempting, because it's Desmond's strongest point and it seems to cut against Rafaela. But she never says skippers learn just as much. Maybe she'd accept the fact and still want recordings for review. One speaker only.
Neither speaker addresses professors' discretion. Rafaela wants a requirement and Desmond wants a restriction, but neither says professors should decide for themselves.
CORRECT. Rafaela: post them online so "every student" can review. Desmond: "only to students with a documented reason." Rafaela says all students should have access; Desmond says no.

questions.stimulus:
Pell: The comet Varga-Lisle has a distinctly green coma, the cloud of gas surrounding its nucleus. Since a green coma usually indicates abundant carbon compounds, Varga-Lisle is probably unusually rich in carbon.

Dahl: So far, Varga-Lisle has been photographed only through the Hardwick Observatory's new filter, which is known to shift the colors of faint objects toward green. Until it is photographed without that filter, we cannot say what color its coma really is.
questions.stem: In responding to Pell, Dahl does which one of the following?
choices: offers an alternative explanation of why comets that are rich in carbon compounds tend to have green comas
raises doubts about the accuracy of the observation on which Pell's conclusion about the comet depends
argues that Varga-Lisle in fact contains less carbon than most comets do, despite how its coma appears
questions whether a green coma is a reliable sign that a comet contains abundant carbon compounds
objects that Pell draws a general conclusion about comets from a single case that may be unrepresentative
questions.explanation: Pell's argument rests on the observation that the coma is green; Dahl says the only photographs were taken through a filter that makes faint objects look green, so the observation may be wrong, as (B) says. (D) is the trap: Dahl doesn't challenge the rule linking green comas to carbon; he challenges whether this coma is green at all. (C) overstates Dahl, who draws no conclusion about the comet's carbon.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Pell) Varga-Lisle is probably unusually rich in carbon. (Dahl) We can't yet say what color the coma really is.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Pell) The coma is green; green comas usually mean abundant carbon. (Dahl) The only photos were taken through a filter that shifts faint objects toward green.

breakdown.analysis: Pell's argument has two pieces: 1. the coma is green (an observation); 2. green usually means carbon (a rule). Which piece does Dahl hit? Not the rule. He never doubts that green means carbon. He hits the observation: maybe the coma only looks green because of the filter. It's like a friend saying, "Your shirt isn't necessarily red; you're looking at it under a red lamp." Prephrase: he challenges the data, not the inference.

choices.note: Dahl never explains why carbon-rich comets are green. He doesn't discuss that link at all.
choices.example: Example of method: Carbon-rich comets look green not because of carbon itself but because carbon compounds break down into gases that glow green in sunlight.

choices.note: CORRECT. Pell's conclusion depends on the coma being green. Dahl points out that the only images came through a green-shifting filter, so the color is in doubt.
Too strong. Dahl says "we cannot say" what color the coma is. He draws no conclusion about how much carbon the comet has.
choices.example: Example of method: In fact, spectra show that Varga-Lisle has less carbon than the average comet, whatever color its coma looks.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Dahl is skeptical, so it's natural to think he's attacking Pell's reasoning. But he leaves the green-means-carbon rule alone. His target is whether this coma is green in the first place.
choices.example: Example of method: Green comas often turn out to come from other gases, so a green coma tells us little about a comet's carbon.

choices.note: Pell's conclusion is about this one comet, not comets in general, and Dahl raises no sampling worry.
choices.example: Example of method: You've studied one green comet and concluded that all green comets are rich in carbon; that comet may be unusual.

questions.stimulus:
Nadia: Many people find bread made by slow sourdough fermentation easier to digest than ordinary yeast bread. The long fermentation breaks down some of the compounds in wheat that cause digestive discomfort.

Ewan: That can't be right. My brother has eaten sourdough bread from the Fallow Street bakery for years, and it upsets his stomach just as much as any other bread does.
questions.stem: Ewan's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: attacks Nadia's motives for praising sourdough bread instead of addressing the reasons she offers for her claim
confuses the claim that a kind of bread is easier to digest with the claim that it is more nutritious
takes for granted that the compounds that cause discomfort in one kind of bread cause discomfort in every kind
treats a claim about what many people experience as if one person's experience could show it to be false
fails to consider the possibility that slow fermentation breaks down compounds in wheat other than those Nadia mentions
questions.explanation: Nadia claims only that many people find sourdough easier to digest; Ewan's one counterexample, his brother, is perfectly consistent with that, so his rejection of her claim treats 'many' as if it meant 'all,' as (D) says. (E) is tempting because it sounds like a careful scientific point, but other compounds have nothing to do with whether one person's experience refutes a claim about many. (B) and (C) describe confusions Ewan never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Ewan) Nadia's claim can't be right.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Nadia) Many people find slow-fermented sourdough easier to digest. (Ewan) My brother's stomach is upset by sourdough as much as by any bread.

breakdown.analysis: Does one upset brother disprove a claim about "many people"? Of course not. Nadia never said everyone digests sourdough easily. It's like saying "Many people like cilantro" and hearing back "That can't be right, my sister hates it." One counterexample sinks an "all" claim, not a "many" claim. We need an answer that says Ewan treats a claim about many as if one case could refute it.

choices.note: Ewan never mentions Nadia's motives. He attacks her claim with a counterexample, badly, but he doesn't attack her.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Nadia only praises sourdough because her cousin owns a bakery, so we can ignore her.

choices.note: Nutrition never comes up. Ewan's point is about digestion, which is exactly what Nadia talked about.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Sourdough is easier to digest, so it must be better for you than other bread.

choices.note: Ewan doesn't reason about which compounds cause discomfort in which breads. He just reports his brother's reaction.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Gluten causes discomfort in wheat bread, so it must cause discomfort in rice bread too.

choices.note: CORRECT. Nadia's claim is about "many people." The brother could be one of the people who don't benefit, and her claim would still be true. Ewan treats a single exception as a refutation.

Tempting, because it sounds like a careful point about the science. But whether fermentation breaks down other compounds has nothing to do with Ewan's mistake. His problem is logical: one case can't disprove a "many" claim.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Fermentation lowers gluten, so it must make bread healthier, ignoring that it may also destroy vitamins.

questions.stimulus:
Farmer: Tractor makers lock the diagnostic software in their machines, so many breakdowns can be fixed only by a licensed dealer, often days away. The law should require makers to give owners access to that software.

Engineer: Owners are already free to fix the mechanical parts of their tractors themselves. But the software also enforces emission limits. If owners could alter it, some would disable those limits to gain power, so access should stay restricted to dealers.
questions.stem: The farmer and the engineer disagree over whether
choices: owners should be permitted to repair the mechanical parts of their own tractors without a dealer
tractor makers should be legally required to let owners have access to their machines' diagnostic software
some owners who could alter the software in their tractors would disable its emission limits
repairs done by licensed dealers are generally more reliable than repairs that tractor owners do themselves
owners are currently able to fix most breakdowns in their tractors without a licensed dealer
questions.explanation: The farmer says the law should require makers to give owners access to the diagnostic software; the engineer says access should stay restricted to dealers, so they disagree over (B). (E) is the trap: the engineer's 'free to fix the mechanical parts' is about what owners are permitted to do, not what they can actually fix, so he never denies the farmer's claim that many breakdowns need a dealer. (A) is the engineer's claim alone, and (C) is his alone too.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Farmer: Makers lock the diagnostic software, so many breakdowns need a dealer; the law should give owners access.; Engineer: Owners are free to fix mechanical parts; the software enforces emission limits, which some owners would disable; keep access with dealers.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Farmer: the law should open the software to owners. Engineer: "access should stay restricted to dealers." That's the clash. The trap lives in the engineer's first line. "Owners are already free to fix the mechanical parts" sounds like a reply to the farmer's complaint that breakdowns need a dealer. But "free to" is about permission, not ability. The farmer's complaint is that the software lock makes many repairs impossible, and the engineer never says owners can actually make them. Watch the switch between what someone is allowed to do and what they're able to do.

choices.note: The engineer says owners are free to do this, but the farmer never addresses mechanical repairs. He probably agrees; either way he isn't on record against it.
CORRECT. The farmer: "The law should require makers to give owners access." The engineer: "access should stay restricted to dealers." Yes versus no.
The engineer's prediction only. The farmer never says what owners would do with the software.
Neither speaker compares the reliability of dealer and owner repairs. The engineer's worry is emissions, not repair quality.

Tempting, and the main trap. The farmer clearly denies this, so it looks like the engineer must affirm it. But the engineer says owners are "free to" fix mechanical parts, which is a point about permission. He never claims owners can fix most breakdowns without a dealer. One speaker committed, the other silent.

questions.stimulus:
Ruel: The blue glass beads found at the hill fort of Dun Carra were imported. Chemical analysis matches their glass to glass from workshops a thousand kilometers to the south, and no glassmaking debris has been found anywhere near the fort.

Imbert: The analysis shows only that the raw glass came from the south. Ingots of raw glass were widely traded, and a local craftsman could have reheated an ingot and shaped beads while leaving almost no debris behind.
questions.stem: Ruel and Imbert disagree over whether
choices: the absence of glassmaking debris near Dun Carra is evidence that the beads were not shaped there
the glass from which the Dun Carra beads were made originally came from workshops far to the south
the beads found at Dun Carra were shaped by a craftsman who lived in the vicinity of the fort
ingots of raw glass were traded widely during the period in which the beads were made
the southern workshops exported finished beads as well as ingots of raw glass
questions.explanation: Ruel cites the absence of debris as a reason to think the beads were imported, which commits him to its being evidence against local shaping; Imbert says beads could be shaped locally while leaving almost no debris, which denies that the missing debris counts against local shaping, so they disagree over (A). (C) is the trap: Imbert says only that a local craftsman could have shaped the beads, not that one did. (B) is common ground, since Imbert grants that the raw glass came from the south.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ruel: The beads were imported; their glass matches southern glass, and there's no glassmaking debris near the fort.; Imbert: The match shows only the raw glass was southern; ingots were traded, and a local craftsman could shape beads leaving almost no debris.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Start with what Imbert concedes: the raw glass came from the south. So the chemistry isn't in dispute. What about Ruel's second clue, the missing debris? Ruel offers it as a reason to think the beads weren't made locally. Imbert answers that local bead-shaping would leave "almost no debris," so finding none tells us nothing. That's the yes and no. Now the trap: does Imbert say the beads WERE made locally? No. He says a craftsman "could have." Showing a possibility isn't asserting a fact.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ruel uses the lack of debris as evidence of import, so he says yes. Imbert says local shaping leaves almost no debris, so the lack of debris isn't evidence against it: he says no.
Agreement. Imbert grants that "the raw glass came from the south." His dispute is about where the beads were shaped, not where the glass came from.

Tempting, and the main trap. Ruel denies this. But Imbert only says a local craftsman "could have" shaped the beads. He's showing Ruel hasn't proved his case, not claiming the opposite. One speaker committed.
Imbert's premise. Ruel never discusses the ingot trade.
Neither speaker says what the southern workshops exported. Ruel's view might suggest finished beads traveled north, but he never states it, and Imbert doesn't address it.

questions.stimulus:
Dr. Amsel: When a physician makes an error that causes a patient no harm, such as giving a dose an hour late, the physician should tell the patient. Patients have a right to know everything that happens in their care.

Dr. Varga: Patients have a right to be told of any error that harms them. But telling patients of every harmless slip would leave many of them anxious and distrustful for no good reason. Physicians should disclose harmless errors only when a patient asks.
questions.stem: Dr. Amsel and Dr. Varga disagree over whether
choices: patients have a right to be told of any errors made in their care that cause them harm
patients have a right to know about everything that happens to them in the course of their care
telling patients about every harmless error would leave many of them anxious and distrustful of their physicians
a physician should tell a patient about a harmless error if the patient specifically asks about it
a physician who harmlessly gives a dose an hour late should tell the patient without being asked
questions.explanation: Amsel says a physician should tell the patient about a harmless error such as a late dose; Varga says harmless errors should be disclosed only when a patient asks, so she denies that the physician should mention the late dose without being asked, and (E) is the point at issue. (B) is the trap: it is Amsel's premise, but Varga never denies that patients have that right; she argues only about when physicians should volunteer information. (A) and (D) are claims both would accept.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Amsel: Tell patients about harmless errors, like a late dose; patients have a right to know everything in their care.; Varga: Patients have a right to know about harmful errors; volunteering every harmless slip breeds anxiety; disclose harmless errors only when asked.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Amsel: tell the patient about the late dose. Varga: tell only "when a patient asks." So the clash is about volunteering. Amsel says yes; Varga says no unless asked. The right answer restates this through Amsel's own example (the late dose) and the phrase "without being asked," which is Varga's "only when asked" turned around. The trap is Amsel's rights claim. Varga affirms a right to know about harmful errors, but she never says patients lack a right to know about harmless ones. Her point is about what doctors should offer, not what patients may learn. Notice she lets patients ask.

choices.note: Agreement. Varga says it outright, and Amsel's "everything" includes harmful errors.

Tempting, and the main trap. Amsel asserts this, and it feels like Varga must reject it. But Varga never denies that patients have a right to know about harmless errors. She lets them find out by asking. Her claim is only that physicians shouldn't volunteer them. One speaker committed.
Varga's reason only. Amsel never says whether disclosure would make patients anxious.
Both would accept this. Varga explicitly allows disclosure when the patient asks, and Amsel, who wants disclosure even without asking, would surely want it then.

CORRECT. Amsel uses this very case: a dose an hour late, no harm, "the physician should tell the patient." Varga says harmless errors should be disclosed "only when a patient asks," so she says no to mentioning it unprompted.

questions.stimulus:
Consultant: The new Merriden concert hall sounds muddy because its ceiling is too high. In every hall I have surveyed with a ceiling over twenty meters high, critics have complained of muddy sound.

Acoustician: Every high-ceilinged hall in your survey also has plaster walls, which reflect sound far more strongly than wood does. Merriden's walls are paneled in wood. So your survey gives us no reason to blame Merriden's ceiling.
questions.stem: The acoustician responds to the consultant by
choices: questioning whether critics are right to describe the sound of the Merriden hall as muddy
arguing that the height of a hall's ceiling has no effect on how the music played there sounds
identifying a factor, absent at Merriden, that may account for the problem in the halls the consultant surveyed
proposing that the wood paneling of Merriden's walls, rather than the height of its ceiling, causes its muddy sound
objecting that the consultant's survey included too few halls to support a conclusion about halls in general
questions.explanation: The consultant blames Merriden's ceiling because high-ceilinged halls he surveyed sound muddy; the acoustician notes that all those halls also had plaster walls, which Merriden lacks, so the plaster rather than the height may explain their muddy sound, as (C) says. (D) is the trap: the acoustician offers an alternative explanation for the surveyed halls, not for Merriden, and the wood walls are the feature that sets Merriden apart, not a cause of its problem. (B) is too strong, since the acoustician says only that the survey gives no reason to blame the ceiling.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Consultant) Merriden sounds muddy because its ceiling is too high. (Acoustician) The survey gives no reason to blame Merriden's ceiling.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Consultant) Every surveyed hall with a ceiling over 20 m drew complaints of muddy sound. (Acoustician) Those halls all have plaster walls, which reflect sound strongly; Merriden's walls are wood.

breakdown.analysis: The consultant's evidence is a pattern: high ceiling goes with muddy sound. The acoustician says those halls share something else, plaster walls, and plaster is a known reflector. So in those halls the plaster might be the real culprit. And Merriden doesn't have plaster. That breaks the link from the surveyed halls to Merriden. Notice the limits. The acoustician doesn't say what's wrong with Merriden, and doesn't say ceiling height never matters. Prephrase: points to a confounding factor in the evidence that Merriden doesn't share.

choices.note: The acoustician never disputes that Merriden sounds muddy. The question is why it does, not whether.
choices.example: Example of method: Only two critics called Merriden's sound muddy, and both reviewed the opening night, when the hall was half empty.

choices.note: Too strong. The acoustician says the survey gives "no reason" to blame the ceiling. That's undercutting evidence, not proving that height has no effect.
choices.example: Example of method: Tests in which the same hall's ceiling was raised and lowered showed no change in clarity, so height doesn't matter.

choices.note: CORRECT. The factor is plaster walls. It may explain the muddy sound in the surveyed halls, and Merriden doesn't have it, so the survey says nothing about Merriden's ceiling.

Tempting, and the main trap. The acoustician does offer an alternative explanation, so this feels right. But it's an alternative explanation for the surveyed halls. Merriden's wood paneling is the reason the explanation doesn't carry over, not a new suspect. The acoustician never says what does cause Merriden's problem.
choices.example: Example of method: The problem isn't Merriden's ceiling; it's the wood paneling, which absorbs too much of the upper range.

choices.note: The acoustician raises no worry about sample size. The objection is that the surveyed halls differ from Merriden in a relevant way.
choices.example: Example of method: You surveyed only six halls, which is far too few to show anything about high ceilings in general.

questions.stimulus:
Odum: Our math department grades on a curve, so in each class only the top fifth of students can receive an A. Since one student's success thus lowers another's chances, the curve discourages students from helping one another. The department should stop grading on a curve.

Brandt: Grades give students a reason to master difficult material, and students who are not graded tend to work less. So the department would be making a mistake if it gave up grading.
questions.stem: Brandt's response to Odum is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that students who help one another learn less than students who compete against one another
fails to consider that students might help one another even in classes that are graded on a curve
presumes, without providing justification, that the curve is the only reason students in the department fail to help one another
treats an argument against one way of assigning grades as if it were an argument against assigning grades at all
rejects Odum's proposal on the grounds that Odum has not shown that dropping the curve would raise students' grades
questions.explanation: Odum argues against grading on a curve, not against grading; Brandt defends grading in general, so his reply treats an objection to one grading method as an objection to all grading, as (D) says. (C) is the trap: it may describe a weakness in the dialogue, but it is Odum, not Brandt, who links the curve to students' failure to help one another. (B) also targets Odum's premise, which Brandt never discusses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Brandt) The department would be making a mistake if it gave up grading.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Odum) The curve sets students against each other, so drop the curve. (Brandt) Grades motivate students; ungraded students work less.

breakdown.analysis: Did Odum propose giving up grading? No. He proposed giving up the curve, one method of assigning grades. Without a curve, the department could still grade on fixed standards. Brandt answers a proposal nobody made. It's like someone saying "We should stop using the scoreboard that only counts the winner's points," and hearing back "Without keeping score, nobody would try." This is called a straw man: knocking down a position the other person doesn't hold. It's a classic; know it. Also, check whose flaw you're describing. The question asks about Brandt.

choices.note: Brandt says nothing about whether helping or competing produces more learning. His claim is about graded versus ungraded students.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Students who compete for grades will obviously outperform students who just help each other, so keep the curve.

choices.note: This is an objection to Odum's premise, not a flaw in Brandt's reasoning. Brandt never discusses whether students help one another.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The curve can't be the problem; Odum just assumes students won't help each other under a curve.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It may describe a weakness in the conversation, but it's Odum who blames the curve for students not helping each other. Brandt never makes that claim. Right flaw, wrong speaker.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Students here don't help one another, so the curve must be the reason.

choices.note: CORRECT. Odum attacks the curve. Brandt defends grading itself. He answers an argument against grading that Odum never made.
Brandt never mentions whether dropping the curve would raise grades. His reason is that grades motivate students.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Odum hasn't shown his plan would raise grades, so we should reject it.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Coastal planners on Tessaly Island regard mangrove forests as wasteland and routinely clear them to make room for resorts. This is shortsighted. Mangrove roots trap sediment and blunt the force of storm waves, so shorelines erode faster where mangroves have been cleared. And a shoreline that is eroding will eventually threaten whatever has been built along it.
questions.stem: The claim that shorelines erode faster where mangroves have been cleared plays which one of the following roles in the ecologist's argument?
choices: It is supported by a claim about mangrove roots and, in turn, provides part of the support for the main conclusion.
It is the argument's main conclusion, and the claim about what mangrove roots do is offered as support for it.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that mangrove roots trap sediment and blunt the force of storm waves.
It is a claim the argument attributes to the coastal planners in order to show that their practice conflicts with their own views.
It is a prediction offered as evidence that the planners' view of mangrove forests is shared by most of the island's residents.
questions.explanation: The main conclusion is the short, unflagged 'This is shortsighted': clearing mangroves for resorts is unwise. The erosion claim is drawn from the facts about mangrove roots ('so') and, combined with the point that erosion threatens what is built along a shore, supports that conclusion, so it is an intermediate conclusion, as (A) says. (B) is the trap: the 'so' makes the erosion claim look like the main point, but it is offered to show why clearing is shortsighted. (C) reverses the support relation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Clearing mangroves to make room for resorts is shortsighted.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mangrove roots trap sediment and blunt storm waves; so shorelines erode faster where mangroves are cleared; and eroding shorelines eventually threaten what's built on them.

breakdown.analysis: Where's the conclusion? It's the three-word sentence "This is shortsighted." Ask which statement supports which. Why is clearing shortsighted? Because cleared shorelines erode faster, and erosion threatens the resorts. Why do they erode faster? Because of what the roots do. So the chain is: 1. roots trap sediment and blunt waves → 2. cleared shores erode faster → (with 3. erosion threatens buildings) → 4. clearing is shortsighted. The claim in the stem is link 2: supported, and supporting. Most students pick (B) because "so" flags the erosion claim as a conclusion. It is one, just not the main one. Lesson: a conclusion indicator marks a conclusion, not necessarily the main conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. The roots claim supports it ("so"), and together with the point about erosion threatening what's built, it supports "This is shortsighted." That's an intermediate conclusion.

Tempting, and the main trap. "So" introduces the erosion claim, and it gets direct support, so it feels like the point. But the ecologist mentions erosion to show why clearing for resorts is shortsighted. That judgment is the main conclusion, and the erosion claim serves it.
Reversed. The roots claim supports the erosion claim, not the other way round.
The planners never say anything about erosion. The ecologist states this claim as her own, to criticize their practice.
Nothing in the argument concerns what residents think. And the erosion claim is offered against the planners' view, not as evidence that the view is popular.

questions.stimulus: Art historian: The bronze horse in the Vell Museum has long been dated to the second century, chiefly because of its thick green patina. But the patina gives us no good reason to accept that date. Although a patina that thick usually takes centuries to form, burying bronze for a few weeks in damp soil treated with certain salts produces the same effect. Forgers have used this technique for generations; therefore, the patina may well be a forger's work.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the art historian's argument?
choices: The bronze horse in the Vell Museum is a recent forgery rather than a work made in the second century.
The thick green patina on the bronze horse may well have been produced by a forger rather than by centuries of exposure.
A patina as thick as the one on the bronze horse usually takes centuries to form on bronze.
Forgers have long known how to give bronze objects thick patinas by burying them in treated soil.
The patina on the bronze horse does not justify the belief that the horse was made in the second century.
questions.explanation: The historian's main point, stated in the second sentence, is that the patina gives no good reason to accept the second-century date; everything after it explains why, so (E) is correct. (B) is the trap: it is flagged by 'therefore' and comes last, but it is an intermediate conclusion offered to show that the patina is no basis for the date. (A) overstates the historian, who says the horse's date is unsupported, not that the horse is a forgery.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The patina gives no good reason to accept the second-century date.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Thick patinas usually take centuries, but treated soil produces one in weeks; forgers have long used this technique; therefore the patina may well be a forger's work.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is background: the horse is dated by its patina. The second sentence, flagged by "But," is the historian's position. Everything after explains it. Why is the patina no reason to accept the date? Because it may well be a forger's work. Why might it be? Because forgers know a fast technique. So "may well be a forger's work" is a step on the way. Most students pick (B) because "therefore" marks it and it comes last. A conclusion indicator tells you a claim is supported, not that it's the main point.

choices.note: Too strong. The historian says the patina "may well be" a forger's work and that it gives no reason to accept the date. Saying a date is unsupported isn't saying the horse is fake.

Tempting, and the main trap. It's flagged by "therefore" and comes last, so it looks like the bottom line. But it's there to explain why the patina gives no good reason for the date. It supports (E), so it can't be the main conclusion.
A premise, and the historian concedes it with "Although." It's background for the point that the same effect can be faked quickly.
A premise. It supports the claim that the patina may be a forger's work.
CORRECT. This restates "the patina gives us no good reason to accept that date." Every later sentence supports it, and it supports nothing else.

questions.stimulus:
Lena: Parla, the language app, should drop its daily-streak feature. Some users who break a long streak quit the app altogether, and a feature that drives learners away is contrary to the app's central purpose, whatever else it does.

Marcus: Some users do quit after breaking a streak. But for each one who does, several others practice daily only because they don't want to lose their streaks. A feature that keeps far more learners practicing than it drives away serves the app's central purpose.
questions.stem: Lena and Marcus disagree over whether
choices: the daily-streak feature leads some of Parla's users who break a long streak to stop using the app
a feature that drives some learners away can still be in keeping with an app's central purpose
the daily-streak feature keeps more of Parla's users practicing than it drives away from the app
most of Parla's users who practice daily do so only because they do not want to lose their streaks
the central purpose of a language app is to keep as many of its users as possible practicing every day
questions.explanation: Lena holds that a feature that drives learners away is contrary to the app's purpose 'whatever else it does'; Marcus holds that such a feature serves the purpose if it keeps far more learners than it loses, so they disagree over the general principle in (B). (C) is the trap: Marcus asserts it, but Lena never disputes the numbers; her 'whatever else it does' makes them irrelevant to her. (D) stretches Marcus's 'several others' per quitter into a claim about most daily users, and (A) is common ground.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Lena: Drop the streak feature; some users quit after breaking a streak, and a feature that drives learners away is contrary to the app's purpose whatever else it does.; Marcus: Some do quit, but several others practice only to keep their streaks; a feature that keeps far more than it loses serves the app's purpose.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Marcus opens by conceding Lena's fact: some users do quit. So the facts about quitting aren't the issue. Look at the principles. Lena: drives learners away → contrary to the purpose, "whatever else it does." Marcus: keeps far more than it drives away → serves the purpose. Imagine a feature that loses one user and keeps ten. Lena says it's contrary to the purpose; Marcus says it serves it. That's the clash. Now the trap: does Lena deny that the feature keeps more users than it loses? She never addresses it. Her "whatever else it does" means the count doesn't matter to her. An answer about the count has only one speaker on record.

choices.note: Agreement. Lena says it, and Marcus concedes it: "Some users do quit after breaking a streak."

CORRECT. Lena: a feature that drives learners away is contrary to the purpose "whatever else it does," so no. Marcus: a feature that keeps far more than it drives away "serves the app's central purpose," so yes, a feature that loses some users can still serve the purpose.

Tempting, and the main trap. Marcus asserts this, so it feels like Lena must deny it. But Lena never disputes the numbers. Her point is that losing learners is disqualifying no matter how many the feature keeps. She could grant the numbers and keep her view. One speaker on record.
Too strong, and Marcus only. He says several users practice for streaks for each one who quits. That doesn't make them most of the daily users. Lena says nothing about it.
Neither speaker defines the app's purpose this way. Marcus's principle is about keeping more learners than you lose, not about maximizing daily practice, and Lena never states the purpose at all.

questions.stimulus:
Councilor Ames: Halbrook should dim its streetlights after midnight. Doing so would cut the city's electricity costs, and less glare would let residents see the stars again. Opponents say dim streets invite crime, but cities that have dimmed their lights have seen no rise in crime.

Councilor Ruiz: Those cities dimmed only residential streets; none dimmed its commercial districts, where most late-night crime occurs. I would support dimming our residential streets, but downtown should stay fully lit.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Ames and Ruiz agree that
choices: Halbrook should dim all of its streetlights after midnight in order to reduce the city's electricity costs
most of the crime committed late at night in Halbrook occurs in the commercial districts of the city
reducing the glare from Halbrook's streetlights at night would allow the city's residents to see the stars
it would be acceptable for Halbrook to dim at least some of its streetlights after midnight
the experience of other cities shows that dimming streetlights at night does not lead to more crime
questions.explanation: Ames wants all of Halbrook's streetlights dimmed after midnight, which includes the residential ones, and Ruiz says she would support dimming the residential streets, so both are committed to (D). (A) is the trap: it differs from (D) by the word 'all,' and Ruiz rejects dimming downtown. (E) is Ames's claim, which Ruiz disputes by noting that those cities never dimmed commercial districts, and (B) is Ruiz's claim alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ames: Dim Halbrook's streetlights after midnight; it saves money and reveals the stars; other cities that dimmed saw no rise in crime.; Ruiz: Those cities dimmed only residential streets, not commercial districts where most late-night crime happens; dim residential streets, but keep downtown fully lit.

breakdown.analysis: For agreement, both speakers must be committed to the claim. On the surface these two are arguing. Ames: dim the lights. Ruiz: not downtown. But look at the overlap. Ames wants every streetlight dimmed, which includes the residential ones. Ruiz says, "I would support dimming our residential streets." So both accept dimming some streets. All → some: if you'd dim every street, you'd accept dimming at least some. The right answer captures that overlap with "at least some," and the trap is the same claim with "all."

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It's Ames's proposal, and it differs from the right answer by one word: "all." Ruiz says downtown "should stay fully lit," so she rejects it.
Ruiz's claim only, and she states it about commercial districts generally. Ames never says where late-night crime occurs.
Ames's point only. Ruiz never mentions glare or the stars.
CORRECT. Ames would dim every street, residential ones included. Ruiz "would support dimming our residential streets." Both accept dimming at least some streets.

Ames says this, but Ruiz challenges it: those cities never dimmed commercial districts, where most late-night crime occurs, so their experience doesn't show what would happen downtown. That's a disagreement, not agreement.

questions.stimulus:
Okafor: Velarix, a large pterosaur, was a scavenger, not a hunter. Its beak lacked the hooked tip that every living bird of prey uses to tear flesh, and an animal without such a tool could not have subdued live prey of any size.

Strand: Many living storks hunt successfully with straight beaks: they swallow small prey whole. Nothing about Velarix's beak would have kept it from hunting that way. I agree, though, that it could not have taken large prey, which would have been impossible to swallow.
questions.stem: Okafor and Strand disagree over whether
choices: Velarix obtained at least some of its food by eating the remains of animals that were already dead
Velarix lacked the ability to capture and eat live prey of a large size
Velarix was capable of capturing and eating at least some live prey of small size
Velarix was a hunter rather than a scavenger of animals that had already died
every living bird of prey uses a hooked beak tip to tear the flesh of the animals it eats
questions.explanation: Okafor says an animal without a hooked tip could not have subdued live prey of any size, so he denies that Velarix could catch small prey; Strand says nothing about Velarix's beak would have kept it from hunting small prey as storks do, which commits him to its being capable of it, so they disagree over (C). (D) is the trap: Strand says only that Velarix could have hunted that way, not that it was a hunter rather than a scavenger. (B) is explicitly agreed, and (A) is Okafor's view alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Okafor: Velarix was a scavenger; no hooked beak tip, and without one it couldn't subdue live prey of any size.; Strand: Storks hunt small prey with straight beaks, swallowing it whole; nothing about Velarix's beak kept it from doing the same; but it couldn't take large prey.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Okafor's rule: no hooked tip → can't subdue live prey of any size. Velarix had no hooked tip, so for Okafor it couldn't catch even small prey. Strand says nothing about Velarix's beak would have kept it from hunting small prey the stork way. That's a claim about ability: Velarix could do it. That's the clash: ability to take small prey. Now the trap. Is Strand saying Velarix WAS a hunter? No. He says it could have hunted, not that it did. Watch the switch from could to did.

choices.note: Okafor's view: a scavenger eats carrion. Strand never says Velarix didn't scavenge; it could have done both. One speaker only.
Agreement, and stated outright. Okafor says no prey of any size, and Strand says, "I agree, though, that it could not have taken large prey."

CORRECT. Okafor's rule rules this out: no hooked tip means no live prey "of any size." Strand says nothing about Velarix's beak would have kept it from hunting small prey by swallowing it whole, which means it could.

Tempting, and the main trap. Okafor denies it, and Strand seems to be defending Velarix as a hunter. But Strand only says it could have hunted that way. He doesn't conclude that it was a hunter, let alone a hunter rather than a scavenger. Ability isn't a verdict.
Okafor's premise. Strand's storks hunt with straight beaks, but he never calls them birds of prey, so he doesn't contradict Okafor's claim about birds of prey.

questions.stimulus:
Restaurateur: Restaurants that abolish tipping and raise menu prices to pay servers a fixed wage drive customers away. Of the six restaurants in Danforth that tried this, four lost so many customers that they restored tipping within a year.

Economist: Those four raised their prices by a fifth or more. The other two, which raised prices by less than a tenth, kept their customers, and they still pay their servers fixed wages today.
questions.stem: The economist responds to the restaurateur by
choices: arguing that the four restaurants would have lost customers that year even if they had never abolished tipping
questioning whether a group of six restaurants is large enough to support a conclusion about restaurants in general
offering evidence that abolishing tipping attracts more new customers to a restaurant than the policy drives away
disputing the restaurateur's account of how many of the six Danforth restaurants restored tipping within a year
citing evidence that the outcome attributed to a policy may depend on how it is implemented
questions.explanation: The restaurateur blames abolishing tipping for the customer losses; the economist shows that only the restaurants with large price increases lost customers, while those that carried out the same policy with small increases kept theirs, so the losses may depend on how the policy was implemented, as (E) says. (B) is the trap: a sample of six is a familiar weakness, but the economist never raises it and instead splits the six by how much they raised prices. (C) overstates the evidence, since the two restaurants kept their customers, not gained new ones.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Restaurateur) Abolishing tipping and raising prices to pay fixed wages drives customers away.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Restaurateur) Four of six Danforth restaurants that tried it lost so many customers they went back. (Economist) Those four raised prices by a fifth or more; the two that raised prices by under a tenth kept their customers and kept the policy.

breakdown.analysis: What does the economist actually do with the six restaurants? He splits them. Big price hikes: lost customers. Small price hikes: kept customers. Same policy, different outcomes, and the difference tracks how the policy was carried out. So it may not be no-tipping as such that drives customers away; it may be the size of the price increase. Notice what he doesn't do: he doesn't dispute the facts, doesn't complain about sample size, and doesn't claim no-tipping wins customers. Prephrase: shows the bad result may depend on how the policy was implemented, not on the policy itself.

choices.note: The economist makes no claim about what would have happened without the policy. He compares restaurants that carried out the policy in different ways.
choices.example: Example of method: Those four restaurants were losing customers before they changed anything, so they'd have lost them anyway.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Six restaurants is a small sample, and that's a textbook objection. But the economist never mentions sample size. He accepts the six and shows what divides them.
choices.example: Example of method: Six restaurants in one town can't tell us anything about restaurants in general.

choices.note: Too strong. The two restaurants "kept their customers." Nothing says they gained new ones or that abolishing tipping attracts more customers than it loses.
choices.example: Example of method: The two that kept the policy saw their business double, so abolishing tipping brings in more customers than it loses.

choices.note: The economist accepts the restaurateur's count: four went back, two didn't. He adds information about price increases.
choices.example: Example of method: Actually, only two of the six restaurants went back to tipping, not four.

choices.note: CORRECT. The outcome is losing customers; the policy is abolishing tipping and paying fixed wages. The economist's evidence shows the losses tracked the size of the price increase, which is a matter of how the policy was carried out.

questions.stimulus: Critic: Wildlife documentaries sometimes present staged scenes, such as a captive animal filmed in a set built to look like its burrow, as if they had been filmed in the wild. Admittedly, such scenes can show behavior that would be nearly impossible to film in nature, and viewers may learn a good deal from them. But a documentary's value lies in viewers' trust that what they see happened as shown. So presenting staged scenes as wild footage undermines what makes such films worth watching.
questions.stem: The claim that viewers may learn a good deal from staged scenes plays which one of the following roles in the critic's argument?
choices: It grants that the scenes the argument discusses have a benefit, without withdrawing the argument's criticism of the way they are presented.
It is offered as support for the claim that a documentary's value lies in viewers' trust that what they see happened as shown.
It is a premise that, together with the claim about viewers' trust, provides support for the argument's conclusion.
It is a claim that the argument attempts to refute by showing that staged scenes seldom depict real animal behavior.
It is a concession used to show that filmmakers should clearly label any staged scenes in their documentaries.
questions.explanation: 'Admittedly' marks the claim as a concession: the critic grants that staged scenes have educational value, then argues with 'But' that presenting them as wild footage still undermines what makes documentaries worth watching, which (A) describes. (C) is the trap: it treats the concession as support for the conclusion, but a point granted in favor of staged scenes cannot help show that presenting them as wild footage is harmful. (E) gives the concession a purpose the argument never draws, since the critic recommends no labeling policy.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Presenting staged scenes as wild footage undermines what makes wildlife documentaries worth watching.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A documentary's value lies in viewers' trust that what they see happened as shown. (Conceded: staged scenes can show hard-to-film behavior and teach viewers a lot.)

breakdown.analysis: "Admittedly" is a flag: here comes a point for the other side. The critic grants that staged scenes have a payoff (viewers learn from them) and then turns with "But" to the reason they're still a problem when passed off as wild. Does the learning claim support the conclusion? Ask yourself: does "viewers learn a lot from staged scenes" help show that presenting them as wild undermines the film? No, it pulls the other way. That's what a concession does. Most students pick (C) because they assume every sentence before "So" is a premise. Lesson: a concession sits in the argument without supporting the conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. "Admittedly" grants a benefit of staged scenes. The argument then keeps its criticism of presenting them as wild footage. Granting a point without giving up the conclusion is exactly a concession.
No connection. The trust claim is a separate premise; nothing about learning supports it.

Tempting, and the main trap. It sits right before the trust premise, and it's easy to treat everything before "So" as support. But learning from staged scenes is a point in their favor; it can't help show that presenting them as wild undermines the film. It's conceded, not used.
The critic doesn't refute this. She grants it, and never claims that staged scenes misrepresent behavior.

Right role, wrong use. It is a concession, but the argument never concludes anything about labeling. Its conclusion is that presenting staged scenes as wild undermines the film's value. Labeling might follow in a reader's mind, but the critic doesn't say it.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Many scholars hold that the road from Varro to Escal was built during the reign of the emperor Tullian, since its milestones bear his name. But a merchant's letter written two decades before Tullian took power describes traveling that very road. The road, then, is older than his reign. As for the milestones, emperors routinely had their names carved on milestones when they had merely repaired an existing road.
questions.stem: The statement that emperors routinely had their names carved on milestones when they had merely repaired an existing road figures in the historian's argument in which one of the following ways?
choices: It is the primary evidence offered for the conclusion that the road from Varro to Escal is older than Tullian's reign.
It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the merchant's letter is cited in order to support.
It is offered as evidence that Tullian's workers repaired the road from Varro to Escal during his reign.
It is used to show that a fact cited for a rival view is compatible with the argument's conclusion.
It is a claim that the scholars use to support their view that the road was built during Tullian's reign.
questions.explanation: The scholars cite the milestones bearing Tullian's name; the historian's evidence for the road's greater age is the merchant's letter, and the claim about emperors' repair inscriptions explains how the milestones could bear Tullian's name even if the road is older, which is what (D) says. (A) is the trap: the claim does help the conclusion, but only by neutralizing the scholars' evidence; the letter is what positively supports it. (C) overreads the claim, which shows the milestones are consistent with a repair, not that Tullian's workers made one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The road from Varro to Escal is older than Tullian's reign.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A merchant's letter from two decades before his reign describes the road. (Answering the scholars' evidence: emperors routinely put their names on milestones of roads they merely repaired.)

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The scholars' evidence: milestones bear Tullian's name. The historian's evidence: the merchant's letter, which is what "then" draws the conclusion from. So what is the milestone sentence doing? It comes after the conclusion, introduced by "As for the milestones," which signals a reply to the scholars. It explains how Tullian's name could be on an older road: he may have repaired it. That doesn't prove the road is old; it removes an obstacle to believing it. Most students pick (A) because the claim plainly helps the historian. But helping by defusing the other side's evidence isn't the same as being the main evidence.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. The claim does help the historian, so "evidence for the conclusion" feels right. But the conclusion is drawn from the merchant's letter ("The road, then, is older"). The milestone claim only explains away the scholars' evidence. On its own it doesn't show the road is old at all.
The main conclusion is that the road is older than Tullian's reign. The merchant's letter supports that, not this general claim about emperors.

Too strong. The historian says emperors routinely carved names on roads they merely repaired, which makes the milestones consistent with a repair. She never claims Tullian's workers actually repaired this road.

CORRECT. The rival view rests on the milestones bearing Tullian's name. The claim shows that fact is compatible with the road being older: an emperor who only repaired a road could still put his name on it.
Reversed. The scholars rely on the milestones. This claim is the historian's reply to them, and it undercuts their view.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: Some define wilderness as land that has never been altered by human activity. But this definition would deny the title to the Corran Highlands, which herders grazed for centuries before abandoning them, even though the highlands have since returned to a condition no ecologist could distinguish from that of land never grazed. And it would grant the title to almost nothing, since air pollution has altered nearly every place on earth.
questions.stem: The philosopher's argument proceeds by
choices: showing that the definition, if applied consistently, would count as wilderness some land that clearly should not be counted as wilderness
arguing that a proposed criterion would withhold a classification from things to which the classification ought to apply
proposing an alternative definition of wilderness that relies on the judgments of ecologists rather than on the land's history
rejecting a definition on the grounds that it would make a term apply both to too many places and to too few
appealing to a single well-known case in order to establish a general claim about how land recovers after human use ends
