questions.explanation: Both of the philosopher's points show that the 'never altered' definition leaves out land that should count as wilderness: the recovered Corran Highlands, and nearly everywhere else once air pollution is considered; (B) describes this abstractly. (A) is the trap: it reverses the direction, charging the definition with including too much, when both examples show it includes too little. (D) is tempting because the philosopher raises two objections, but 'grant the title to almost nothing' is a second complaint that the definition is too narrow, not a complaint that it is too broad.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Implied) Defining wilderness as land never altered by humans is inadequate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: It would exclude the Corran Highlands, which are indistinguishable from never-grazed land; and it would include almost nothing, since air pollution has altered nearly everywhere.

breakdown.analysis: This is a definition tested against cases. Ask: is the philosopher saying the definition is too broad (lets in things that shouldn't count) or too narrow (shuts out things that should)? First case: the Highlands look exactly like untouched land but get excluded. Too narrow. Second point: "grant the title to almost nothing." Also too narrow; it shuts out nearly everything. Both objections push the same way. Prephrase: argues the definition excludes cases that ought to be included. Watch for the answer that flips the direction, and the one that splits the two objections into opposite complaints.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It's the classic too-broad objection, and "if applied consistently" sounds like what the philosopher does. But neither example shows land wrongly counted as wilderness. Both show land wrongly left out. Wrong direction.
choices.example: Example of method: Defining wilderness as land with no buildings would count a freshly clear-cut forest as wilderness, which it plainly isn't.

choices.note: CORRECT. The criterion is "never altered by human activity." The classification is "wilderness." The Highlands, and almost everywhere else, ought to qualify but wouldn't. Both points show the definition withholding the title where it belongs.
The philosopher offers no new definition. Ecologists appear only to show that the Highlands are indistinguishable from untouched land.
choices.example: Example of method: Instead, call land wilderness when ecologists cannot tell it apart from land never used by people.

choices.note: Tempting, because there are two objections and one sounds like it's about quantity. But "grant the title to almost nothing" is a complaint that the term would apply to too few places. Neither objection says too many.
choices.example: Example of method: The definition would count city parks as wilderness while excluding remote valleys once farmed, so it's both too broad and too narrow.

choices.note: The Highlands case is used against a definition, not to support a general claim about how land recovers. And the philosopher draws no conclusion about recovery in general.
choices.example: Example of method: The Corran Highlands recovered fully after grazing ended, so all grazed land recovers once herders leave.

questions.stimulus: Solar farm manager: We used to pay a crew to mow the grass that grows beneath our solar panels. This year we stopped mowing and instead leased the land to a farmer whose sheep now graze there. The sheep have kept the grass as short as the mowing did, and the lease earns us money instead of costing us any. So grazing sheep is a better way for us to control the grass than mowing was.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Would sheep raised on land beneath solar panels produce as much wool as sheep raised on open pasture?
Do other solar farms in the region still pay crews to mow the grass that grows beneath their panels?
Does the grass beneath the panels grow more slowly in the shade than grass in open fields does?
Do the sheep grazing beneath the panels cause any damage to the panels or to the wiring that connects them?
Would the farmer be willing to keep leasing the land if the lease payments were raised?
questions.explanation: The manager compares sheep and mowing on two points, grass height and cost, and concludes that sheep are better overall. The argument ignores any new cost the sheep might bring, and (D) asks about exactly that: damage to the panels would weaken the argument, and no damage would strengthen it. (E) is the tempting choice because it is about money, but a yes would only add a bonus and a no would not undo the savings the manager already has. (A) and (B) concern the farmer’s wool and other solar farms, not this farm’s choice.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Grazing sheep is a better way for the solar farm to control the grass than mowing was.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The sheep keep the grass as short as mowing did; the lease earns money, while mowing cost money.

breakdown.analysis: Better in every way that matters? The manager checked two things, grass height and cost, and declared sheep the winner. But sheep are big animals walking around expensive equipment. If they chew wires or crack panels, the savings could vanish. It’s like saying a teenager is a better babysitter than the agency because she’s cheaper and the kids like her, without asking whether she lets them play with matches. We want a question whose answer could go either way and push the argument in opposite directions: “Do the sheep cause damage?”

choices.note: Wool is the farmer’s business, not the solar farm’s. Whether the sheep are good wool producers doesn’t change whether grazing is better for the manager. Irrelevant.
What other farms do doesn’t tell us what’s best for this one. They might not have heard of the idea. Irrelevant.
Slow-growing grass would affect mowing and grazing alike. And the manager already tells us the sheep keep the grass as short as mowing did. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. This is the hidden cost. If the sheep damage panels or wiring, the money from the lease could be wiped out by repairs, and grazing may not be better at all. If they cause no damage, the manager’s comparison holds up. Either answer changes how strong the argument is.

Tempting, because it’s about money. But it’s one-sided. If the farmer would pay more, that’s a bonus; if not, the manager still earns the current lease and still saves the mowing cost. Neither answer touches the gap.

questions.stimulus: Driving instructor: Our school offers an optional course in night driving. Last year, students who took the course had far fewer accidents in their first year of licensed driving than did students who skipped it. So the course makes new drivers safer, and we should require every one of our students to take it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Does the night-driving course cost students more than the school’s other optional courses do?
Were the students who chose to take the course already more cautious drivers than those who skipped it?
Did any of the students who took the night-driving course have an accident in their first year of driving?
Do other driving schools in the area also offer optional courses in night driving to their students?
Would requiring the course make it harder for the school to schedule its regular driving lessons?
questions.explanation: The students chose whether to take the course, so the difference in accidents might reflect who signed up rather than what the course taught. (B) asks about that: if the course takers were already more cautious, the argument is weakened; if they were not, the course looks responsible. (C) is tempting but asks only whether any course taker had an accident, and a few accidents are consistent with far fewer overall. (A), (D), and (E) do not bear on whether the course makes drivers safer.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The night-driving course makes new drivers safer, so all students should be required to take it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Students who took the optional course had far fewer first-year accidents than students who skipped it.

breakdown.analysis: Who signs up for an optional safety course? Probably careful people. If the careful kids chose the course, they’d have fewer accidents anyway, course or no course. It’s like noticing that people who buy bike helmets crash less and concluding that helmets prevent crashes. We need a question that tells us whether the two groups were alike to begin with.

choices.note: The course’s price doesn’t tell us whether it works. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If the course takers were already more cautious, their lower accident rate could be due to who they are, not what they learned, and the argument is weak. If they weren’t, the course is the likely reason, and the argument is strong. Two answers, two directions.

Tempting, but “any” is too weak to matter. The argument says course takers had far fewer accidents, not zero. Whether one or two of them crashed tells us nothing about whether the course caused the difference.
Other schools offering the course doesn’t show that it works. Irrelevant.

This bears on whether requiring the course is convenient, not on whether the course makes drivers safer, which is the claim the requirement rests on. One-sided at best: a yes adds a small cost, and a no tells us nothing.

questions.stimulus: Last spring, heavy snowmelt sent the Tarvin River higher than in any spring on record. Rafting outfitters along the river had predicted a busy season, since high water makes the river’s rapids more exciting. Yet the outfitters booked far fewer rafting trips last spring than they do in an ordinary spring.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Officials closed the river to rafting for much of last spring because the high water made it unsafe.
Rafters who book trips on the Tarvin River generally prefer exciting rapids to calmer stretches of water.
Several of the outfitters raised the prices of their rafting trips slightly before last spring began.
The high water last spring was caused by an unusually large amount of snow that fell over the winter.
Most of the people who book rafting trips on the Tarvin River live in cities within a day’s drive of it.
questions.explanation: High water should have drawn more rafters, but if it was so high that officials closed the river for much of the spring, few trips could be booked at all. That is (A). (C) is the tempting choice because higher prices can reduce demand, but a slight increase does not account for far fewer bookings in a season that should have been unusually busy. (B) makes the puzzle worse, and (D) only explains why the water was high.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The river was the highest on record, which should have made rafting more exciting and popular, but outfitters booked far fewer trips than usual.

breakdown.analysis: How can the thing that should help the outfitters end up hurting them? Maybe the same high water had a downside. Too much of a good thing is a common answer to paradoxes. It’s like a restaurant expecting a rush during a big snowstorm because people love hot soup, then finding the roads closed. Prephrase: the high water itself kept people off the river.

choices.note: CORRECT. The very thing that made the rapids exciting also made them dangerous enough to close the river. If the river was closed for much of the spring, there were few trips to book. Both facts now fit together.
This explains why the outfitters expected a busy season. It makes the drop in bookings even more surprising. Deepens the puzzle.
Tempting, because price can affect demand. But “slightly” is the problem. A small price bump can’t explain far fewer bookings in a season that should have been unusually popular.
This explains why the water was high, which we already knew. It says nothing about why bookings fell.
Where customers live was true in ordinary springs too. A fact that didn’t change can’t explain a change. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: At Varo Ridge, an inland settlement occupied about 3,000 years ago, archaeologists have found hearths containing large quantities of fish bones. The nearest seacoast is more than 100 kilometers from Varo Ridge. Therefore, the people of Varo Ridge must have obtained their fish through trade with coastal communities.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most helpful to determine in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: How many hearths in total have archaeologists found at the site of the Varo Ridge settlement?
Did coastal communities of that era eat fish more often than the people of Varo Ridge did?
Were there any rivers or lakes near Varo Ridge 3,000 years ago that held fish?
Did the people of Varo Ridge also trade with other communities for goods other than food?
Did the people of Varo Ridge cook their fish in the same way that coastal communities cooked theirs?
questions.explanation: The argument assumes the sea was the only source of fish. (C) tests that: if nearby rivers or lakes held fish, the people could have caught their own and the argument is weakened; if not, trade with the coast becomes the likely explanation. (D) is tempting because it is about trade, but a yes would show only that they traded for something, and a no would not rule out trading for fish. The other choices do not bear on where the fish came from.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The people of Varo Ridge got their fish by trading with coastal communities.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Their hearths contain lots of fish bones; the sea is more than 100 kilometers away.

breakdown.analysis: Do fish only live in the sea? Of course not. Rivers and lakes have fish too. The argument treats “far from the sea” as “far from fish.” It’s like finding fresh apples in a city apartment and concluding they must have been shipped from a farm, without checking whether there’s a market downstairs. We need a question that tests whether a local source of fish existed.

choices.note: The number of hearths doesn’t tell us where the fish came from. Irrelevant.
How much fish the coastal people ate says nothing about how fish got to Varo Ridge. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If nearby rivers or lakes held fish, the people of Varo Ridge could have caught their own, and the argument falls apart. If there were no such waters, trade with the coast is the best explanation left. Either answer moves the argument.

Tempting, because it’s about trade. But it’s one-sided. A yes shows they traded for something, not for fish. A no doesn’t rule out trading for fish. The real question is whether they needed to trade at all.
Cooking methods don’t tell us where the fish came from. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Our town’s public pool loses about $60,000 each summer. Last summer roughly 40,000 swimmers paid the pool’s $3 admission fee. If we raise the fee to $5, the extra $2 per swimmer will bring in $80,000, more than enough to cover the losses. So raising the admission fee will end the pool’s losses.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the pool lose more money last summer than it lost in the summer before?
Would far fewer people swim at the pool if the admission fee were raised to $5?
Do the neighboring towns charge more than $3 for admission to their public pools?
Does the town operate any other recreational facilities that also lose money each year?
Do most of the town’s residents want the public pool to remain open in future summers?
questions.explanation: The $80,000 figure assumes that 40,000 swimmers will keep coming at the higher price. (B) asks whether that is so: if attendance would drop sharply, the extra revenue could fall short; if it would not, the plan works. (C) is tempting, but higher fees elsewhere would only suggest that $5 is reasonable, and lower fees elsewhere would not show that swimmers would stay away. The remaining choices do not affect whether the fee increase covers the losses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Raising the pool’s fee from $3 to $5 will end its losses.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The pool loses about $60,000 a summer; 40,000 swimmers paid last summer; an extra $2 each would bring in $80,000.

breakdown.analysis: Will 40,000 people still show up if the price goes up by two-thirds? The math only works if attendance holds. It’s like a café deciding to double coffee prices and counting on selling the same number of cups. We need a question about how swimmers would react to the higher fee.

choices.note: The pool loses “about $60,000 each summer.” Whether last summer was a little worse than the one before doesn’t change whether the new fee covers the loss. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If far fewer people would swim at $5, the extra revenue could easily fall below $60,000, and the plan fails. If attendance would hold, $80,000 covers the losses. That’s the assumption the math rests on.

Tempting, because it hints at whether $5 is a normal price. But it’s indirect and one-sided. Swimmers in this town might still stop coming, and a lower fee elsewhere wouldn’t show that they would. It doesn’t settle the attendance question.
Other facilities losing money is a different problem. Irrelevant.
Residents can want the pool open and still refuse to pay $5 to swim. Doesn’t tell us whether the fee will cover the losses.

questions.stimulus: Lexicographer: The word ‘brackle,’ meaning a sudden summer hailstorm, appears in several letters written in the Tessan Valley in the 1790s. No earlier written use of the word has been found anywhere. So the word most likely originated in the Tessan Valley.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Is the word ‘brackle’ still used by people living in the Tessan Valley today?
Were the letters that use the word written by people with little formal schooling?
Do any modern dictionaries include the word ‘brackle’ among their entries?
Did people in the Tessan Valley in the 1790s have other words for sudden summer storms?
Have many letters and other writings survived from other regions from the 1790s and earlier?
questions.explanation: The argument infers the word’s birthplace from the fact that no earlier use has been found elsewhere. That silence means something only if plenty of writing from elsewhere survives to be searched. (E) asks about exactly that: if little survives, the lack of earlier uses tells us almost nothing; if a great deal survives, the lack is telling. (A) is the tempting choice, but whether people use the word today has no bearing on where it started.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: ‘Brackle’ most likely originated in the Tessan Valley.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: It appears in 1790s letters from the valley; no earlier written use has been found anywhere.

breakdown.analysis: “No earlier use has been found.” Found where? If almost nothing written elsewhere survives, of course no one has found the word there. Not finding something only counts when you had a real chance to find it. It’s like saying a song was first sung at your school because the only old recordings anyone has are from your school’s talent shows. We need a question about how much writing from other places is available to search.

choices.note: Tempting, because it connects the word to the valley. But current use tells us nothing about where the word began. Words travel and settle in new places all the time.
The writers’ schooling doesn’t tell us where the word came from. Irrelevant.
Whether today’s dictionaries list the word says nothing about its origin. Irrelevant.
Other words for storms could exist alongside ‘brackle’ no matter where it began. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If lots of writing from elsewhere survives and none of it uses the word earlier, the valley is a strong candidate. If very little survives, the absence of earlier uses is just a gap in the record. That decides whether the argument’s main evidence means anything.

questions.stimulus: In the year after the city of Corvale opened its bike-share program, the number of cars entering the downtown area each weekday fell by about 8 percent. During that year, riders made an average of 3,000 bike-share trips downtown each weekday. Clearly, the bike-share program is responsible for the drop in downtown car traffic.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did most of the people taking bike-share trips downtown formerly make those same trips by car?
Did the number of bike-share trips taken downtown grow steadily over the course of the year?
Are the people who use the bike-share program younger, on average, than people who drive downtown?
Is the bike-share program operated by the city itself or by a private company under contract?
Would adding bike-share stations in other neighborhoods also reduce car traffic in those neighborhoods?
questions.explanation: Bike-share trips reduce car traffic only if they replace car trips. (A) asks whether they did: if most riders formerly drove, the program plausibly explains the drop; if they formerly walked or took the bus, the 3,000 trips took few cars off the road and something else must explain it. (E) is the tempting choice, but it asks about other neighborhoods in the future, not about what caused this drop downtown.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bike-share program caused the 8 percent drop in downtown car traffic.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Car traffic fell after the program opened; riders made about 3,000 bike-share trips downtown each weekday.

breakdown.analysis: Three thousand bike trips is a lot, but who was taking them? If those riders used to walk or ride the bus, not one car came off the road. A bike trip only cuts car traffic if it replaces a car trip. It’s like a gym crediting its new juice bar for a drop in soda sales across town, when the juice buyers never drank soda. We need a question about what the riders did before.

choices.note: CORRECT. If most riders used to drive, the program took cars off the road and the argument looks good. If most used to walk or ride transit, the program barely touched car traffic, and something else must explain the drop. This is the link the argument needs.
Steady growth versus bursts doesn’t tell us whether the bike trips replaced car trips. Irrelevant.
Riders’ ages don’t affect whether their trips replaced car trips. Irrelevant.
Who runs the program has nothing to do with what caused the traffic drop. Irrelevant.
Tempting, because it’s about the program’s effect on traffic. But it asks about other neighborhoods in the future. The argument is about what caused this drop, downtown, last year.

questions.stimulus: Sweet corn growers in the Ostra region who mounted roost boxes for bats, which feed on the moths whose larvae damage corn, report that larva damage to their crops fell by nearly half over the next two years. So the bats drawn to the roost boxes are responsible for the reduction in damage.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do the bats that use the roost boxes also feed on insects that do not harm corn?
Are bats more effective at catching moths than are the birds that also feed on moths?
Did damage also fall on the region’s corn farms that had no roost boxes?
Were roost boxes for bats mounted by corn growers in other regions as well as in Ostra?
Did a few of the roost boxes on the growers’ farms remain empty throughout the two years?
questions.explanation: Damage could have fallen for reasons that had nothing to do with bats, such as weather that hurt the moths. (C) supplies the needed comparison: if damage fell just as much on farms without roost boxes, the bats are not the explanation; if it did not, the boxes look responsible. (E) is tempting, but a few empty boxes are fully consistent with bats in the other boxes doing the work. (A) and (B) do not bear on what caused the drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Bats drawn to the roost boxes caused the drop in larva damage.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After growers mounted bat boxes, larva damage on their farms fell by nearly half over two years.

breakdown.analysis: Did damage fall everywhere? Moth numbers rise and fall with weather and other things. If farms without boxes saw the same drop, the bats didn’t do it. This is the missing comparison group. It’s like taking vitamin C, getting over your cold in a week, and crediting the vitamin, without asking how long colds last for people who don’t take it. We need a question that checks the farms without boxes.

choices.note: What else the bats eat doesn’t change whether they reduced corn damage. They can eat other insects and moths too. Irrelevant.
Comparing bats to birds doesn’t tell us whether the bats caused this drop. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If farms without boxes saw damage fall just as much, something region-wide caused the drop, and the bats get no credit. If those farms saw no drop, the boxes are the likely reason. That’s the comparison the argument skipped.
Boxes in other regions tell us nothing about what happened in Ostra. Irrelevant.
Tempting, because empty boxes sound like evidence against the bats. But “a few” is too weak to matter. Bats in the other boxes could still be doing all the work.

questions.stimulus: The Kesterly Bridge needs $12 million in repairs. About 17,000 vehicles cross the bridge each day, so a toll of $1 per crossing would raise the full amount in about two years. Thus, a $1 toll on the Kesterly Bridge is a practical way to pay for the needed repairs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Was the Kesterly Bridge built more recently than most of the other bridges in the region?
Have tolls on any of the other bridges in the region ever been set at more than $1?
Do most of the drivers who cross the Kesterly Bridge each day live within the region?
Would many drivers who now cross the bridge switch to a toll-free route if a toll were charged?
Do most of the drivers who cross the bridge agree that the bridge is in need of repairs?
questions.explanation: The two-year estimate assumes that 17,000 vehicles will keep crossing once there is a toll. (D) tests that assumption: if many drivers would switch to a free route, the toll would raise far less and the plan looks impractical; if few would, the estimate holds. (E) is tempting, but drivers can agree the bridge needs repairs and still avoid paying for it, so a yes would not secure the revenue. The other choices do not bear on how much the toll would raise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A $1 toll is a practical way to pay for the $12 million in repairs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 17,000 vehicles cross daily, so $1 each would raise $12 million in about two years.

breakdown.analysis: Will 17,000 vehicles still cross once they have to pay? If there’s a free bridge a few miles away, many drivers will use it. The math assumes traffic stays the same. It’s like a parking lot that starts charging and expects every car that used to park free to keep coming. We need a question about whether drivers would avoid the toll.

choices.note: The bridge’s age doesn’t change how much a toll would raise. Irrelevant.
Toll levels elsewhere don’t tell us whether drivers here would keep crossing. Irrelevant.
Whether drivers are local doesn’t settle whether they’d pay or detour. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If many drivers would detour to a free route, the toll raises much less than $12 million in two years, and the plan isn’t practical. If few would, the math holds. This is the assumption the revenue estimate depends on.
Tempting, because support sounds like willingness to pay. But it’s one-sided. Drivers can agree the repairs are needed and still take the free route. Agreement doesn’t put money in the toll booth.

questions.stimulus: Tenants’ association president: We slipped a questionnaire under the door of every apartment in our building, and 70 percent of the tenants who returned it said they want the laundry room to stay open overnight. So most of the building’s tenants want the laundry room kept open overnight.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do other apartment buildings in the neighborhood keep their laundry rooms open overnight?
Were tenants who want overnight laundry hours more likely than other tenants to return the questionnaire?
How many washing machines and dryers are there in the building’s laundry room?
Would keeping the laundry room open overnight raise the building’s electricity costs?
Did any of the tenants who returned the questionnaire say that they never use the laundry room?
questions.explanation: The conclusion is about all the building’s tenants, but the evidence comes only from those who chose to reply. (B) asks whether the replies were skewed: if tenants who wanted overnight hours were more eager to respond, the 70 percent overstates support; if not, the result is likely representative. (D) is tempting because it raises a real drawback, but it bears on whether the room should stay open, not on what most tenants want.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of the building’s tenants want the laundry room open overnight.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of the tenants who returned a questionnaire said they want overnight hours.

breakdown.analysis: Who bothers to fill out a questionnaire? Mostly people who care about the issue. If the tenants who want late-night laundry were the ones eager to reply, 70 percent of replies could be a small share of the building. This is a self-selected sample. It’s like judging a restaurant by its online reviews, which come mostly from people who loved it or hated it. We need a question about whether the people who replied were typical.

choices.note: Other buildings’ hours say nothing about what tenants here want. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If supporters were more likely to reply, the 70 percent overstates support, and the conclusion is weak. If replies came evenly from all kinds of tenants, the sample probably reflects the building. This tests whether the sample is representative.
The number of machines doesn’t tell us what tenants want. Irrelevant.
Tempting, because it’s a real drawback to the idea. But the conclusion isn’t that the room should stay open; it’s that most tenants want it to. Cost is a different question.
Some respondents might not use the laundry room. So? They can still have an opinion, and a few of them wouldn’t change whether the sample represents the building.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago the city of Kellam installed flashing warning lights at its busiest mid-block crosswalks. Studies show that such lights make drivers much more likely to stop for pedestrians, and Kellam’s own measurements confirm that drivers now stop far more often at those crosswalks. Yet more pedestrians have been struck at those crosswalks since the lights were installed than in the two years before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Drivers in Kellam stop for pedestrians more often at crosswalks with warning lights than at crosswalks without them.
Most of the pedestrians struck at the lighted crosswalks were crossing during the evening rush hour, when traffic is heaviest.
The lights were installed at the crosswalks where pedestrians had most often been struck in the years before.
Many drivers in Kellam say that the flashing lights make them more alert when they approach a crosswalk.
Many pedestrians who once crossed elsewhere on those streets now cross only at the lighted crosswalks.
questions.explanation: The lights can make each crossing safer while the number of people struck rises, if many more people now cross there. (E) says exactly that: pedestrians who used to cross elsewhere now funnel to the lighted crosswalks, so a lower risk per crossing applies to far more crossings. (C) is the trap because it seems to explain why those crosswalks see many accidents, but those same crosswalks were the most dangerous before too, so it gives no reason for the count to rise after the lights went up. (A) and (D) only restate or reinforce that the lights work.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The new lights make drivers stop far more often at these crosswalks, but more pedestrians have been struck there since the lights went up than before.

breakdown.analysis: How can a crossing get safer while more people get hit there? Watch the measure. The stimulus gives a count of people struck, not a rate. If many more people now use those crosswalks, the count can rise even though each crossing is safer. It’s like a town adding lifeguards at one beach, after which everyone swims there instead of at the unguarded coves, so more rescues happen at that beach. Prephrase: more pedestrians are crossing at the lighted crosswalks now. Most students pick (C) because “those were the dangerous spots” sounds like an explanation. It fails because those crosswalks were the dangerous spots before the lights too; it explains why their numbers are high, not why they went up.

choices.note: This restates that the lights work. It makes the rise in people struck even more puzzling.
Rush-hour timing would have been true before the lights as well. It describes when accidents happen, not why there are more of them now.

Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like selection bias. But the comparison in the stimulus is between the same crosswalks before and after. If they were already the most dangerous spots, that explains high numbers in both periods, not an increase. If anything, the worst spots should improve the most once lights go up.
This says the lights work as intended, which deepens the puzzle rather than resolving it.

CORRECT. If pedestrians who used to cross wherever they liked now cross only at the lights, those crosswalks carry far more pedestrians. Each crossing can be safer while the total number struck there still rises. Both facts fit.

questions.stimulus: Historian: The account books of St. Aubert’s priory show that the quantity of candles the priory purchased fell by more than half between 1347 and 1352. Some scholars attribute this to a rise in the price of wax, but wax prices in the region held steady throughout those years. So the decline most likely reflects a sharp fall in the number of people living at the priory.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the priory’s purchases of bread, cloth, and other everyday goods also fall during those years?
Did the number of people living at the priory rise again in the decades that followed 1352?
Did the scholars who blame the price of wax examine the priory’s account books for themselves?
Was wax produced in the region also sold to buyers in other regions during those years?
Did other priories in the region keep account books as detailed as those kept at St. Aubert’s?
questions.explanation: If the priory lost many of its residents, its purchases of nearly everything should have fallen, not just candles. (A) tests this indirectly: a sharp drop in bread and cloth too would support a population decline, while steady purchases of those goods would point to some cause specific to candles. (B) is the trap because it concerns the priory’s population, but what happened after 1352 cannot show whether the number of residents fell between 1347 and 1352. (C) attacks the scholars, whose view the argument has already rebutted with the price data.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The drop in candle purchases most likely reflects a sharp fall in the number of people living at the priory.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Candle purchases fell by more than half from 1347 to 1352; wax prices held steady, which rules out the scholars’ price explanation.

breakdown.analysis: The historian knocks out one explanation (wax prices) and jumps to another (fewer people). But are those the only two options? Maybe the priory started making its own candles, or cut back on lighting. How could we tell? If people really left, the priory should have bought less of everything. It’s like guessing your roommate moved out because the grocery bill dropped. Check whether the toilet paper and electricity bills dropped too. We need a question that tests whether other purchases fell. Most students pick (B) because it’s about the number of residents, which is what the conclusion is about. But it asks about the wrong years. A later recovery tells us nothing about whether the population fell during 1347–1352.

choices.note: CORRECT. If bread and cloth purchases also fell sharply, that’s what we’d expect if there were far fewer mouths to feed and bodies to clothe, so the argument gets stronger. If those purchases held steady, the drop is specific to candles, and something other than population is likely behind it. Either answer moves the argument.

Tempting, and the main trap. It mentions the priory’s population, which is what the conclusion is about. But the argument is about what happened between 1347 and 1352. Whether numbers recovered later tells us nothing about whether they fell during those years.
This questions the scholars. But the historian has already rejected their view with the wax-price evidence. How they did their research doesn’t affect whether the population explanation is right.
Where the region’s wax was sold doesn’t matter. What matters for the scholars’ view is what wax cost, and the stimulus says the price held steady.
Other priories’ record keeping tells us nothing about why this priory bought fewer candles. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: In the Teral highlands, sheep farmers who keep guard dogs lose a larger percentage of their flocks to wolves each year, on average, than do farmers who keep no guard dogs. Yet field trials have shown that a guard dog greatly reduces the number of wolf attacks on the flock it protects.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Some breeds of guard dog are considerably more effective than others at driving wolves away from a flock.
Wolves in the Teral highlands attack sheep far more often in the winter months than in the summer months.
Teral farmers who keep guard dogs typically have much larger flocks than do Teral farmers who keep none.
Teral farmers usually acquire guard dogs only after their flocks have suffered repeated attacks by wolves.
Guard dogs in the Teral highlands occasionally injure sheep while chasing wolves away from a flock.
questions.explanation: If farmers get guard dogs only after wolves have repeatedly attacked their flocks, the dog owners are the farmers who face the most wolves. A dog can cut their losses a great deal and still leave them losing more than farmers in areas wolves rarely visit, which is (D). (C) is the trap: larger flocks would mean more sheep lost in total, but the stimulus compares percentages of flocks, so flock size does not explain the gap. (E) concerns injuries from dogs, not losses to wolves.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Guard dogs greatly reduce wolf attacks on a flock, but farmers with guard dogs lose a larger percentage of their flocks to wolves than farmers without them.

breakdown.analysis: If the dogs work, why do dog owners lose more? Maybe the dog owners aren’t a random group. Who would buy a guard dog? The farmers with a wolf problem. Their losses could be cut sharply by the dog and still be higher than the losses of farmers with no wolves nearby. It’s like noticing that people who own fire extinguishers have more kitchen fires; maybe the people who cook a lot are the ones who buy extinguishers. Prephrase: the dog owners face far more wolves to begin with. Most students pick (C) because bigger flocks mean more sheep lost. But the stimulus says “percentage.” Flock size is already accounted for.

choices.note: Differences among breeds don’t explain why dog owners as a group do worse than farmers with no dogs at all.
Wolves attacking more in winter affects all farmers alike. A fact that applies to both groups can’t explain a difference between them.
Tempting, and the main trap. A bigger flock would lose more sheep in total. But the comparison is by percentage of the flock, so size is already factored out. Watch the switch from a count to a rate.

CORRECT. The dog owners are the farmers whose flocks wolves target. A dog can reduce their losses and still leave them above farmers who rarely see wolves. The dogs work; they just went to the hardest-hit farms.
Injuries caused by dogs aren’t losses to wolves, and the stimulus is about losses to wolves. Doesn’t touch the paradox.

questions.stimulus: Three years ago the Dunlin youth football league banned tackling for players under twelve, allowing only flag football at those ages. Since then, the number of concussions reported among the league’s under-twelve players has fallen by 40 percent. Therefore, tackling must have caused a large share of the concussions suffered by the league’s youngest players before the ban.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do players over twelve in the league suffer concussions more often than players under twelve do?
Were some of the concussions reported before the ban caused by collisions that did not involve tackling?
Did the number of children playing in the league’s under-twelve division change substantially after the ban?
Do concussions in children under twelve usually take longer to heal than those in older players?
Did most of the league’s coaches support the decision to ban tackling for its younger players?
questions.explanation: The 40 percent drop is a drop in the number of concussions, not in the rate per player. (C) asks whether the number of players changed: if many families left the division after the ban, fewer players alone could explain fewer concussions; if enrollment held steady or grew, the drop points to tackling. (B) is the trap, since it seems to question whether tackling was the cause, but some concussions coming from other collisions is consistent with tackling causing a large share. (A) concerns the wrong group.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Tackling caused a large share of under-twelve concussions before the ban.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After tackling was banned for players under twelve, the number of reported concussions among them fell by 40 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Fewer concussions out of how many kids? The stimulus gives a count, not a rate. If lots of families pulled their kids out after the switch to flag football, fewer players alone would mean fewer concussions. It’s like a store bragging that shoplifting fell by half after it moved, when the new location gets half the customers. We need a question about whether the number of players changed. Most students pick (B) because it seems to question the tackling explanation. But the conclusion says tackling caused “a large share,” not all. Some non-tackling concussions fit that perfectly.

choices.note: This compares the wrong groups. The argument is about under-twelve players before and after the ban, not about older players.

Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like an alternative cause. But “some” is too weak to matter. The conclusion only claims a large share came from tackling, which allows some from other collisions. A yes or a no leaves the argument where it was.

CORRECT. If enrollment dropped sharply, the drop in concussions could come from having fewer players, and the argument is weak. If enrollment held steady or grew, the drop reflects a real fall in the rate, and tackling looks responsible. This is the count-versus-rate gap.
How long concussions take to heal doesn’t affect how many occurred or what caused them. Irrelevant.
Coaches’ support for the ban doesn’t tell us whether tackling caused the concussions. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: A year ago the town of Marrow Point banned stores from handing out thin plastic grocery bags, which had made up a noticeable share of the plastic items in the town’s household trash. Yet in the year since the ban took effect, the total weight of plastic in Marrow Point’s household trash has risen.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Since the ban, many residents have bought heavy plastic bags to line their trash cans, a use for which they formerly reused thin grocery bags.
During the past year, the town’s recycling program stopped accepting several kinds of plastic packaging that it had previously collected.
The number of households in Marrow Point grew substantially during the year after the ban took effect.
Many stores responded to the ban by selling thick plastic bags, labeled as reusable, that customers often throw away after one use.
Thin plastic grocery bags weigh much less than most of the other plastic items that people commonly throw away at home.
questions.explanation: Four choices give a reason the weight of plastic trash could rise despite the ban: heavier trash-can liners (A), plastic diverted from recycling into trash (B), more households (C), and heavier bags that are still thrown away (D). (E) explains only why removing grocery bags would reduce the weight of plastic trash by a small amount; it gives no reason for the weight to go up, so it is the exception. (B) and (C) are the traps here, since they do not mention bags at all, but each adds plastic to the trash.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The town banned thin plastic grocery bags, a noticeable share of its plastic trash, but the total weight of plastic in household trash went up.

breakdown.analysis: In an EXCEPT question, four answers resolve the puzzle and the right answer doesn’t. So we’re hunting for the one that leaves the rise unexplained. A good resolver gives a source of extra plastic in the trash. Watch for the answer that explains only half: why the ban might not help much, without explaining why things got worse. It’s like cutting out dessert and gaining weight. “Desserts weren’t many calories” explains why you didn’t lose much. It doesn’t explain the gain. The traps here are (B) and (C), which don’t mention bags at all, so they look off topic. But they’re the resolvers students most often reject by mistake.

choices.note: This resolves it. People used to reuse thin grocery bags as trash liners. Now they buy heavy liners instead, so more plastic, by weight, goes into the trash.
This resolves it, though it looks off topic. Plastic that used to go to recycling now goes into household trash, which adds weight even if fewer bags are thrown away.
This resolves it. The stimulus gives a total weight, not a per-household amount. More households means more trash overall, which can outweigh the bags that were removed.
This resolves it. Thick “reusable” bags weigh more than thin ones. If people throw them out after one use, the ban can raise the weight of plastic trash.
CORRECT. This explains only why the ban would make a small difference by weight. It doesn’t explain why the weight rose. A small reduction is still a reduction, so the puzzle remains.

questions.stimulus: Plant manager: Six months ago our factory replaced its paper sign-in sheets with electronic time clocks, and since then the number of late arrivals on record has tripled. Admittedly, we hired more workers during that period, but our workforce grew by only 10 percent. So our employees have clearly become less punctual.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the factory hire more new workers during the past six months than it did during the six months before that?
Under the old system, did workers write down their own arrival times on the sign-in sheets?
Do late arrivals by the factory’s workers cause delays in its production schedule?
Did installing the electronic time clocks cost the factory more than it had expected?
Are most of the factory’s recorded late arrivals concentrated among workers on its early-morning shift?
questions.explanation: The tripling compares records from two different systems, so it shows a change in punctuality only if both systems recorded lateness equally well. (B) gets at this: if workers wrote down their own times, late arrivals were probably underreported before and the tripling may be an artifact of honest clocks; if someone else recorded the times, the comparison is fairer. (A) is the trap because hiring is what the manager concedes, but a 10 percent rise in the workforce is too small to explain a tripling no matter when the hiring happened. (E) concerns which workers are late, not whether lateness increased.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The factory’s employees have become less punctual.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Recorded late arrivals tripled after electronic time clocks replaced paper sign-in sheets; the workforce grew only 10 percent, which can’t explain the rise.

breakdown.analysis: The manager rules out one explanation (more workers) but misses a bigger one: the measuring tool changed. Paper sheets and electronic clocks may not catch lateness the same way. If workers used to write their own times, a lot of “8:00” might really have been 8:10. It’s like switching from a bathroom scale you can nudge with your toe to a doctor’s scale, and concluding you gained weight. We need a question about how lateness was recorded before. Most students pick (A) because it’s about hiring, the factor the manager raised. But the manager already gave us the number: 10 percent. That can’t produce a tripling, whatever the timing of the hires.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It’s about the concession the manager already handled. The workforce grew only 10 percent, and that can’t triple the late arrivals. Comparing this hiring to earlier hiring doesn’t change that.

CORRECT. If workers recorded their own times, lateness was probably underreported before, and the tripling may just reflect an honest clock. If someone else recorded arrivals carefully, the old and new numbers are comparable, and the argument holds. This tests whether the comparison is fair.
Whether lateness causes production delays is about its consequences, not about whether it increased. Irrelevant.
The clocks’ cost has nothing to do with whether workers became less punctual. Irrelevant.
Which shift has the late arrivals doesn’t tell us whether lateness rose overall. Whatever the shifts, the question is whether the old records can be compared with the new ones.

questions.stimulus: In the year after the state of Calder began requiring all motorcycle riders to wear helmets, the number of motorcyclists killed in accidents in the state fell sharply. During that same year, however, the number of motorcyclists admitted to Calder hospitals with serious injuries rose.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many crashes that cause fatal head injuries to riders without helmets cause only serious, nonfatal injuries to riders who wear them.
In the year after the helmet law took effect, the number of motorcycles registered in Calder fell by nearly a fifth.
Most motorcycle accidents in Calder involve collisions with cars rather than crashes involving only the motorcycle.
Some riders in Calder continued to ride without helmets after the law took effect, despite the risk of fines.
Before the law took effect, riders who chose to wear helmets tended to ride more cautiously than riders who did not.
questions.explanation: If helmets turn many would-be fatal crashes into survivable ones, some riders who once would have died now reach the hospital seriously hurt. That cuts deaths and adds serious-injury admissions at the same time, which is (A). (B) is the trap: fewer motorcycles on the road would explain the drop in deaths, but it would also mean fewer injuries, so it makes the rise in hospital admissions harder to explain. (D) and (E) do not account for either change.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: After helmets became mandatory, motorcycle deaths fell sharply, but hospital admissions for serious injuries rose.

breakdown.analysis: Shouldn’t a safety law reduce both deaths and injuries? Not if it works by changing one into the other. A rider who would have died might now survive with a broken skull. That rider moves from the death count to the hospital count. It’s like a new ambulance service getting more heart attack patients to the hospital alive. Hospital admissions for heart attacks go up, even though fewer people are dying. Prephrase: helmets turn deaths into serious injuries. Most students pick (B) because fewer riders explains fewer deaths. But fewer riders should also mean fewer injuries, so it explains one side and makes the other worse.

choices.note: CORRECT. Riders who would have died now survive, often with serious injuries. Those survivors raise hospital admissions while lowering deaths. Both facts are explained by the same thing.

Tempting, and the main trap. Fewer motorcycles would explain fewer deaths. But fewer riders should also mean fewer injuries, so this makes the rise in admissions even harder to explain. It resolves one side and deepens the other.
What kind of crash is most common was likely true before the law too. It doesn’t explain why deaths and injuries moved in opposite directions.
Some riders breaking the law would make the law less effective. That explains neither the fall in deaths nor the rise in injuries.
This is about cautious riders before the law. It doesn’t explain anything that happened after it.

questions.stimulus: In a ten-year study, adults who ate beans or lentils at least four times a week were 30 percent less likely to develop heart disease than adults who rarely ate them. The two groups did not differ in how much they exercised or in how many of them smoked. So eating beans or lentils frequently reduces a person’s risk of developing heart disease.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Among the adults who ate beans or lentils frequently, did those who exercised regularly develop heart disease less often than those who did not?
Were the adults in the study typical of adults in general in their overall rates of heart disease?
Do beans and lentils contain any nutrients that cannot be obtained from other common foods?
Did the adults who ate beans or lentils frequently eat less red meat than those who rarely ate them?
Did some of the adults who ate beans or lentils frequently develop heart disease during the study?
questions.explanation: The study rules out exercise and smoking but not other differences in diet. People who eat beans often may eat less of something harmful, and (D) asks whether they ate less red meat: if so, that difference rather than the beans could explain the lower risk; if not, the beans look responsible. (A) is the trap: it brings up exercise, a classic confounder, but the groups were already matched on exercise, so a comparison within the bean-eating group can't show whether the beans made the difference. (B) and (E) do not bear on whether the beans caused the difference.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eating beans or lentils frequently reduces the risk of heart disease.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Frequent bean and lentil eaters were 30 percent less likely to develop heart disease; the groups didn’t differ in exercise or smoking.

breakdown.analysis: The study ruled out two alternative causes, but did it rule out everything? Someone who eats lentils four times a week is probably eating them instead of something else. If that something else is red meat, the benefit may come from what they skip, not what they eat. It’s like crediting a new phone for your better sleep, when the real change is that you stopped scrolling at midnight on the old one. We need a question about some other way the two groups differed. Most students pick (A) because it targets a group difference, the right kind of gap. But the stimulus already answered it: the groups exercised the same.

choices.note: Tempting because exercise is a classic confounder. But the two groups were already matched on exercise, so comparing exercisers with non-exercisers inside the bean-eating group says nothing about whether beans themselves made the difference. Either answer leaves the argument where it was.

Whether the study group matches the general population in heart disease rates doesn’t affect the comparison between bean eaters and others within the study. A textbook-sounding sampling worry that doesn’t touch this argument.
The argument doesn’t claim beans are the only source of their benefit. Beans could lower risk even if their nutrients exist elsewhere. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If frequent bean eaters ate less red meat, the lower risk could come from avoiding meat, and the argument weakens. If both groups ate similar amounts of red meat, that alternative is ruled out, and the beans look responsible. The answer pushes in opposite directions.
“Some” bean eaters getting heart disease is consistent with a 30 percent lower risk. Lower risk isn’t zero risk.

questions.stimulus: Building inspector: The fire alarm in the Harlan Building failed to sound during last Tuesday’s drill. An alarm of this kind fails only if its backup battery is dead or its control wiring is faulty. The wiring was tested on the Sunday before the drill and found to be in perfect order. Therefore, the alarm’s backup battery must have been dead at the time of the drill.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Does a dead backup battery always cause an alarm of this kind to fail to sound?
Have the fire alarms in other buildings the inspector has examined ever failed during drills?
Was any work done on the Harlan Building’s electrical system between Sunday and the drill?
Would the alarm have sounded during the drill if both its battery and its wiring had been sound?
Did the occupants of the Harlan Building leave the building as instructed during the drill?
questions.explanation: Failure requires a dead battery or faulty wiring, so the battery conclusion follows only if the wiring was still sound on Tuesday. The test showed it was sound on Sunday, and (C) asks whether anything happened in between: if electrical work was done, the wiring may have been damaged and the argument weakens; if none was done, the wiring very likely stayed sound. (A) is the trap because it sounds like the key conditional, but it reverses it: the argument needs ‘fails only if dead battery or bad wiring,’ not ‘a dead battery always causes failure.’ (D) restates the given premise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The backup battery was dead at the time of the drill.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The alarm failed; failure → dead battery OR faulty wiring; the wiring tested fine on Sunday.

breakdown.analysis: Lay out the logic. Fail → battery dead OR wiring faulty. The alarm failed, so one of the two was true on Tuesday. The wiring was fine on Sunday. Fine on Sunday doesn’t mean fine on Tuesday. That two-day gap is the only hole. It’s like proving your car keys are in the kitchen because they were there Sunday and they’re not in the bedroom. We need a question that tells us whether the wiring could have changed. Most students pick (A) because it sounds like checking the conditional. But it reverses it. The argument uses fail → (battery or wiring). Whether a dead battery always causes failure is the reverse direction, and the argument never relies on it.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It reverses the conditional. The argument needs “if it fails, the battery or wiring is bad,” which is given. Whether a dead battery is enough to cause failure is the reverse, and it doesn’t matter: the alarm did fail, and we’re working backward from that.
Other buildings’ alarms don’t tell us what went wrong in this one. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If electrical work was done after Sunday, the wiring may have been damaged, and the wiring is back in play as the cause, so the argument weakens. If nothing was done, the wiring was almost certainly still sound, and the battery is the only remaining cause. This fills the two-day gap.
This just restates the premise in contrapositive form: if both are sound, it doesn’t fail. We already know the answer is yes. A question the argument already answers can’t help evaluate it.
Whether people evacuated properly has nothing to do with why the alarm failed. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Across the Orvald region, the average yield of sugar beets per hectare was higher this year than last year. Yet on nearly every farm in the region that grew sugar beets in both years, the yield per hectare was lower this year than last.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: This year’s growing season in the Orvald region was considerably drier than last year’s growing season.
The farms in the Orvald region that grow sugar beets also grow wheat and barley in rotation with them.
The total weight of sugar beets harvested in the Orvald region was lower this year than it was last year.
Most of the region’s sugar beet farmers planted the same varieties of seed this year as they did last year.
Many of the farms with the region’s lowest beet yields last year grew no sugar beets this year.
questions.explanation: A regional average depends on which farms are counted. If the farms with the poorest yields stopped growing beets, they drop out of this year’s average, which can then rise even though nearly every farm still growing beets did worse. That is (E). (A) is the trap: a drier season explains why individual farms’ yields fell, but it would pull the regional average down too, so it leaves the rise unexplained. (C) is consistent with both facts but explains neither.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The region’s average beet yield per hectare rose, but nearly every farm that grew beets in both years had a lower yield.

breakdown.analysis: How can an average go up when almost every member goes down? Change who’s in the group. The second fact covers only farms that grew beets both years. If the worst farms quit, they leave the average, and the average can rise even while everyone who stayed did a bit worse. It’s like a class average rising after the weakest students drop the course, even though every remaining student scored a little lower on the final. Prephrase: low-yield farms stopped growing beets. Most students pick (A) because it explains the falling farm yields. But a bad season would drag down the regional average too. It explains one fact and contradicts the other.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. A drier season explains why individual farms did worse. But it should pull the regional average down too. It explains one side and leaves the rise in the average even more puzzling.
Crop rotation applies in both years. It doesn’t explain why the regional average and farm yields moved in opposite directions.

Consistent with the facts, but not an explanation. A lower total doesn’t tell us why the average per hectare rose while individual farms fell. Notice it fits nicely with the right answer: if poor farms quit, the total could drop too.
Using the same seed rules out one possible change. It explains nothing.

CORRECT. The poorest farms left the group. With them gone, this year’s average is drawn only from better farms, so it can top last year’s average even though each of those farms did a bit worse. Both facts fit.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: The Corran salamander breeds only in pools that form each spring from melting snow. Five years ago, a drainage ditch was dug that keeps such pools from forming in the eastern half of the Corran meadows, though not in the western half. The number of salamander egg masses found in the meadows each spring has not declined since then. So the salamanders must have shifted their breeding to the western half.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Were salamander egg masses found in the eastern half of the meadows before the ditch was dug?
Has the number of Corran salamanders breeding outside the Corran meadows also stayed the same?
Do spring pools still form each year in the western half of the Corran meadows?
Will plants that need spring pools eventually disappear from the eastern half of the meadows?
Do salamanders hatched in the western half survive to adulthood as often as those hatched in the eastern half once did?
questions.explanation: A shift to the western half presupposes that the salamanders used to breed in the eastern half. (A) tests that hidden precondition: if egg masses were found there before the ditch, the steady count suggests they moved west; if none were, there was nothing to shift and the conclusion fails. (E) is the trap because it compares the two halves, but survival to adulthood is a different question from where the salamanders breed. (C) is already answered by the stimulus, which says the ditch does not stop pools from forming in the west.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The salamanders shifted their breeding to the western half of the meadows.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: They breed only in spring pools; the ditch stopped pools forming in the east but not the west; the number of egg masses hasn’t fallen.

breakdown.analysis: “Shifted” means they used to be somewhere else. Did they ever breed in the east? Maybe the eastern pools were too shallow, or too short-lived, and every egg mass was always in the west. Then the ditch changed nothing for the salamanders, and nothing moved. It’s like concluding your neighbor started parking on the street because her driveway was blocked, when she never parked in the driveway. We need a question that checks whether there were eastern breeders before. Most students pick (E) because it compares east and west, which feels on target. But it asks how many young survive, not where the adults breed.

choices.note: CORRECT. If egg masses used to be found in the east, they must now be laid somewhere else, and the steady count points west. The argument is strong. If none were ever found in the east, the salamanders had nothing to shift away from, and the conclusion fails. This tests what “shifted” assumes.
Breeding outside the meadows is a different population. It doesn’t tell us whether the meadow salamanders moved within the meadows.
The stimulus already answers this. The ditch keeps pools from forming in the east “though not in the western half,” so the western pools still form. A question with a known answer can’t help.
What will happen to eastern plants in the future says nothing about where salamanders breed now. Irrelevant.

Tempting, and the main trap. It compares the two halves, so it looks relevant. But survival to adulthood is about what happens after the eggs hatch. The argument is about where the eggs are laid. Wrong question.

questions.stimulus: In the Tavel forest, wooden nest boxes with small entrance holes are much less likely to be raided by predators than are boxes with large entrance holes. Nevertheless, the songbirds that nest in the forest’s small-hole boxes fledge fewer young per nest, on average, than do the songbirds that nest in its large-hole boxes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Predators in the Tavel forest raid nests in natural tree cavities more often than they raid nests in boxes.
Boxes with large entrance holes let in more rain, which can chill the eggs and newly hatched chicks inside.
Far fewer small-hole boxes than large-hole boxes have been put up by the people who maintain the forest.
Small entrance holes admit only the forest’s smallest songbirds, which lay fewer eggs per clutch than larger songbirds.
Songbirds in the Tavel forest prefer nest boxes whose entrance holes face away from the prevailing wind.
questions.explanation: The two kinds of box are used by different birds. If only the smallest species can fit through small holes, and those species lay fewer eggs, their nests produce fewer young even though predators rarely reach them, which is (D). (C) is the trap: fewer small-hole boxes would mean fewer young from those boxes in total, but the stimulus compares young per nest, so the number of boxes is irrelevant. (B) makes large-hole boxes look worse, which deepens the puzzle.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Small-hole boxes are much safer from predators, but birds nesting in them fledge fewer young per nest than birds in large-hole boxes.

breakdown.analysis: If small holes keep predators out, why do those nests produce fewer young? Ask who’s inside. A small hole doesn’t just keep out predators; it keeps out bigger birds. So the two kinds of box hold different species. If the small species lay fewer eggs, they’ll fledge fewer young no matter how safe the box is. It’s like noticing that compact cars have fewer passengers per trip than minivans and blaming the car’s safety features. Prephrase: different, less productive birds use the small-hole boxes. Most students pick (C) because fewer boxes means fewer young. But the stimulus says “per nest.” The number of boxes drops out of a per-nest average.

choices.note: Natural cavities aren’t part of the comparison. This tells us nothing about why one kind of box produces fewer young than the other.
This makes the large-hole boxes look worse, so they should produce fewer young, not more. Deepens the puzzle.
Tempting, and the main trap. Fewer boxes would mean fewer young in total. But the comparison is per nest, so the number of boxes doesn’t matter. Count versus rate.

CORRECT. The small holes sort the birds by size. The small species that fit through lay smaller clutches, so their nests fledge fewer young even with less predation. The boxes are safer; the occupants are just less productive.
A preference for boxes facing away from the wind would affect both kinds of box. It doesn’t explain a difference between them.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Over the past decade, the average price of a new home in Brisa has risen by 40 percent. Over the same period, the average household income in Brisa has also risen by 40 percent. So, for Brisa’s households, new homes are no less affordable today than they were a decade ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the average price of existing homes in Brisa also rise by 40 percent over the past decade?
Did the incomes of most Brisa households rise by roughly as much as the average household income did?
Did the number of new homes built in Brisa each year increase over the past decade?
Are new homes in Brisa more affordable than new homes in the cities that border it?
Did average household income in Brisa rise faster in the first half of the decade than in the second half?
questions.explanation: An average income can rise by 40 percent because a small number of households earn far more, while most households gain little. (B) asks whether typical incomes kept pace: if most households’ incomes rose much less than the average, new homes have become less affordable for most of them; if most rose about as much, the argument holds. (A) is the trap because it looks like a check on housing prices, but the conclusion is about new homes, so the price of existing homes is beside the point. (E) concerns timing within the decade, which does not change the ten-year comparison.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: New homes are no less affordable for Brisa’s households than they were a decade ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The average new-home price rose 40 percent; average household income also rose 40 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Averages hide a lot. If a few households got very rich, the average income could jump 40 percent while most families’ incomes barely moved. Then most households would find new homes much less affordable. It’s like saying everyone in the room got richer when a billionaire walks in. The average is up; nobody else’s wallet changed. We need a question about whether typical households kept pace with the average. Most students pick (A) because it’s about prices, the other half of affordability. But it swaps “existing” for “new,” and the conclusion is only about new homes.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It looks like a check on prices. But the argument is about new homes, and their price is given. What existing homes cost is a different market.

CORRECT. If most households’ incomes rose about 40 percent, the price-to-income ratio held for them, and the argument stands. If most rose far less, the average was pulled up by a few high earners, and new homes are less affordable for most households. That’s the gap between the average and the typical household.
How many homes were built doesn’t change how a home’s price compares with a household’s income. Irrelevant.
A comparison with other cities doesn’t tell us whether affordability in Brisa changed over time.
The argument compares the start and end of the decade. How income rose in between doesn’t change that comparison.

questions.stimulus: Kerrow Cutlery makes two lines of kitchen knives: a standard line and a premium line that had always been priced well above it. Last year Kerrow cut the price of its premium knives to match the price of its standard knives, without changing either line in any other way. Yet in the following months, sales of Kerrow’s premium knives fell.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: For many years, Kerrow’s standard knives have sold in much greater numbers than its premium knives have.
Kerrow’s main competitors cut the prices of their own premium knives by similar amounts at about the same time.
Kerrow announced the price cut in the same magazines in which it regularly advertises its standard knives.
Kerrow’s premium knives cost the company considerably more to produce than its standard knives do.
Many knife buyers judge a knife’s quality mainly by comparing its price with other knives’ prices.
questions.explanation: If buyers judge a knife’s quality largely by its price relative to other knives, then once the premium knives cost the same as the standard ones, many buyers would stop seeing them as better and would be less inclined to choose them. That is (E), and it lets a price cut reduce sales. (B) is the trap: if competitors cut their prices too, Kerrow’s cut would bring no advantage, but that explains only why sales did not rise, not why they fell. (D) concerns Kerrow’s profits, not its sales.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Kerrow cut the price of its premium knives to the standard-line price, with no other change, but premium sales fell.

breakdown.analysis: Lower price, same product, fewer sales? Something about the lower price must have made the knives less attractive. What does price tell a shopper? For many, a high price signals quality. Take away the price gap and the premium knife looks like just another knife. It’s like a fancy restaurant offering its tasting menu at fast-food prices; some diners start wondering what’s wrong with the food. Prephrase: buyers took the lower price as a sign of lower quality. Most students pick (B) because competitor price cuts sound like a reason for weak sales. But matching cuts would only cancel Kerrow’s advantage. That explains no gain, not a drop.

choices.note: This was true before the price cut too. A long-standing fact can’t explain a change.

Tempting, and the main trap. If rivals cut prices similarly, Kerrow’s cut brings no edge, so sales might stay flat. But flat isn’t falling. This explains why the cut didn’t help, not why sales dropped.
Where the cut was announced doesn’t explain why sales fell. At worst, fewer buyers heard about it, which would mean no gain, not a loss.
Tempting in a different way. This explains why the cut might hurt Kerrow’s profits. But the puzzle is about sales, not profit.

CORRECT. If buyers judge quality by comparing prices, a premium knife priced like a standard one no longer looks premium. Fewer people want it, so sales fall even though the knife didn’t change. Both facts fit.

questions.stimulus: Urban planner: A good test of whether a neighborhood suits young families is whether its homes are within a ten-minute walk of a public playground. By that test, the Marlow neighborhood suits young families well. Nearly every home in Marlow lies within half a kilometer of a playground, measured in a straight line, and most adults can walk half a kilometer in well under ten minutes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Are there more public playgrounds in Marlow than there are in any other neighborhood of the city?
Do most young families in Marlow in fact walk their children to the neighborhood’s playgrounds?
Do highways or rail lines separate many Marlow homes from the playgrounds nearest to them?
Are Marlow’s playgrounds as well equipped as the public playgrounds in the city’s other neighborhoods?
Is being near a playground more important to most young families than being near a good school?
questions.explanation: The test is about walking time, but the evidence is a straight-line distance. Those match only if people can walk roughly straight to the playground. (C) asks whether barriers stand in the way: if highways or rail lines force long detours, many homes may be far more than ten minutes away on foot; if not, the straight-line figure is a fair guide. (B) is the trap because it seems to test whether the playgrounds are really walkable, but the test asks whether homes are within a ten-minute walk, not whether families actually make the walk. (D) and (E) concern the playgrounds’ quality and the test’s importance, not whether Marlow passes it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Marlow suits young families well, by the test of having homes within a ten-minute walk of a playground.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly every home is within half a kilometer of a playground in a straight line; most adults walk that distance in well under ten minutes.

breakdown.analysis: “Measured in a straight line.” Nobody walks in a straight line through a highway. The test is about walking time, and the evidence is straight-line distance. If a rail yard sits between a home and the playground, a half-kilometer gap could be a twenty-minute walk around it. It’s like saying your office is close because you can see it from your window, when the river in between has no bridge for a mile.
