We need a question that checks whether the straight line matches the real route. Most students pick (B) because it seems to test walkability in real life. But the test is about whether homes are within a ten-minute walk, not whether families walk there. “Can” isn’t “do.”

choices.note: Comparing Marlow with other neighborhoods doesn’t matter. The test is about walking time from each home, not about ranking neighborhoods.

Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like checking the real-world walk. But the test asks whether homes are within a ten-minute walk, not whether families make that walk. Parents might drive out of habit even if the walk is short. “Can” isn’t “do.”

CORRECT. If highways or rail lines block the straight path, the real walk could be much longer than half a kilometer, and many homes might fail the ten-minute test. If no such barriers exist, the straight-line distance is a fair stand-in, and Marlow passes. This targets the gap between the evidence and the test.
How well equipped the playgrounds are isn’t part of the test. Irrelevant.
This questions how much the test matters, but the argument applies the test as given. Ranking playgrounds against schools doesn’t tell us whether Marlow passes it.

questions.stimulus: Six years ago, to protect the trout in Lake Orrin, the province banned commercial net fishing on the lake. The limits on how many trout recreational anglers may take from the lake have not changed since then. Yet surveys show that the lake’s trout population is now substantially smaller than it was before the ban took effect.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Before the ban, trout were the most valuable of the fish that commercial fishers caught in Lake Orrin.
In the years just before the ban, commercial fishers had already been catching far fewer trout in Lake Orrin than in earlier decades.
Some of the commercial fishers who formerly worked on Lake Orrin now fish instead on other lakes in the province.
Most of the fish caught in the commercial nets on Lake Orrin were pike, which feed heavily on young trout.
The number of recreational anglers fishing on Lake Orrin has remained about the same since the ban.
questions.explanation: If the nets mostly caught pike, which eat young trout, the ban mainly protected the trout’s predators. More pike would eat more young trout, so the trout population could shrink even though no one nets trout anymore. That is (D). (B) is the trap: if commercial fishers were already catching few trout, the ban would do little to help, but that explains only why the population did not grow, not why it fell. (A) and (E) make the decline harder to explain.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Commercial net fishing was banned to protect the trout, and angling limits didn’t change, but the trout population is now substantially smaller.

breakdown.analysis: How does removing a threat leave the trout worse off? Maybe the nets were doing the trout a favor. What else did the nets catch? If they kept the trout’s predators in check, the ban freed those predators. It’s like getting rid of the barn cats to protect the chickens’ feed and then losing the feed to mice. Prephrase: the nets had been removing something that harms trout. Most students pick (B) because it explains why the ban didn’t help. But “didn’t help” isn’t “made things worse.” It leaves the decline unexplained.

choices.note: If trout were the nets’ most valuable catch, the nets were taking lots of trout, so the ban should have helped them. Deepens the puzzle.

Tempting, and the main trap. If the nets were already catching few trout, the ban wouldn’t do much, so the population might hold steady. But the puzzle is that it fell. This explains a lack of improvement, not a decline.
Where the fishers went doesn’t affect Lake Orrin’s trout. Irrelevant.
CORRECT. The nets were mostly removing pike, which eat young trout. Ban the nets and the pike population grows, so more young trout get eaten. The ban backfired, and the decline makes sense.
Steady angling pressure rules out one alternative explanation. That makes the decline harder to explain, not easier.

questions.stimulus: Analyst: Some credit the high-speed wireless network built in Tamsin County three years ago for the county’s surge in new home-based businesses. Admittedly, such businesses have multiplied in Tamsin since the network was completed. But they have multiplied just as quickly in neighboring Corvel County, where no such network was built. So the network is not responsible for Tamsin’s surge.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Does the signal from Tamsin’s new network reach many homes in Corvel County?
Did building the new wireless network create a large number of jobs in Tamsin County?
Has the government of Corvel County considered building a high-speed wireless network of its own?
Were there more home-based businesses in Tamsin than in Corvel before the network was built?
Do the new home-based businesses in Tamsin earn more, on average, than the new ones in Corvel?
questions.explanation: The analyst treats Corvel as a county without the network, so Corvel’s matching surge seems to show that the network made no difference. That comparison works only if Corvel really lacked access to the network. (A) asks whether the network’s signal reaches Corvel homes: if it does, Corvel’s surge may come from the same network and the argument collapses; if it does not, Corvel is a fair comparison. (D) is the trap because it compares the two counties, but ‘multiplied just as quickly’ is a rate of growth, so the starting numbers do not matter. (B) concerns jobs, not home-based businesses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new network is not responsible for Tamsin’s surge in home-based businesses.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Concession: the businesses multiplied after the network was built. But they multiplied just as quickly in Corvel, where no network was built.

breakdown.analysis: The whole argument rests on Corvel as the comparison group: no network, same surge, so the network didn’t matter. But “built in Tamsin” isn’t the same as “used only in Tamsin.” Wireless signals don’t stop at county lines. If Corvel homes get the signal, Corvel had the network too, and its surge supports the network theory instead of undercutting it. It’s like testing whether a new streetlight reduced crime on your block by comparing it with the next block, which is lit by the same light. We need a question about whether Corvel really lacked the network. Most students pick (D) because it compares the counties. But “multiplied just as quickly” is a rate, so the starting numbers don’t matter.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the signal reaches many Corvel homes, Corvel isn’t a network-free county at all, and its surge could be the network’s work too. The argument collapses. If the signal doesn’t reach Corvel, the comparison is fair, and the argument gets stronger. This tests the comparison group.
Construction jobs are a different effect. Whether the network created jobs doesn’t tell us whether it caused the surge in home-based businesses.
What Corvel’s government has considered doesn’t change whether Corvel had access to the network during the surge. Irrelevant.

Tempting, and the main trap. It compares the two counties, which feels like checking the comparison. But the argument says the businesses “multiplied just as quickly,” a rate of growth. Starting from different numbers doesn’t change whether they grew at the same rate.
How much the businesses earn is a different question from what caused them to start. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Portable fire extinguishers can put out most small household fires. Yet a study based on the Brensk fire department’s records of house fires found that homes with an extinguisher on hand suffered fire damage amounting to a larger percentage of the home’s value, on average, than did homes without one.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Most of the extinguishers sold for household use are designed to put out several different kinds of fire.
Homes in Brensk that have fire extinguishers are, on average, larger and more valuable than homes without them.
Most of the house fires recorded in Brensk began in the kitchen rather than in other parts of the home.
Many Brensk residents who own extinguishers keep them where they cannot be reached quickly during a fire.
Fires that residents put out themselves before calling firefighters rarely appear in the Brensk fire department’s records.
questions.explanation: The study used only the fire department’s records. If fires that residents put out themselves rarely reach those records, the records leave out the cases where an extinguisher worked, so the recorded fires in homes with extinguishers are mostly the ones the extinguisher could not stop. That is (E). (B) is the trap: bigger, more valuable homes would explain more damage in dollars, but the study measured damage as a percentage of the home’s value. (D) explains why an extinguisher might fail to help, but not why homes with one would fare worse.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Extinguishers can put out most small fires, but in the fire department’s records, homes with extinguishers suffered more damage, as a share of home value, than homes without.

breakdown.analysis: Where did the data come from? The fire department’s records. Which fires get into those records? The ones firefighters are called to. If a resident puts out a small fire with an extinguisher, nobody calls, and that success never shows up. The records for extinguisher homes are mostly the fires that got out of hand. It’s like judging a hospital’s skill by its death records alone: the patients it cured never appear. Prephrase: the successes are missing from the data. Most students pick (B) because bigger homes mean bigger damage. But the stimulus measured damage as a percentage of value, which cancels out home size.

choices.note: If extinguishers handle many kinds of fire, they should help more, not less. Deepens the puzzle.

Tempting, and the main trap. Bigger, pricier homes would suffer more damage in dollars. But the study measured damage as a percentage of each home’s value, so home value is already factored out. Count versus rate again.
Kitchens being the most common starting point applies to homes with and without extinguishers. It doesn’t explain a difference between them.
Tempting in a different way. Hard-to-reach extinguishers would explain why they don’t help. But it doesn’t explain why homes with them fare worse than homes without them. No help isn’t harm.

CORRECT. Fires that residents put out with an extinguisher rarely reach the records. So the recorded fires in extinguisher homes are mostly the ones that got away from them, which are bigger fires. The extinguishers can work and the records can still look bad.

questions.stimulus: Cheesemaker: Several recent batches of our aged cheddar have developed a bitter aftertaste. The only change we have made to our cheesemaking process this year is that we now age the wheels in a new limestone cellar rather than on wooden shelves in the barn. Therefore, aging the cheese in the limestone cellar must be what made those batches bitter.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the cheesemaker’s argument depends?
choices: Cheddar aged on wooden shelves never develops a bitter aftertaste, no matter how long the wheels are left to age there.
The milk used for the recent batches did not differ from the milk used earlier in any way that could cause bitterness.
Most of the customers who bought cheddar from the recent batches noticed the bitter aftertaste and complained about it.
Limestone cellars are used by most of the cheesemakers in the region who produce the highest-quality aged cheddar for sale.
The bitterness in the recent batches would have been stronger still if the wheels had been aged for a longer time.
questions.explanation: The cheesemaker rules out other causes only within the cheesemaking process, so the argument needs the ingredients, which lie outside that process, not to be the culprit. That is (B): if the milk changed in a way that could cause bitterness, the cellar is no longer the only suspect. (A) is tempting but far stronger than needed; the shelves could occasionally yield bitter cheese and the cellar could still be to blame for these batches. (C), (D) and (E) do not bear on what caused the bitterness.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Aging in the limestone cellar made the recent batches bitter.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Recent batches are bitter; the only change to the cheesemaking process this year is the move to the limestone cellar.

breakdown.analysis: The only change to the process? Fine. But is the process the only thing that could make cheese bitter? What about what goes into it? The argument rules out other causes inside the process and quietly ignores everything outside it, like the milk. It’s like saying “I changed nothing about how I bake, so the new oven ruined the bread,” when the flour supplier also changed. We need an answer that says nothing outside the process, such as the milk, explains the bitterness. Negate each choice and see whether the argument falls apart.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a clean before-and-after contrast. But it’s far too strong. Negate it: shelf-aged cheddar sometimes turns bitter. The cellar could still be what caused these batches to turn. The argument survives, so this isn’t required.
choices.negation: Cheddar aged on wooden shelves sometimes develops a bitter aftertaste.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the milk for the recent batches did differ in a way that could cause bitterness. Now there’s a second suspect outside the process, and the cellar is no longer the only explanation. The argument collapses, so it depends on this.
choices.negation: The milk used for the recent batches differed from the milk used earlier in a way that could cause bitterness.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether customers noticed or complained has nothing to do with what caused the bitterness. Negate it and the causal claim is untouched.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the customers who bought cheddar from the recent batches noticed the bitter aftertaste and complained.

choices.note: So? What top cheesemakers use tells us nothing about why these batches went bitter. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: Limestone cellars are not used by most of the cheesemakers who produce the highest-quality aged cheddar.

choices.note: Interesting fact, but not relevant. The argument is about the cause of the bitterness, not how bitterness changes with aging time. Negate it and nothing happens.
choices.negation: The bitterness in the recent batches would not have been stronger if the wheels had been aged longer.

questions.stimulus: Under Tolliver’s public art program, the arts commission may approve a mural only if the mural is to be painted on a city-owned building and its design has been presented at a public hearing. The design for the mural proposed for the Garnet Street warehouse was presented at a public hearing last month. Even so, the commission cannot approve that mural.
questions.stem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every mural that is to be painted on a city-owned building and whose design has been presented at a hearing is approved by the commission.
Several residents who attended last month’s public hearing objected to the design of the proposed warehouse mural.
The commission has not approved any mural this year that was to be painted on a privately owned building.
The Garnet Street warehouse is not one of the buildings in Tolliver that the city owns.
The arts commission has rejected other murals in the past that were proposed for warehouses in Tolliver.
questions.explanation: Approval requires two things: a city-owned building and a public hearing. The hearing requirement is met, so the only way to guarantee the mural cannot be approved is for the other requirement to fail, which is exactly what (D) says. (A) is the tempting reversal: it tells us when murals are approved, not when they can’t be, and in any case it would point toward approval. (B), (C) and (E) are facts about objections and past decisions that don’t touch the rule’s requirements.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The commission cannot approve the Garnet Street warehouse mural.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Approve → city-owned building AND design shown at hearing; the warehouse mural’s design was shown at a hearing.

breakdown.analysis: Map it out. Approve → (city-owned AND hearing). Contrapositive: NOT city-owned OR NO hearing → can’t approve. We know the hearing happened, so that escape route is closed. The only way to get “cannot approve” is the other one: the building isn’t city-owned. Prephrase: the warehouse isn’t city property. It’s like a club rule: you can enter only if you have a ticket and you’re on the list. You’re on the list. If you’re still not getting in, it must be because you lack a ticket.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses all the right terms. But this reverses the rule: it says when a mural IS approved. We need to know when one can’t be. And even if it were true, it says nothing about whether this warehouse is city-owned, so the conclusion still doesn’t follow.
So? Objections at a hearing aren’t part of the rule. The rule asks only whether the design was presented, and it was. Objections don’t make approval impossible.
This is a pattern from this year, not a fact about the warehouse. We still don’t know who owns the warehouse, so the conclusion doesn’t follow.
CORRECT. Not city-owned → the first requirement fails → the commission cannot approve the mural. Combined with the rule, the conclusion is airtight.
Past rejections don’t prove anything about this mural. Those warehouses might not have been city-owned, or the commission might have simply declined. Nothing here guarantees “cannot approve.”

questions.stimulus: Lightning poses the greatest danger to climbers who are above the tree line. For that reason, a mountain guide should cancel a scheduled summit climb if afternoon thunderstorms are forecast, unless the climbing party is able to reach the summit and get back below the tree line before noon.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Thunderstorms are forecast for this afternoon, and Rafe’s slow-moving party cannot get back below the tree line before noon, so Rafe should cancel today’s climb.
No thunderstorms are forecast for this afternoon, so Ines should not cancel her party’s summit climb, even though the party moves slowly.
Thunderstorms are forecast for this afternoon, but Dana’s party can be back below the tree line well before noon, so Dana must lead the climb as planned.
Because Marco canceled a climb last week when storms were forecast, he should cancel every future climb for which storms are forecast.
Lena’s party could not have returned below the tree line before noon, so she should have canceled yesterday’s climb, even though no storms were forecast.
questions.explanation: The principle says: storms forecast and the party can’t be back below the tree line by noon → cancel. Only (A) supplies both facts and draws the verdict “cancel.” (C) is the tempting trap: the exception means the principle no longer requires canceling, but it never says the guide must go ahead. (B) and (E) involve no storm forecast, where the principle says nothing, and (D) ignores the exception for fast parties.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Afternoon storms forecast AND party can’t be back below the tree line by noon → cancel the climb.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment that meets both conditions and concludes the guide should cancel.

breakdown.analysis: “Unless” sets up an exception. Translate: storms forecast → cancel, unless back by noon. So: storms AND NOT back by noon → cancel. The principle only ever tells you to cancel. It never tells you to climb. So the right answer must: 1. have storms forecast; 2. have a party that can’t be back below the tree line by noon; 3. conclude “cancel.” Any answer that concludes “go ahead” can’t be supported by this rule.

choices.note: CORRECT. Storms forecast: check. Party can’t be back by noon: check. Verdict is cancel: check. Every condition is met and the verdict matches.
No storms are forecast, so the principle doesn’t apply at all. It never says when you should NOT cancel. The verdict here has no support from the rule.

Tempting. Dana fits the exception, so the rule doesn’t require her to cancel. But “not required to cancel” isn’t “must climb.” The principle only produces cancellations. Watch the difference between an exception and a command.
Too broad. The rule has an exception for parties that can be back by noon, and this judgment wipes it out. It also rests on what Marco did last week, which the principle doesn’t care about.
No storms were forecast, so the first condition fails. Being slow alone never triggers a cancellation under this principle.

questions.stimulus: Communications director: A study of printed newsletters found that readers remembered more of an article when it was set in a serif typeface than when it was set in a sans serif typeface. Our city’s website currently displays all public notices in a sans serif typeface. So switching the website to a serif typeface would help residents remember more of the notices they read there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the communications director’s argument?
choices: Most residents who read public notices on the city’s website would prefer that those notices be set in a serif typeface rather than a sans serif one.
Serif typefaces are easier to read than every other kind of typeface, whether in print or on a screen.
The advantage in recall that serif type gives to readers of printed text does not disappear when text is read on a screen.
Residents read the city’s public notices on its website more often than they read the notices in printed form.
The study of printed newsletters included readers from a wide range of ages and educational backgrounds.
questions.explanation: The evidence is about print; the conclusion is about a website. The argument needs the print result to carry over to screens, and (C) is the minimal version of that: the recall advantage doesn’t vanish on a screen. (B) is the tempting trap, but it is much stronger than needed and is about ease of reading, not recall. (E) would make the study more convincing but isn’t required, and (A) and (D) are about preference and frequency, not memory.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Switching the website to a serif typeface would help residents remember more of the notices.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A study of printed newsletters found better recall for serif type; the website now uses sans serif.

breakdown.analysis: Print isn’t a screen. Why should a paper study tell us anything about a website? The argument jumps from one medium to another and assumes the effect comes along. It’s like testing a running shoe on a track and assuming it grips just as well on ice. We need an answer that says the recall advantage still holds on a screen. Use the negation test: if negating the answer kills the argument, it’s required.

choices.note: Preference isn’t memory. Negate it (most residents wouldn’t prefer serif) and they could still remember more with serif type. The argument is untouched.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most residents who read public notices on the website would prefer them in a serif typeface.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like strong support for serif type. But it’s way too strong (“every other kind,” print AND screen), and it’s about ease of reading, not recall. Negate it: serif isn’t the easiest of all typefaces. Serif could still beat sans serif for recall on screens. Not required.
choices.negation: Serif typefaces are not easier to read than every other kind of typeface in both print and on a screen.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the recall advantage disappears on a screen. Then switching the website’s typeface does nothing for memory, and the conclusion collapses. That’s the gap between print and screen, filled minimally.
choices.negation: The advantage in recall that serif type gives to readers of printed text disappears when text is read on a screen.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The claim is about notices read on the website. How often people read print versions doesn’t matter. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: Residents do not read the public notices on the website more often than they read them in printed form.

choices.note: This would make the study more trustworthy, but it isn’t required. Negate it: the study had a narrow group of readers. That weakens the evidence a bit, but the argument doesn’t depend on it. A narrow sample could still show a real effect. Helpful isn’t the same as necessary.
choices.negation: The study of printed newsletters did not include readers from a wide range of ages and educational backgrounds.

questions.stimulus: To transmit through the Hollis Radio Club’s mountaintop repeater, a club member must hold an advanced operator’s license. Every club member who holds an advanced license has also passed the club’s emergency-procedures exam. Therefore, Kofi Mensah, a member of the club, has passed the emergency-procedures exam.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
choices: Kofi Mensah has transmitted through the club’s mountaintop repeater at least once.
Every club member who has passed the emergency-procedures exam holds an advanced operator’s license.
Some members of the Hollis Radio Club who hold advanced licenses transmit through the repeater regularly.
Kofi Mensah has been studying for the advanced operator’s license and plans to take its test soon.
Most of the members of the Hollis Radio Club have transmitted through the mountaintop repeater.
questions.explanation: The chain is: transmits through the repeater → advanced license → passed the exam. Nothing yet connects Kofi to the start of the chain, and (A) does: if he has transmitted, he must hold the license and so must have passed the exam. (B) is the tempting reversal; it runs from the exam to the license and so can’t get us to the exam. (C), (D) and (E) never place Kofi in the chain.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Kofi has passed the emergency-procedures exam.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Transmit through repeater → advanced license; advanced license → passed exam; Kofi is a member.

breakdown.analysis: Build the chain: Transmit → License → Exam. The conclusion is about Kofi reaching “Exam.” But we know nothing about Kofi except that he’s a member. We need to put him somewhere on the chain. Getting him to “Transmit” or “License” does the job. Prephrase: Kofi has transmitted through the repeater, or Kofi holds an advanced license.

choices.note: CORRECT. Kofi transmitted → he holds an advanced license → he passed the exam. The chain runs all the way to the conclusion.
Tempting, because it links the two terms. But it reverses the given link: it runs Exam → License. We already know License → Exam. Neither gets Kofi onto the chain, so nothing follows about him.
Says nothing about Kofi. Facts about some other members can’t prove anything about him.
This actually suggests Kofi does NOT yet hold the advanced license. Either way, it doesn’t place him on the chain.
“Most” members isn’t Kofi. He could be in the minority who never transmitted. Too weak to guarantee the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Sports commentator: The league’s video review officials were right to let stand the goal awarded in last night’s match. The replay footage came from a camera angle that did not clearly show whether the ball had fully crossed the goal line, and the referee on the field had an unobstructed view of the play.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the sports commentator’s reasoning?
choices: Whenever replay footage clearly shows that a ruling made on the field was mistaken, the video review officials should overturn that ruling.
A league should install additional cameras so that replay footage shows every part of the goal line clearly.
Video review should be used only for goals that are scored during the final ten minutes of a match.
Video review officials should consult the on-field referee before they make any decision about a disputed goal.
An on-field ruling should be overturned on video review only if the footage clearly shows it to be wrong.
questions.explanation: The commentator concludes the goal should stand because the footage wasn’t clear. (E) makes clear footage a requirement for overturning, so unclear footage means the ruling stays. (A) is the tempting reversal: it says when a ruling must be overturned, but it says nothing about what to do when the footage is unclear. (B) is about future equipment, (C) introduces timing we aren’t told about, and (D) is about procedure rather than the verdict.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Officials were right to let the goal stand.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The footage didn’t clearly show whether the ball crossed the line; the referee had a clear view.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. The conclusion is “leave the call alone,” and the key fact is “the footage wasn’t clear.” So we want a rule like: don’t overturn unless the footage clearly shows a mistake. In arrows: overturn → footage clearly shows error. Contrapositive: footage not clear → don’t overturn. That’s exactly the commentator’s move.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s the same idea with the arrow pointing the wrong way. It says clear footage → overturn. Here the footage wasn’t clear, so this rule is silent. It can’t justify leaving the goal in place.
This is advice about the future. It doesn’t say what officials should do with unclear footage now.
We don’t know when the goal was scored, and the commentator never mentions timing. This rule can’t connect to the conclusion.
This is about how officials should go about deciding, not what they should decide. It doesn’t justify letting the goal stand.
CORRECT. Overturn only if the footage clearly shows error. The footage didn’t, so the ruling shouldn’t be overturned, which is just what the commentator concludes.

questions.stimulus: Each oyster filters large volumes of water as it feeds, removing algae as it does so. Every summer, algae blooms in Merrick Bay starve the water of oxygen and kill fish. The state should therefore allow more oyster farms in the bay, since additional farms would reduce the summer blooms.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Oysters remove more algae from the water than does any other kind of shellfish that could be farmed in the bay.
Algae blooms are the only cause of the fish deaths that occur in Merrick Bay each summer.
The oysters on additional farms would remove algae quickly enough to make the summer blooms at least somewhat smaller.
Most of the people who fish in Merrick Bay would support a decision by the state to allow more oyster farms.
Oyster farms in Merrick Bay earn their owners more money than do other kinds of businesses located on the bay.
questions.explanation: Each oyster removes algae, but the plan works only if the added oysters remove enough of it to make a dent in a bay-wide bloom. (C) states that minimal requirement. (B) is the tempting choice, but the argument doesn’t need blooms to be the only cause of fish deaths; reducing one cause is still worth doing. (A) is too strong, and (D) and (E) are about support and profit, not about the blooms.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The state should allow more oyster farms, since they would reduce the summer blooms.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Oysters filter water and remove algae; summer algae blooms kill fish in the bay.

breakdown.analysis: So each oyster eats some algae. Does that mean more farms would shrink a whole bay’s bloom? A teaspoon removes water too, but you can’t bail out a lake with one. The argument needs the added oysters to make a real difference at the scale of the bloom. Prephrase: the new oysters would remove enough algae to make the blooms smaller.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument doesn’t compare oysters to other shellfish. Negate it (some other shellfish removes more algae) and oyster farms could still reduce the blooms.
choices.negation: Oysters do not remove more algae than every other kind of shellfish that could be farmed in the bay.

choices.note: Tempting, because fish deaths are why the blooms matter. But the argument doesn’t need blooms to be the ONLY cause. Negate it: something else also kills fish. Shrinking the blooms would still help. Not required.
choices.negation: Algae blooms are not the only cause of the fish deaths in Merrick Bay each summer.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the new oysters wouldn’t remove algae fast enough to make the blooms any smaller. Then the claim that more farms “would reduce the summer blooms” is false, and the recommendation loses its reason.
choices.negation: The oysters on additional farms would not remove algae quickly enough to make the summer blooms any smaller.

choices.note: Popularity isn’t the issue. The argument is about whether the farms would shrink the blooms. Negate it and nothing changes.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the people who fish in the bay would support allowing more oyster farms.

choices.note: Wrong dimension: money, not algae. Negating it doesn’t touch the argument.
choices.negation: Oyster farms in the bay do not earn more money than other kinds of businesses on the bay.

questions.stimulus: At the Ardley Culinary Institute, only apprentices whose dishes are served at the annual Founders’ Dinner receive the Gold Ladle award. Every apprentice whose dish is served at the Founders’ Dinner has trained under one of the institute’s head chefs. It follows that every apprentice who receives the Gold Ladle this year has worked at least one shift in the institute’s banquet kitchen.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every apprentice who has worked a shift in the banquet kitchen has trained under one of the institute’s head chefs.
Every apprentice who trained under one of the head chefs has worked at least one banquet-kitchen shift.
Some of the apprentices whose dishes are served at the Founders’ Dinner have worked shifts in the banquet kitchen.
Most apprentices who have worked a shift in the banquet kitchen have had dishes served at the Founders’ Dinner.
No apprentice who has not trained under one of the institute’s head chefs has ever received the Gold Ladle award.
questions.explanation: The premises give Gold Ladle → dish served → trained under a head chef. The conclusion ends at “worked a banquet shift,” a term that appears only there, so we need trained under a head chef → worked a banquet shift. That is (B). (A) is the tempting reversal of that bridge, (C) and (D) are too weak, and (E) just restates what the premises already establish.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Every Gold Ladle winner this year has worked a banquet-kitchen shift.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Gold Ladle → dish served at the dinner; dish served → trained under a head chef.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Gold Ladle → Dish served → Trained under head chef → ??? → Banquet shift. The conclusion’s new term is “banquet shift.” It shows up nowhere in the premises. We need a bridge from the last link we have (trained under a head chef) to the new term. Prephrase: everyone who trained under a head chef has worked a banquet shift.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses exactly the two right terms. But it runs backward: Banquet shift → Trained. We need Trained → Banquet shift. Knowing that banquet workers trained under head chefs doesn’t tell us that head-chef trainees worked banquets.
CORRECT. Trained → Banquet shift completes the chain: Gold Ladle → Dish → Trained → Banquet shift.
“Some” is too weak. The Gold Ladle winners could all be among the ones who never worked a banquet shift.
Wrong direction and too weak. It goes from banquet workers toward the dinner, and only for “most.” It doesn’t guarantee anything about the winners.
This is already true given the premises (Gold Ladle → Trained, in contrapositive form). Restating what we know doesn’t add the missing term, “banquet shift.”

questions.stimulus: An online seller should give a buyer a full refund for a returned item if the item was misdescribed in the seller’s listing, or if the buyer sends the item back undamaged within thirty days of its delivery. A seller that follows this policy treats buyers fairly without exposing itself to abuse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Corinne sent back an undamaged lamp forty days after it was delivered, and the lamp’s listing was accurate, so the seller should give her a full refund.
The listing for Abdul’s coat was accurate, but he sent the coat back torn a week after delivery, so the seller should give him a full refund.
The teapot Petra bought was misdescribed in the seller’s listing, so the seller should give her a full refund even if she decides to keep the teapot.
Although Yusuf sent his chair back seven weeks after it was delivered, the listing had misstated its dimensions, so the seller should give him a full refund.
Hana sent back an undamaged rug two weeks after it was delivered, so the seller should give her a full refund only if the rug was misdescribed.
questions.explanation: A returned item earns a full refund if either it was misdescribed or it came back undamaged within thirty days. Yusuf’s chair was returned and misdescribed, so the late return doesn’t matter, as (D) says. (C) is the tempting trap: the misdescription is there, but the principle covers returned items, and Petra may keep hers. (A) and (B) meet neither condition, and (E) adds a requirement the principle doesn’t impose on an undamaged return made within thirty days.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Item returned AND (misdescribed OR undamaged within 30 days) → full refund.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment where a returned item meets at least one of the two conditions and the verdict is a full refund.

breakdown.analysis: This is an “or” rule: either condition is enough. But both conditions sit inside a bigger frame: the item is returned. So the right answer needs: 1. the item comes back; 2. it was misdescribed, OR it came back undamaged within 30 days; 3. the verdict is a full refund. Watch for answers that meet one condition but break the frame, and for answers that pile on extra conditions.

choices.note: Accurate listing, so not misdescribed. Forty days is past thirty. Neither condition is met, so the principle doesn’t support a refund.
Accurate listing, and the coat came back torn. Within a week, yes, but not undamaged. Neither condition is met.
Tempting, since misdescription alone is enough. But the principle is about refunds for returned items. Petra might keep the teapot, and then the rule doesn’t apply. Half-right isn’t right.
CORRECT. The chair was returned and misdescribed. That’s one full condition, so the timing doesn’t matter. Full refund.
Hana returned it undamaged within thirty days, so she already qualifies. This judgment adds a misdescription requirement the principle doesn’t impose. It contradicts the rule instead of following it.

questions.stimulus: Maple producers in Ardane County made far less syrup this spring than they do in a typical year. Sap flows most freely when freezing nights alternate with thawing days, and this March brought far fewer freezing nights than usual. So the scarcity of freezing nights must be what reduced the county’s syrup production this year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: The number of freezing nights in March is the only factor that affects how freely the sap of maple trees flows.
Maple producers in neighboring counties also made less syrup this spring than they do in a typical year.
Next spring is likely to bring more freezing nights to Ardane County than this spring did.
Syrup made from sap collected in a spring with few freezing nights is darker than syrup made in other years.
Ardane County’s producers did not tap substantially fewer maple trees this spring than they do in a typical year.
questions.explanation: The argument blames the weather for a drop in total syrup, so it must assume there wasn’t some other reason the total fell, such as fewer trees being tapped. (E) rules that out. (A) is tempting but too strong: other factors can affect sap flow and the weather could still be what caused this year’s drop. (B) would help a little but isn’t required, and (C) and (D) are irrelevant to the cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Fewer freezing nights reduced the county’s syrup production this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Production was far lower than usual; sap flows best with freeze-thaw cycles; March had far fewer freezing nights.

breakdown.analysis: The weather explanation is plausible, but is it the only one? Total syrup depends on how much sap each tree gives AND how many trees get tapped. If producers tapped half as many trees, production would drop no matter the weather. It’s like blaming a slow sales month on rain when the store was also closed for a week. We need an answer that rules out another cause of the drop. Negate each choice and see if the argument breaks.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like it shores up the weather explanation. But “only factor” is too strong. Negate it: other things also affect sap flow. The freezing nights could still be what caused this year’s drop. Not required.
choices.negation: The number of freezing nights in March is not the only factor that affects how freely maple sap flows.

choices.note: This might corroborate the weather story, but it isn’t required. Negate it: neighbors made normal amounts. Their weather may have been different, so the argument still stands.
choices.negation: Maple producers in neighboring counties did not make less syrup this spring than usual.

choices.note: A prediction about next year has nothing to do with what caused this year’s drop.
choices.negation: Next spring is not likely to bring more freezing nights than this spring did.

choices.note: Syrup color is irrelevant to the amount produced. Negate it and nothing happens.
choices.negation: Syrup made in a spring with few freezing nights is not darker than syrup made in other years.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: producers tapped substantially fewer trees. Now there’s another explanation for the low total, and the weather might not be the cause at all. The argument falls apart.
choices.negation: Ardane County’s producers tapped substantially fewer maple trees this spring than they do in a typical year.

questions.stimulus: A hot-air balloon flight should not be launched if surface winds at its landing site are expected to exceed fifteen kilometers per hour. Whenever a cold front passes through the Arlen Valley, surface winds throughout the valley exceed that speed. So this afternoon’s scheduled flight should not be launched.
questions.stem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: This afternoon’s flight will land in the Arlen Valley, through which a cold front is expected to pass this afternoon.
Whenever surface winds in the Arlen Valley exceed fifteen kilometers per hour, a cold front is passing through the valley.
Most balloon flights that are launched when a cold front is expected end with landings that damage the balloon.
Several balloon pilots in the Arlen Valley have launched flights this year despite forecasts of strong surface winds.
Cold fronts pass through the Arlen Valley more often in the afternoon than at any other time of day.
questions.explanation: Strong winds expected at the landing site → don’t launch, and a cold front in the valley → strong winds there. To reach “don’t launch” for this flight, we need its landing site in the valley and a front expected there, which (A) supplies. (B) is the tempting reversal; it tells us what strong winds indicate, not whether strong winds are coming. (C) and (D) are about outcomes and other pilots, and (E) is a general tendency, not a forecast for today.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: This afternoon’s flight should not be launched.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Winds expected over 15 km/h at landing site → don’t launch; cold front in the valley → winds over 15 km/h in the valley.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Cold front in valley → strong winds in valley → (if you land there) strong winds at landing site → don’t launch. The premises are general. Nothing ties them to this afternoon’s flight. We need two facts about this flight: it lands in the valley, and a front is expected there this afternoon. Then the chain runs straight to “don’t launch.”

choices.note: CORRECT. Landing in the valley + front expected → strong winds expected at the landing site → don’t launch. Every link is in place.
Tempting, because it connects winds and fronts. But it’s the reverse: strong winds → front. We need a reason to expect strong winds this afternoon, and this doesn’t give one.
This adds a new consequence (damaged balloons) instead of placing today’s flight in the chain. We still don’t know whether a front is expected or where the flight lands.
What other pilots did has nothing to do with whether this flight should launch.
“More often in the afternoon” isn’t a forecast for this afternoon. And we still don’t know where the flight lands.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant owner: Our servers should share a portion of their tips with the kitchen staff. Diners decide how much to tip largely on the basis of how good the food was, and it is the cooks, not the servers, who are chiefly responsible for the quality of the food.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the restaurant owner’s argument?
choices: Servers should be paid a wage high enough that their income does not depend on the tips they receive from diners.
Diners ought to base the amount they tip on the quality of the service they receive rather than on the quality of their food.
Workers who are chiefly responsible for what customers are rewarding with a tip should receive a share of that tip.
Cooks should be paid more than servers whenever the cooks’ work takes longer to learn than the servers’ work does.
A restaurant should not require its servers to share tips with others unless a majority of its servers agree to it.
questions.explanation: The owner’s facts are that tips reward the food and the cooks are responsible for the food; the conclusion is that cooks should get part of the tips. (C) links those facts to that verdict. (B) is tempting because it is about what tips should reward, but it pushes against the owner’s reasoning instead of supporting it. (A) and (D) are about wages, and (E) adds a voting condition that would, if anything, block the owner’s proposal.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Servers should share some of their tips with the kitchen staff.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Diners tip mostly based on the food; the cooks are chiefly responsible for the food.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. The conclusion is “cooks get a share of the tips,” and the reason is “the tip is really paying for the cooks’ work.” So the principle is: if your work is what the tip rewards, you should get part of it. It’s like a group project where the teacher praises the slides. The person who made the slides should get the credit.

choices.note: This is about servers’ wages, not about who should get tips. It doesn’t lead to sharing with the kitchen.
Tempting, because it’s about what tips should reward. But it says diners should tip for service, which points toward servers keeping their tips. It works against the owner.
CORRECT. The cooks are chiefly responsible for the food, and the food is what diners reward. So the cooks should get a share. That’s the owner’s conclusion.
Wrong dimension: wages and training time, not tips. It doesn’t justify sharing tips.
This adds a condition (servers must agree) that the owner never addresses, and it would restrict the policy rather than justify it.

questions.stimulus: Luthier: In blind listening tests, professional violinists consistently preferred violins whose tops were carved from spruce cut in winter to violins whose tops were carved from spruce cut in summer. Apart from the wood of their tops, the violins in the tests were identical. So the season in which spruce is cut affects how a violin made from it sounds.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the luthier’s argument depends?
choices: Violins whose tops are carved from winter-cut spruce sell for higher prices than violins made from summer-cut spruce.
The winter-cut and summer-cut spruce in the tests did not come from forests that differ in ways that affect sound.
Professional violinists are better able than amateur players to hear small differences in the sound of violins.
The season in which spruce is cut affects the sound of a violin more than does any other feature of the wood.
Most violin makers who know about the results of the tests now carve violin tops only from spruce cut in winter.
questions.explanation: The tests held everything constant except the wood, but “the wood” differs in more than its cutting season. If the winter wood and summer wood came from forests that produce different-sounding spruce, the forest, not the season, could explain the preference. (B) rules that out. (D) is the tempting too-strong version: the season needn’t be the biggest factor, only a real one. (A), (C) and (E) concern price, amateurs and other makers’ choices.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The season spruce is cut in affects how a violin made from it sounds.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Blind tests: players preferred violins with winter-cut spruce tops; the violins differed only in the wood of their tops.

breakdown.analysis: “Differed only in the wood” sounds airtight. But the wood can differ in more ways than its cutting season. What if all the winter spruce came from one forest and all the summer spruce from another? Then the forest could explain the difference. It’s like comparing summer and winter apples when the winter apples all came from a better orchard. We need an answer that rules out another difference between the two batches of wood.

choices.note: Price isn’t sound. Negate it (winter-spruce violins don’t sell for more) and the test results still point to the season.
choices.negation: Violins with winter-cut spruce tops do not sell for higher prices than violins with summer-cut spruce tops.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the two batches came from forests that differ in ways that affect sound. Now the forest could explain the preference, and the season might do nothing. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The winter-cut and summer-cut spruce used in the tests came from forests that differ in ways that affect sound.

choices.note: The argument doesn’t mention amateurs. Negate it (professionals aren’t better than amateurs at this) and the professionals’ preferences still show a difference in sound.
choices.negation: Professional violinists are not better able than amateur players to hear small differences in sound.

choices.note: Tempting, but too strong. The luthier only says the season has some effect, not the biggest effect. Negate it: some other feature of the wood matters more. The season can still matter. Not required.
choices.negation: The season in which spruce is cut does not affect the sound more than every other feature of the wood does.

choices.note: What other makers do afterward has no bearing on whether the season affects the sound.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most violin makers who know the results now use only winter-cut spruce.

questions.stimulus: Any compost pile whose center stays at 55 degrees Celsius or higher for three days in a row kills the weed seeds it contains. Ruth turned her compost pile once a week throughout the summer. Therefore, the weed seeds in Ruth’s compost pile have been killed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
choices: Every compost pile whose center stays at 55 degrees Celsius or higher for three days in a row has been turned once a week.
Most compost piles that are turned once a week throughout the summer reach 55 degrees Celsius at their centers.
Weed seeds that survive in a compost pile can sprout in any garden where that compost is later spread.
Any compost pile turned weekly all summer has a center that stays at 55 degrees Celsius or higher for three straight days.
Ruth’s compost pile contained fewer weed seeds at the end of the summer than it contained at the beginning of it.
questions.explanation: The premise says hot for three days → seeds killed, and we only know Ruth turned her pile weekly. We need turned weekly → hot for three days, which (D) supplies. (A) is the tempting reversal; it runs from heat to turning. (B) is too weak twice over (“most,” and reaching 55 degrees isn’t staying there three days), (C) is about what happens afterward, and (E) allows some seeds to survive.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The weed seeds in Ruth’s pile have been killed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Center at 55°C+ for three days in a row → seeds killed; Ruth turned her pile weekly all summer.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Turned weekly → ??? → Hot for 3 days → Seeds killed. “Turned weekly” appears only in the premise about Ruth; “hot for 3 days” only in the rule. Bridge them: every pile turned weekly stays hot for three days. Then Ruth’s pile was hot, so its seeds are dead.

choices.note: Tempting, since it links the right two ideas. But it runs Hot → Turned. We need Turned → Hot. Knowing that hot piles were turned doesn’t tell us that Ruth’s turned pile got hot.
Too weak. “Most” piles leaves room for Ruth’s to be an exception. And reaching 55°C isn’t the same as staying there for three days in a row.
Irrelevant. This is about what surviving seeds might do later, not about whether Ruth’s seeds were killed.
CORRECT. Turned weekly → stays hot for three days → seeds killed. Ruth’s pile was turned weekly, so the conclusion follows.
Fewer seeds isn’t zero seeds. Some could still be alive, so this doesn’t prove they’ve been killed.

questions.stimulus: A person should be listed as an author of a scientific paper only if that person helped to design the research the paper reports or helped to write the paper itself. People who contributed to the research in other ways, however valuable their contributions, should instead be thanked in the paper’s acknowledgments.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Because Ana helped to write the paper on soil bacteria, she should be listed as one of that paper’s authors.
Because Dev designed the experiment but did not help to write the report, he should be thanked in the acknowledgments rather than listed as an author.
Because Mira supplied the funding for the study, she should be listed as an author, since without her the research could not have been done.
Because Lars both helped to design the study and helped to write the paper, he should be listed as the paper’s first author.
Because Rui only collected data, without helping to design the study or to write the paper, he should not be listed as an author.
questions.explanation: “Only if” makes designing or writing a requirement for authorship: author → designed or wrote. Rui did neither, so he shouldn’t be listed, as (E) says. (A) is the tempting reversal; meeting a necessary condition doesn’t guarantee authorship. (B) contradicts the principle, since designing qualifies Dev’s work as more than an “other” contribution, (C) lists someone who did neither, and (D) ranks authors, which the principle never addresses.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Listed as author → helped design OR helped write. Contrapositive: did neither → not listed.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment that follows: someone who neither designed nor wrote should not be listed.

breakdown.analysis: “Only if” introduces a necessary condition. Author → (design OR write). So the rule can tell you who should NOT be an author (anyone who did neither), but it never tells you who SHOULD be. It’s like “you can vote only if you’re registered.” Being registered doesn’t mean you voted. The right answer must 1. describe someone who neither designed nor wrote, and 2. conclude they shouldn’t be listed.

choices.note: Tempting, since Ana meets the condition. But meeting a necessary condition isn’t enough. “Only if” doesn’t work in reverse. The principle never says who must be listed.
This contradicts the principle. Designing the research is one of the two qualifying contributions, so Dev’s design work isn’t one of the “other ways” that belong in the acknowledgments.
Mira neither designed nor wrote, so the principle says she should NOT be listed. This judgment goes the opposite way.
The principle says nothing about author order. “First author” goes beyond the rule.
CORRECT. Rui did neither, so by the contrapositive he shouldn’t be listed. This is exactly the verdict the principle produces.

questions.stimulus: The rusty skimmer, a dragonfly, lays its eggs only in ponds that contain no fish. Ten years ago, every pond in the Orrel Heath preserve was stocked with trout. So the rusty skimmer does not currently lay its eggs anywhere in the Orrel Heath preserve.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
choices: Trout eat the larvae of rusty skimmers whenever those larvae are present in the ponds where the trout live.
Every pond that is now in the Orrel Heath preserve still contains at least some fish.
Most of the ponds in the Orrel Heath preserve that were stocked with trout ten years ago still contain trout.
Rusty skimmers laid their eggs in many of the preserve’s ponds before those ponds were stocked with trout.
Every pond in which rusty skimmers lay their eggs is a pond that contains no fish of any kind.
questions.explanation: Skimmers lay eggs only in fish-free ponds, so they lay none in the preserve if no pond there is now fish-free. The premises only say the ponds were stocked ten years ago; fish could have died out since, or new ponds could have formed. (B) closes both holes. (C) is the tempting but too-weak version, since the leftover ponds could be fish-free, and (E) merely restates the first premise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rusty skimmers don’t currently lay eggs anywhere in the preserve.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Skimmer lays eggs → pond has no fish; every pond in the preserve was stocked with trout ten years ago.

breakdown.analysis: Lays eggs here → fish-free pond. Contrapositive: no fish-free pond → no eggs. So we need: there’s no fish-free pond in the preserve now. But the premise is ten years old. Did the trout survive? Has a new pond formed since? Stocked then isn’t the same as fish now. It’s like saying “every apartment was rented in 2015, so none is vacant today.” Prephrase: every pond in the preserve now has fish.

choices.note: This explains why skimmers avoid fish, but it doesn’t tell us any pond still has fish. If some pond lost its trout, skimmers could breed there.
CORRECT. Every current pond has fish → no fish-free pond → no skimmer eggs anywhere in the preserve. It handles both the trout dying out and new ponds.
Tempting, because it updates the ten-year-old fact. But “most” leaves some ponds possibly fish-free, and skimmers could lay eggs in those. Too weak for a sufficient assumption.
History. What skimmers did before the stocking says nothing about whether the ponds have fish today.
This just restates the first premise. It adds nothing about whether the preserve’s ponds have fish now.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: A company that advertises a product as ‘handmade’ deceives its customers if machines perform any step in making the product that those customers believe is done by hand. Velloway Candles advertises its candles as handmade, but it uses a machine to pour the melted wax into molds. Therefore, Velloway deceives its customers.
questions.stem: The ethicist’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Velloway’s customers believe that the melted wax for its candles is poured into the molds by hand.
Some of Velloway’s customers believe that at least one step in making its candles is done by hand.
Velloway’s customers would be less willing to buy its candles if they knew that a machine pours the wax.
Pouring melted wax into molds is a step that machines perform more consistently than people do.
Most companies that advertise their candles as handmade use machines for at least one step in making them.
questions.explanation: Deception requires a machine step that the customers believe is done by hand. We know a machine pours the wax, so we need the customers to believe the pouring is done by hand, which is (A). (B) is the tempting weak version: a belief that some step is handmade could be about a step that really is done by hand. (C) concerns motive, not deception, and (D) and (E) are irrelevant comparisons.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velloway deceives its customers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Advertised as handmade AND a machine does a step customers believe is done by hand → deceives; Velloway advertises “handmade” and a machine pours the wax.

breakdown.analysis: The rule needs three things: 1. “handmade” advertising (yes); 2. a step done by machine (yes, pouring); 3. customers believe that same step is done by hand (missing). Prephrase: Velloway’s customers believe the pouring is done by hand. Careful: the belief has to match the machine step. A belief about some other step doesn’t count.

choices.note: CORRECT. Now all three conditions are met for the pouring step, so by the rule, Velloway deceives its customers.
Tempting, but too weak twice. It’s “some” customers, and it’s “at least one step.” That step might be wicking or packing, done by hand for real. It doesn’t link the belief to the machine step.
This is about what customers would do if they knew, not about what they believe. The rule turns on belief, so this doesn’t trigger it.
Irrelevant comparison. Whether machines pour more consistently has nothing to do with deception.
What other companies do doesn’t tell us what Velloway’s customers believe.

questions.stimulus: The bronze coin unearthed last month at the Avel site bears the seal of the mint at Tirra. Historical records show that the Tirra mint closed permanently in the year 410 and never reopened. So the coin must have been made no later than 410.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every coin that was made at the Tirra mint before the mint closed bears the mint’s seal.
Few coins bearing the Tirra seal have been found at sites as far from Tirra as the Avel site is.
No coin bearing the seal of the Tirra mint was made anywhere other than at that mint.
Most coins bearing the Tirra seal that experts have examined turned out to be genuine products of that mint.
The Avel site was inhabited during the years in which the Tirra mint was still producing coins.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from “bears the Tirra seal” to “made at the Tirra mint,” and that move fails if someone else, such as a later forger, could have stamped the seal. (C) closes the gap: seal → made at the mint, and the mint stopped working in 410. (A) is the tempting reversal (made at the mint → seal). (D) is too weak, since “most” leaves room for this coin to be a copy, and (E) only shows the coin could be early.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The coin was made no later than 410.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The coin bears the Tirra mint’s seal; the mint closed for good in 410.

breakdown.analysis: So it has the seal. Does that mean the Tirra mint made it? Someone could have copied the seal later. A designer logo on a handbag doesn’t prove the designer made the bag. The argument needs: seal → made at the Tirra mint. Then, since the mint stopped in 410, the coin is from 410 or earlier.

choices.note: Tempting, because it ties the mint and the seal together. But it runs Made at Tirra → Seal. We need Seal → Made at Tirra. Every genuine coin having the seal doesn’t stop fakes from having it too.
Rarity at distant sites doesn’t tell us when this coin was made.
CORRECT. Seal → made at the Tirra mint → made while it was open → no later than 410.
Too weak. “Most” examined coins were genuine leaves room for this one to be a later copy. A sufficient assumption has to guarantee the conclusion.
Being inhabited back then makes an early date possible, but it doesn’t rule out a later date.

questions.stimulus: Every mushroom species that grows on fallen birch trunks in the Larrow Woods is safe to eat. All of the mushrooms Odette gathered this morning belong to the white-gilled species that she found growing beside the stream. So all of the mushrooms Odette gathered this morning are safe to eat.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Some of the mushrooms Odette gathered this morning were growing on fallen birch trunks lying beside the stream.
Every mushroom species in the Larrow Woods that is safe to eat is one that grows on fallen birch trunks.
The stream beside which Odette found the white-gilled species runs through the middle of the Larrow Woods.
Odette has never gathered a mushroom that later turned out to be unsafe for anyone to eat.
The white-gilled species Odette found beside the stream is one that grows on fallen birch trunks in the Larrow Woods.
questions.explanation: The rule is about species: grows on fallen birch in the Larrow Woods → safe. Odette’s mushrooms are all one species, so we need that species to be one that grows on fallen birch in the Larrow Woods, which is (E). (A) is the tempting choice, but it says only that some of her mushrooms grew on birch, and the stream may not even be in the Larrow Woods. (B) reverses the rule, and (C) places the stream without linking the species to birch.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: All the mushrooms Odette gathered are safe to eat.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Species grows on fallen birch in Larrow Woods → safe; all of Odette’s mushrooms are the white-gilled species from the stream.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Odette’s mushrooms → white-gilled species → ??? → grows on fallen birch in Larrow Woods → safe. The missing link is between “the white-gilled species” and “grows on fallen birch in the Larrow Woods.” Notice the rule is about species, not individual mushrooms, and it’s about the Larrow Woods specifically. Prephrase: the white-gilled species is one that grows on fallen birch in the Larrow Woods.

choices.note: Tempting, because it mentions fallen birch. But we don’t know the stream is in the Larrow Woods, and the rule is about species anyway. Saying some of her mushrooms grew on birch somewhere doesn’t place the species in the rule.
This reverses the rule: Safe → grows on birch. It tells us nothing about whether the white-gilled species is safe.
Location alone isn’t enough. Even if the stream is in the Larrow Woods, we don’t know the white-gilled species grows on fallen birch.
Her track record isn’t proof. Past luck can’t guarantee that this morning’s mushrooms are safe.
CORRECT. The white-gilled species grows on fallen birch in the Larrow Woods → it’s safe → all of Odette’s mushrooms, which belong to it, are safe.

questions.stimulus: Heritage fund officer: Our fund will pay to restore a historic pipe organ only if the restoration keeps the organ’s original pipes. Old organ pipes sound properly only at the wind pressure for which they were originally made, and the restoration proposed for the organ at St. Aldric’s would raise its wind pressure well above that level. So our fund will not pay for that restoration.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the heritage fund officer’s argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any restoration after which an organ’s original pipes would sound properly counts as one that keeps the organ’s original pipes.
Most restorations that raise an organ’s wind pressure leave at least some of the organ’s original pipes unable to sound properly.
The fund has in the past refused to pay for restorations that would have raised an organ’s wind pressure.
A restoration does not keep an organ’s original pipes if those pipes would no longer sound properly once it is finished.
The only change that the proposed restoration would make to the organ at St. Aldric’s is to raise its wind pressure.
questions.explanation: The premises give: raise pressure → pipes won’t sound properly, and fund pays → original pipes kept. The gap is between “won’t sound properly” and “not kept,” and (D) bridges it in that direction, so the chain runs to “no payment.” Most students pick (A) because it links the same two ideas, but it runs the other way (sounds properly → kept), and its contrapositive (not kept → won’t sound properly) never yields “not kept.” (B) is too weak, and (C) and (E) don’t connect the pipes’ sound to keeping them.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The fund will not pay for the St. Aldric’s restoration.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Fund pays → original pipes kept; pipes sound properly → original wind pressure; the restoration raises the pressure well above the original.

breakdown.analysis: What’s the sneaky gap? The pipes stay physically in the organ, so in what sense aren’t they “kept”? The argument needs a link from “won’t sound properly” to “not kept.” Chain it: Raise pressure → won’t sound properly → ??? → not kept → fund won’t pay. (The last step is the contrapositive of Pays → Kept.) Prephrase: if the pipes won’t sound properly after a restoration, that restoration doesn’t count as keeping them. Watch the direction. The trap here uses the same two terms with the arrow reversed.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it because it pairs “sound properly” with “keeps the pipes.” But it says Sound properly → Kept. Its contrapositive is Not kept → won’t sound properly. We need Won’t sound properly → Not kept. This version never gets us to “not kept,” so it never gets us to “won’t pay.”
Too weak. “Most” restorations, and only “some” pipes. Even if it applies here, we still need a link from bad-sounding pipes to “not kept.”
Past refusals don’t guarantee anything about this decision. The fund’s rule turns on keeping the pipes, and this doesn’t connect to that.
CORRECT. Won’t sound properly → not kept. Chain: raise pressure → won’t sound properly → not kept → fund won’t pay. The conclusion is guaranteed.
Irrelevant. Knowing raising the pressure is the only change doesn’t tell us whether the restoration keeps the original pipes.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: Gray rock lizards on Selwin Island spend far less time basking in the sun than gray rock lizards on the nearby mainland. Some researchers attribute this to the island’s many hawks, which prey on basking lizards. But on the island’s northern cliffs, where no hawks nest or hunt, the lizards bask just as little as they do elsewhere on the island. So the hawks are not the reason island lizards bask less.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the biologist’s argument depends?
choices: It is not the case that the cliff lizards bask little mainly because of a trait inherited from ancestors that hawks preyed upon.
Island lizards bask less than mainland lizards do mainly because air temperatures on Selwin Island are higher than on the mainland throughout the year.
Hawks on Selwin Island catch more gray rock lizards each year than do all of the island’s other predators combined.
On the mainland, gray rock lizards bask less in areas where hawks nest than they do in areas where hawks are absent.
The northern cliffs are home to more gray rock lizards than is any other part of Selwin Island.
questions.explanation: The biologist treats the hawk-free cliffs as a control: lizards there bask little without hawks, so hawks aren’t the reason. But if the cliff lizards’ caution is inherited from ancestors shaped by hawk predation, hawks are still the reason, just not the hawks living there now. (A) denies this. Most students pick (B) because it gives a tidy alternative explanation that supports the biologist; but negating it changes nothing, so it is helpful, not required. (C) and (E) are irrelevant, and (D) would, if anything, support the researchers.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Hawks are not the reason island lizards bask less than mainland lizards.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Researchers blame hawks; on the northern cliffs, with no hawks, lizards bask just as little as elsewhere on the island.

breakdown.analysis: The cliffs look like a perfect control group: no hawks, same low basking, so hawks don’t matter. But does a hawk-free cliff today mean the lizards there are free of hawk influence? Their behavior could be built in, inherited from ancestors that lived with hawks. It’s like a family that still locks every door though they moved from a high-crime city to a safe village. Crime is still why they lock up. The obvious gap (hawks hunting there anyway) is already closed by “no hawks nest or hunt.” So the hidden gap is history. We need: the cliff lizards’ low basking isn’t a hawk-shaped inheritance.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the cliff lizards bask little mainly because of a trait inherited from hawk-hunted ancestors. Then hawk predation IS the reason, and the cliffs prove nothing. The argument collapses. Note the defender form: it just rules out one way the cliffs could mislead.
choices.negation: The cliff lizards bask little mainly because of a trait inherited from ancestors that hawks preyed upon.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it. It gives a neat alternative cause, so it would strengthen the biologist a lot. But it isn’t required. Negate it: warmer air isn’t the reason. The argument never relied on any particular alternative; it only claims hawks aren’t the cause. Helpful isn’t necessary.
choices.negation: Island lizards do not bask less than mainland lizards because of higher air temperatures on the island.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How many lizards hawks catch compared with other predators doesn’t tell us whether hawks explain the basking difference.
choices.negation: Hawks on the island do not catch more lizards than all the island’s other predators combined.

choices.note: This would support the researchers’ hawk theory, so it isn’t something the biologist assumes. Negating it only helps the biologist.
choices.negation: On the mainland, lizards do not bask less where hawks nest than where hawks are absent.

choices.note: Population size on the cliffs doesn’t matter. The comparison works whether the cliffs hold many lizards or few.
choices.negation: The northern cliffs are not home to more lizards than every other part of the island.

questions.stimulus: Journal editor: Admittedly, the reviewers we consulted found no errors in Dr. Okoye’s paper, and her earlier work has always held up. Nonetheless, we should not publish the paper. Its central result depends entirely on a data set that Dr. Okoye has declined to share, so no researcher outside her laboratory has any way to check that result.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the journal editor’s reasoning?
choices: A journal should publish any paper in which its reviewers find no errors, provided that the paper’s data are available to other researchers.
Only papers whose central results can be checked by researchers outside the authors’ own laboratories should be published.
Researchers ought to share the data underlying their published findings with any qualified researcher who asks to see those data.
A journal should give more weight to the findings of its reviewers than to the reputation of a paper’s author.
A paper whose central result conflicts with earlier findings should not be published until that result has been independently replicated.
questions.explanation: The editor’s verdict is “don’t publish,” and the reason is that no outside researcher can check the central result. (B) makes outside checkability a necessary condition for publication, so the paper fails it. Most students pick (C) because it captures the editor’s complaint about withholding data, but it tells researchers what to do and says nothing about what a journal should publish. (A) reverses the logic, giving conditions for publishing; (D) would favor publication; and (E) depends on a conflict with earlier findings that the editor never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The journal should not publish Dr. Okoye’s paper.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Concession: reviewers found no errors and her past work held up. But: the central result rests on unshared data, so no outside researcher can check it.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, and the conclusion is about the journal: don’t publish. The reason is “no one outside her lab can check the result.” So we need: can’t be checked from outside → don’t publish. In “only” form: published → checkable from outside. The concession (no errors, good track record) is there to tempt you toward principles about reviews and reputation. The reason that does the work is checkability.

choices.note: This reverses the direction. It says when to publish (no errors AND shared data). Okoye’s data aren’t shared, so this rule is silent. It can’t produce “don’t publish.”

CORRECT. “Only” marks the necessary condition: published → checkable from outside. Contrapositive: not checkable → not published. Okoye’s result can’t be checked from outside, so the journal shouldn’t publish. The “only” form hides it a bit, but it’s exactly the editor’s step.

Tempting, and most students pick it because it matches the editor’s frustration with Okoye. But look at who the rule is about: researchers, not journals. It says Okoye ought to share. It says nothing about whether a journal should publish a paper when she doesn’t.
This would point toward publishing, since the reviewers found no errors. It works against the editor.
