Partial match. It needs a conflict with earlier findings, and the editor never says the result conflicts with anything.

questions.stimulus: Public works director: Last winter, for the first time, we treated the city’s residential streets with a brine spray instead of rock salt, and accidents on those streets fell by a third compared with the winter before. Some attribute the decline to light snowfall last winter, but last winter’s snowfall was in fact about average for the city. So the brine spray deserves the credit.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the public works director’s argument?
choices: Accidents on the city’s main roads, which were treated with rock salt both winters, became more frequent last winter.
Brine spray costs the city less per kilometer of street treated than rock salt did in previous winters.
Most residents who drive on the city’s residential streets noticed that those streets were less icy last winter.
Brine spray prevents ice from forming on streets more effectively than rock salt does at every temperature.
It is not the case that the winter before last brought the city far more snowfall than an average winter does.
questions.explanation: The director rebuts the weather explanation by showing last winter was average, but the comparison is with the winter before. If that winter was unusually snowy, an average winter would produce fewer accidents with no help from brine. (E) rules this out. Most students pick (A) because a rise on the rock-salt roads would be a convincing control; but negating it (main-road accidents didn’t rise) does no damage, so it is sufficient-style support, not a requirement. (B) is about cost, (C) is helpful but not needed, and (D) is far too strong.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The brine spray caused the drop in residential-street accidents.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Accidents fell by a third compared with the previous winter; critics blame light snow, but last winter’s snowfall was about average.

breakdown.analysis: The director answers “it was a light winter” with “no, it was average.” Average compared to what? The accident drop is measured against the winter before. If that one was a monster winter, then going from terrible to average would cut accidents with no help from brine. It’s like crediting a new tutor for a jump in test scores when last year’s test fell during a week you had the flu. The obvious weather objection is answered; the hidden one sits in the comparison year. We need: the winter before wasn’t far snowier than average.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it. A rise on the rock-salt roads would be a great control group. But required? Negate it: main-road accidents didn’t rise (maybe they held steady). That doesn’t show the brine did nothing. It’s support that would help, not an assumption the argument needs.
choices.negation: Accidents on the city’s main roads did not become more frequent last winter.

choices.note: Cost has nothing to do with whether brine caused the drop.
choices.negation: Brine spray does not cost less per kilometer than rock salt did.

choices.note: This would be nice corroboration, but it isn’t required. Residents might not notice how icy the streets are, and the brine could still have worked.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most residents noticed that the streets were less icy last winter.

choices.note: Too strong. Brine needn’t beat salt at every temperature, only enough to explain last winter’s drop. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: Brine spray does not prevent ice more effectively than rock salt at every temperature.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the winter before last brought far more snow than average. Then the drop in accidents could be just a return to normal weather, and the brine gets no credit. The argument collapses. Note the defender form: it closes the one weather loophole the director’s rebuttal left open.
choices.negation: The winter before last brought the city far more snowfall than an average winter does.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A graduate student who has completed at least one year of study should receive a travel stipend to attend a conference if the student will present a paper there or serves on the conference’s organizing committee, but in either case only if the student has not received a stipend within the past two years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?
choices: Noor, a third-year graduate student, will present a paper at a conference this spring, and although she received a stipend last year, she should receive another one now.
Felix, who began graduate study four months ago, will present a paper at a conference and has never received a stipend, so he should receive one.
Although Ines will not present a paper at the Calder conference, she is a second-year student on its organizing committee who has never had a stipend, so she should receive one.
Bram, a fourth-year student, has received no stipend in three years, but since he will neither present a paper nor serve as an organizer, he should not receive one.
Tova, a second-year graduate student, will present a paper at a conference, so she should receive a stipend if she also serves on its organizing committee.
questions.explanation: A stipend is warranted when the student 1. has a year of study, 2. presents or organizes, and 3. has had no stipend in two years. Ines meets all three, and not presenting doesn’t matter because organizing is an alternative; that is (C). Most students pick (D) because every fact in it is correct, but the principle only says when a student should get a stipend and never when one should be denied, so (D)’s verdict has no support. (A) violates the two-year limit, (B) the one-year requirement, and (E) leaves the stipend history unknown.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: 1+ year of study AND (presents OR organizes) AND no stipend in past 2 years → should receive a stipend. Also: should receive → no stipend in past 2 years.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment that meets every condition and concludes the student should get a stipend, or that denies a stipend only on the two-year ground.

breakdown.analysis: List the conditions the right answer must satisfy: 1. at least one year of study; 2. presents a paper OR serves as an organizer (either one is enough); 3. no stipend in the past two years; 4. verdict: should receive. The principle’s “only if” also lets you deny a stipend to someone who got one recently, but nothing else in the rule ever says “should not receive.” So any answer that denies a stipend for some other reason is going beyond the rule. Watch for answers that open with a fact that sounds disqualifying but isn’t.

choices.note: Noor got a stipend last year, so she fails the two-year condition. The principle says she should NOT receive one now. This judgment contradicts it.
Four months isn’t a year of study. Felix fails the first condition, so the principle doesn’t support a stipend.

CORRECT. Second-year: condition 1 met. Organizer: condition 2 met (presenting isn’t required, since it’s an “or”). Never had a stipend: condition 3 met. Verdict: should receive. The opening “will not present” is bait; it doesn’t matter.

Tempting, and most students pick it: every fact is right and Bram doesn’t qualify. But failing to qualify isn’t the same as being disqualified. The principle never says when a student should not receive a stipend, except when one was received within two years, and Bram hasn’t had one. So “should not receive” goes beyond the rule.

We don’t know whether Tova received a stipend in the past two years, so the verdict isn’t supported. And making the stipend depend on organizing adds a condition she doesn’t need, since presenting is already enough.

questions.stimulus: Five years ago, 40 percent of the tea harvested in the Darjan hills was sold abroad. Last year, 60 percent of the Darjan harvest was sold abroad, even though several new tea-growing regions now compete for foreign buyers. Clearly, then, the amount of Darjan tea sold abroad has grown over the past five years.
questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: The total amount of tea harvested in the Darjan hills did not decline at all over the past five years.
Foreign buyers generally prefer Darjan tea to the tea produced in the newer tea-growing regions.
Less Darjan tea was consumed within the Darjan region last year than was consumed there five years ago.
Last year’s Darjan harvest was not less than two-thirds the size of the Darjan harvest five years earlier.
The price that foreign buyers pay for Darjan tea has risen over the past five years.
questions.explanation: A bigger share of a smaller harvest can be a smaller amount. With a harvest of H then and h now, the amount sold abroad grows only if 0.6h is more than 0.4H, that is, if h is more than two-thirds of H. (D) states that minimal requirement. Most students pick (A) because “the harvest didn’t shrink” is the natural prephrase; but the argument survives a modest decline (say 10 percent), so (A) would be enough without being required. negating (C) would only help the argument; (B) and (E) are irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The amount of Darjan tea sold abroad has grown.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The share sold abroad went from 40 percent of the harvest to 60 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Percent isn’t amount. 60 percent of a small pie can be less than 40 percent of a big pie. Run numbers: harvest of 100 tons five years ago means 40 tons abroad. Last year, for 60 percent to beat 40 tons, the harvest must exceed 66.7 tons. A harvest of 60 tons gives only 36 tons abroad. So the argument needs: the harvest didn’t fall below two-thirds of what it was. Notice how little that is. It doesn’t need the harvest to stay level. This is the classic percentage-vs-amount gap; know it.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it, because “the harvest didn’t shrink” is the obvious prephrase. But it’s stronger than needed. Negate it: the harvest fell a little, say from 100 to 90 tons. Then 54 tons went abroad versus 40, and the conclusion holds. Sufficient, not necessary.
choices.negation: The total amount of tea harvested in the Darjan hills declined at least somewhat over the past five years.

choices.note: Buyer preference doesn’t tell us whether the amount sold abroad went up. Negate it and the numbers still decide the question.
choices.negation: Foreign buyers do not generally prefer Darjan tea to tea from the newer regions.

choices.note: Not required. Negate it: local consumption didn’t fall. The local share dropped from 60 to 40 percent, so that could happen only if the harvest grew by at least half, which makes the amount sold abroad even bigger. Negating it helps the argument.
choices.negation: It is not the case that less Darjan tea was consumed in the region last year than five years ago.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: last year’s harvest was less than two-thirds the earlier one. Then 60 percent of it is less than 40 percent of the earlier harvest, and the amount sold abroad fell. The conclusion is false. This is the minimal condition.
choices.negation: Last year’s Darjan harvest was less than two-thirds the size of the harvest five years earlier.

choices.note: Price is a different dimension from amount. Negate it and the argument is unaffected.
choices.negation: The price foreign buyers pay for Darjan tea has not risen over the past five years.

questions.stimulus: Under the rules of the Fenmoor Herding Association, no dog may compete in the open class at its sheepdog trials unless the dog has placed in a novice trial. Every dog that has placed in a novice trial within the past two years is eligible for the association’s breeding registry. Brack is not eligible for the registry. So Brack may not compete in this year’s open class.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Brack has not competed in any novice trial that was held more than two years ago.
Brack has not placed in any novice trial that was held during the past two years.
Every dog that is eligible for the association’s breeding registry has placed in a novice trial within the past two years.
Most dogs that compete in the open class have placed in a novice trial at some point within the past two years.
Dogs that placed in a novice trial more than two years ago rarely go on to compete in the open class.
questions.explanation: Not eligible → hasn’t placed in a novice trial in the past two years, but Brack could still have placed in one earlier, and any placing qualifies a dog for the open class. (A) closes that door indirectly: a dog that never competed in an older novice trial can’t have placed in one. Most students pick (B), but it is already implied by the premises, so it adds nothing; Brack’s old placings are still unaccounted for. (C) reverses the registry rule, and (D) and (E) are too weak.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brack may not compete in this year’s open class.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Open class → placed in a novice trial (ever); placed in past 2 years → eligible for registry; Brack is not eligible.

breakdown.analysis: Contrapositive of the registry rule: Not eligible → didn’t place in the past two years. So Brack hasn’t placed recently. But the open-class rule asks whether he ever placed, at any time. The gap is the window more than two years back. We need Brack to have no older placing either. It’s like a store that gives a discount to anyone who has ever been a member: knowing you haven’t been a member this year doesn’t settle it. Look for an answer that rules out an old placing, possibly in disguise.

choices.note: CORRECT. If Brack never competed in a novice trial more than two years ago, he can’t have placed in one. Add the premises (no placing in the past two years) and he never placed at all, so he can’t enter the open class. It’s phrased as “competed” rather than “placed,” which hides it, but it’s even stronger than we need.

Tempting, and most students pick it, because it sounds exactly like what’s missing. But the premises already give us this: not eligible → no placing in the past two years. Restating it adds nothing. The older placings are still unaccounted for.
This reverses the registry rule (Eligible → placed recently). Brack isn’t eligible, so this tells us nothing about him.
“Most” open-class dogs is too weak, and it’s about recent placings, which Brack lacks anyway. It doesn’t rule out a dog with an older placing competing.
“Rarely” isn’t “never.” Brack could be one of the rare ones with an old placing who does compete.

questions.stimulus: Crowdfunding platform spokesperson: The backers of the Lumen desk lamp project are not entitled to refunds, even though the lamps reached them more than a year late. The project’s creators told backers about each delay as soon as they learned of it, and the lamps that were finally delivered matched the original description in every respect.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the spokesperson’s reasoning?
choices: If the creators of a crowdfunded project hide problems from backers or deliver something other than what they had described, the backers are entitled to refunds.
The creators of a crowdfunded project should tell backers about any delay in the project as soon as they learn of it.
Backers of a crowdfunded project are entitled to a refund if the product is delivered more than two years after its promised date.
People who back a crowdfunded project should recognize that they are taking a risk and should not expect the product to arrive on time.
Unless the creators of a crowdfunded project withheld information from backers or delivered something different from what they described, the backers are not entitled to refunds.
questions.explanation: The spokesperson concludes “no refunds” from two facts: nothing was withheld and the product matched its description. (E) says that unless one of those things went wrong, backers are not entitled to refunds, so the verdict follows. Most students pick (A) because it names exactly the same two conditions, but it states when refunds are owed, and its conditions aren’t met here, so it is silent about this case. (B) is a duty of creators, (C) is silent about a one-year delay, and (D) is about expectations rather than entitlement.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Lumen backers are not entitled to refunds.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lamps were over a year late, but the creators disclosed each delay promptly, and the lamps matched the description.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says: no refunds. The facts are “no hiding, no mismatch.” So we need: no hiding AND no mismatch → no refund. In “unless” form: no refund unless they hid something or delivered something different. The trap is the same two conditions pointing the other way: hiding or mismatch → refund. That rule never tells you what happens when neither occurred. Watch the arrow.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it: same two conditions, same topic. But it says (hide OR mismatch) → refund. Here neither happened, so this rule is silent. It can’t produce “not entitled.” That’s a reversed conditional.
This is a duty creators have, and these creators met it. It doesn’t say what follows for refunds.
Silent here: the lamps were about a year late, not two. A rule granting refunds above two years doesn’t deny them below it.
This is about what backers should expect, not what they’re entitled to. Expecting a delay doesn’t mean you have no claim to a refund.

CORRECT. “Unless” form: refund → (withheld OR mismatch). Contrapositive: nothing withheld AND no mismatch → no refund. Both facts hold, so backers aren’t entitled. Exactly the spokesperson’s conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Policy analyst: The government’s new subsidy for rural broadband service will not slow the movement of people from rural towns to cities. Surveys show that people who have left rural towns overwhelmingly cite a lack of jobs, not poor internet service, as their reason for leaving. Better internet service would no doubt make rural life more convenient, but convenience is not what those who leave are seeking.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the policy analyst’s argument?
choices: Most people who have left rural towns for cities would have stayed if suitable jobs had been available near their homes.
The broadband subsidy will cost more per rural household than any other program designed to slow rural migration.
Poor internet service is the reason that rural residents give least often when asked why they are moving to cities.
Better internet service would not enable any rural residents who would otherwise leave for lack of work to find work without moving.
A lack of jobs is the only reason for which the residents of rural towns ever decide to leave their towns and move to cities.
questions.explanation: The analyst assumes that because people leave for jobs rather than for internet service, better service can’t keep them. But better service could bring the jobs, through remote work or new local businesses, and then it would slow migration. (D) denies that. It sounds strong, but the conclusion is absolute (“will not slow”), so even a few people kept home would sink it. Most students pick (E) or (A), which echo “jobs”; but (E) is far too strong, and negating either does no harm. (B) and (C) are irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The broadband subsidy will not slow migration from rural towns to cities.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Leavers cite lack of jobs, not poor internet, as their reason; better internet would only make rural life more convenient.

breakdown.analysis: People leave because of jobs, not internet. Fine. But can internet affect jobs? Remote work, online businesses, new employers who need fast connections. If broadband creates work, it attacks the very reason people leave. It’s like saying “people quit the gym because of the hours, not the parking, so a new parking lot won’t help” when the new lot lets the gym stay open later. The analyst assumes internet and jobs are separate. We need: better service won’t let would-be leavers find work at home. Note: the conclusion is absolute, so the assumption can be strong too.

choices.note: Tempting, because it backs up the survey’s focus on jobs. But it isn’t required. Negate it: most leavers wouldn’t have stayed even with jobs. That doesn’t make the subsidy any more likely to slow migration. Not needed.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most people who have left would have stayed if suitable jobs had been available.

choices.note: Cost compared with other programs has nothing to do with whether this one slows migration.
choices.negation: The subsidy will not cost more per household than every other program designed to slow migration.

choices.note: Too specific. Internet service needn’t be the least-cited reason; the argument only needs it not to be the main one. Negate it and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: Poor internet service is not the reason rural residents give least often.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: better internet service would let some would-be leavers find work without moving. Then the subsidy slows migration, and the conclusion is false. Strong wording is fine here because the conclusion (“will not slow”) is absolute.
choices.negation: Better internet service would enable at least some rural residents who would otherwise leave for lack of work to find work without moving.

choices.note: Tempting, since it echoes “jobs,” but way too strong. Negate it: some people move for other reasons too, like family or schools. The argument survives. And even if it were true, the analyst would still need internet service not to create jobs.
choices.negation: A lack of jobs is not the only reason that rural residents ever move to cities.

questions.stimulus: It is wrong for anyone to accept a gift from a person whose application he or she will soon be deciding on, unless every other applicant seeking the same decision has been told about the gift beforehand. Without such disclosure, the other applicants have no way to raise concerns about the fairness of the decision.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle stated above?
choices: Before choosing among applicants for a studio lease, Renata accepted a gift from one applicant but first told every other applicant about it, so accepting the gift was not wrong.
Tomas accepted wine from a candidate whose application he would decide on the next day and told his fellow managers but no other candidate, so he acted wrongly.
Ilse accepted a gift from an applicant whose application she had already rejected, without telling any other applicant, so her accepting the gift was wrong.
Because Omar told no one that a contractor whose bid he would soon review had given him a gift, Omar should now withdraw from reviewing the contractors’ bids.
Priya accepted a gift from an applicant whose application a colleague would soon decide on, and she told no other applicant, so accepting the gift was wrong.
questions.explanation: The principle condemns accepting a gift from an applicant you will soon decide on unless every other applicant was told. Tomas told his colleagues, but not the other candidates, so the exception fails and his acceptance was wrong, as (B) says. Most students pick (A) because Renata satisfies the exception; but an exception only removes the principle’s verdict of “wrong” and never establishes “not wrong.” (C) involves a decision already made, (D) draws a different verdict (withdrawal), and (E) involves someone who isn’t the decision-maker.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Accept gift from an applicant you will soon decide on AND not every other applicant told beforehand → wrong.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment that meets every condition and concludes the acceptance was wrong.

breakdown.analysis: Unpack the “unless”: accepting is wrong unless every other applicant was told. So the rule only ever outputs “wrong.” The right answer needs: 1. the person accepts a gift; 2. from an applicant whose application that same person will soon decide; 3. not every other applicant was told beforehand; 4. verdict: wrong. Telling the wrong audience doesn’t count, and meeting the exception doesn’t make anything right. It’s like “you’ll be fined unless you have a permit.” Having a permit means no fine under this rule, but it doesn’t mean everything you did was legal.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it: Renata did exactly what the exception asks. But the exception only switches off the verdict of “wrong.” The principle never says anything is “not wrong.” Maybe accepting gifts is wrong for some other reason. This judgment goes beyond the rule.

CORRECT. Tomas accepted a gift from a candidate he’d decide on the next day (soon). He told his colleagues, but the principle requires telling every other applicant, and he told none of them. So the exception fails and the verdict is wrong. The disclosure to the managers is bait.
Ilse had already decided, so she wasn’t someone who “will soon be deciding.” The principle doesn’t cover this case.
Wrong verdict. The principle says accepting the gift is wrong. It says nothing about withdrawing from the review.
Priya isn’t the one deciding; a colleague is. The principle covers the decision-maker who accepts the gift, so it doesn’t apply to her.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Strengthen, Weaken, Inference & Parallel

questions.stimulus: Manager of Pinecrest Lanes: Last winter we replaced the old wooden surfaces of our bowling lanes with synthetic ones. Since then, the average score bowled at Pinecrest has risen by about twelve pins per game. The synthetic surfaces, which hold the lane oil more evenly than wood does, are clearly what has improved our customers' scores.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the manager's argument?
choices: Many longtime bowlers at Pinecrest say that they prefer the feel of the old wooden lanes to that of the new synthetic ones.
Synthetic lane surfaces cost more to install than wooden surfaces do, but they are less expensive to maintain over the years.
At other alleys that switched to synthetic lanes, average scores rose by similar amounts, while scores at alleys that kept wood did not.
Pinecrest began offering free weekly coaching sessions to its league bowlers at about the time the synthetic lanes were installed.
The number of games bowled at Pinecrest each week has grown steadily since the synthetic lanes were installed last winter.
questions.explanation: The manager infers that the new surfaces caused the higher scores from a before-and-after change at one alley. (C) supplies the missing comparison: alleys that made the same switch saw the same rise, and alleys that did not switch saw none, which makes some other local cause much less likely. (D) is the trap; it is relevant, but it offers a rival cause (coaching) and so weakens the argument. (A) is about preference, not scores.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The synthetic lane surfaces caused the rise in Pinecrest's average scores.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Scores rose about twelve pins per game after the switch; synthetic surfaces hold oil more evenly.

breakdown.analysis: Scores went up after the lanes changed. So what? Lots of things could have changed at the same time. This is a classic before-and-after causal argument, and the easiest way to strengthen it is to show the same cause producing the same effect somewhere else, or to rule out a rival cause. It's like saying a new fertilizer grew your tomatoes: you'd believe it more if neighbors who used it got the same result and neighbors who didn't got nothing. We need an answer that ties higher scores to the synthetic surface itself.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What bowlers like isn't what makes them score higher. The argument is about scores, not taste.
Wrong dimension. Cost and upkeep have nothing to do with whether the surfaces raised scores.
CORRECT. Same switch elsewhere, same jump in scores; no switch, no jump. That pattern points to the surface as the cause rather than something peculiar to Pinecrest.
Tempting, because it's about the scores. But it hands you a rival cause: free coaching started at the same time. That weakens the claim that the lanes did it. Always check the direction.
So? More games bowled says nothing about why each game scores higher. If anything, more practice is another possible cause.

questions.stimulus: The cones of the Kerrin pine open and release their seeds only after they have been exposed to the intense heat of a fire. In the Dunlin Hills, every fire for the past eighty years has been put out before it could spread, and during that time almost no young Kerrin pines have appeared there, although mature Kerrin pines remain common.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: The suppression of fires in the Dunlin Hills has probably reduced the number of new Kerrin pines that have taken root there.
If fires were allowed to burn freely in the Dunlin Hills, the Kerrin pine would soon become the most common tree in the region.
Fire suppression has also reduced the number of young trees of other species in the Dunlin Hills over the past eighty years.
Kerrin pines are more common in regions where fires burn freely than in any other kind of region where the tree grows.
Mature Kerrin pines in the Dunlin Hills are more likely than young ones to be killed when a fire does break out there.
questions.explanation: Seeds are released only after intense fire heat, fires have been stopped for eighty years, and almost no young pines have appeared; together these strongly support the modest causal claim in (A). (B) is the tempting overreach: the facts say nothing about how fast the pine would spread or how it would compare with other trees. (C), (D) and (E) bring in other species, other regions or mortality rates the facts never mention.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Kerrin pine cones release seeds only after intense fire heat; 2. In the Dunlin Hills, fires have been put out before spreading for eighty years; 3. In that time almost no young Kerrin pines have appeared; 4. Mature Kerrin pines are still common.

breakdown.analysis: Put the facts side by side: no fire heat means no seeds released, no big fires for eighty years, and hardly any young pines. The obvious, modest conclusion is that stopping fires has cut down on new pines. That's the kind of answer most-strongly-supported questions reward: it connects two facts and doesn't claim more than they show. Watch for answers that predict the future or rank the pine against other trees.

choices.note: CORRECT. No intense heat means the cones stay shut, and the fires have been stopped for eighty years, so the lack of young pines is very likely the result. "Probably" keeps the claim at the right strength.

Tempting, because it runs the same logic forward. But "soon" and "most common tree in the region" go far beyond the facts. We know nothing about other trees or how fast pines would spread. Too strong.
We don't know this. The facts are only about Kerrin pines. Other species may not need fire at all.
Unsupported comparison. The facts describe one place. Nothing ranks fire-prone regions against every other kind.
No information about which trees die in a fire. This brings in something new.

questions.stimulus: Salon owner: In January we began playing soft classical music in our salon, and since then the average tip our stylists receive has risen by about 15 percent. Nothing about the way our stylists do their work has changed in that time. Evidently, then, the music puts our customers in a more generous mood.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the salon owner's argument?
choices: Several regular customers have said that they would rather hear popular music than classical music while they are in the salon.
Stylists at salons in the area that play no music at all also receive tips from most of the customers they serve.
The stylists say that the music has made their long workdays at the salon noticeably more pleasant than they used to be.
In January the salon also raised its prices by about 15 percent, and customers' tips are generally a fixed percentage of the bill.
Customers who book longer appointments at the salon tend to leave larger tips than customers who book shorter ones do.
questions.explanation: The owner concludes that the music caused tips to rise, having ruled out only changes in how the stylists work. (D) offers an alternative cause that fully accounts for the increase: prices rose 15 percent and tips track the bill, so tips would rise 15 percent with or without the music. (C) is tempting but still credits the music, and (A) is about preference, not tipping.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The classical music makes customers more generous.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Average tips rose about 15 percent after the music started; the stylists' work hasn't changed.

breakdown.analysis: Tips went up after the music started. But is the music the only thing that changed? The owner rules out one rival (how the stylists work), but not others. A weakener here will give another reason tips rose. Think of it like this: your paycheck went up the month you started wearing a lucky tie. Maybe it was the raise everyone got that month. We want the salon's version of that raise.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Some customers preferring other music doesn't tell us whether the music changed how much people tip.
So? Customers elsewhere tip too. That doesn't explain why tips at this salon rose 15 percent.

Tempting, because it suggests a mechanism (happier stylists, better service). But that path still runs through the music, so it doesn't weaken the claim that the music raised tips. It might even help it.
CORRECT. Prices went up 15 percent at the same time, and tips are a percentage of the bill. That alone explains a 15 percent rise in tips, no generous mood required.
Interesting fact, but we don't know appointment lengths changed. Without that, it doesn't explain the rise.

questions.stimulus: The Ellwood Glassworks makes only two products: drinking glasses and vases. This year the glassworks produced 15 percent more vases than it produced last year. Even so, the total number of items it produced this year was smaller than the total number it produced last year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: This year the Ellwood Glassworks produced more vases than it produced drinking glasses.
The Ellwood Glassworks produced fewer drinking glasses this year than it produced last year.
Demand for the glassworks' drinking glasses fell this year, while demand for its vases rose.
The glassworks earned less money from the sale of its products this year than it earned last year.
Next year the Ellwood Glassworks will produce fewer drinking glasses than it produced this year.
questions.explanation: Only two products exist, vase output went up, and total output went down; the only way the total can fall while one part rises is for the other part to fall, so (B) must be true. (A) could be false, since glasses may still outnumber vases. (C) supplies an unproven cause, and (D) and (E) concern money and next year, which the facts never address.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. The glassworks makes only glasses and vases; 2. Vase output rose 15 percent this year; 3. Total output this year was lower than last year.

breakdown.analysis: Total = glasses + vases. Vases went up, but the total went down. What had to happen? Glasses had to go down, and by more than vases went up. Quick example: last year 100 glasses + 100 vases = 200. This year 115 vases; total under 200, so glasses must be under 85. That's the must-be-true. Everything else is a guess about causes, money or the future.

choices.note: We don't know this. In the example above, 115 vases and 80 glasses works, but so does 30 vases rising to about 35 alongside 200 glasses falling to 150. The count comparison could go either way.
CORRECT. Two products, one went up, the total went down, so the other must have gone down. That's arithmetic.
Tempting, because it's a natural story. But the facts are about how many were made, not why. Maybe a furnace broke. An unsupported causal claim.
Money is never mentioned. Fewer items could still bring in more revenue if prices rose.
A prediction. The facts cover only this year and last year.

questions.stimulus: County commissioner: A survey of people attending this year's Ludlow County Fair found that 78 percent of them favor spending county funds on a new livestock arena at the fairgrounds. The survey questioned more than 600 people, so its results are reliable. Clearly, most residents of Ludlow County favor building the new arena.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the commissioner's argument?
choices: The new livestock arena would cost the county more than any other building project it has undertaken in the past decade.
Some of the people questioned at the fair said that they had not yet decided whether they favored building the arena.
Most surveys of Ludlow County residents conducted in recent years have questioned fewer than 600 people.
Several county commissioners have stated publicly that they intend to vote against spending county funds on the arena.
The survey was conducted at the fair's livestock barns, where most of the people questioned were exhibitors who would use the arena.
questions.explanation: The commissioner generalizes from fair attendees to all county residents and defends the survey only on size. (E) shows the sample is unrepresentative: most respondents were exhibitors who stand to benefit from the arena. (C) is the trap, but it only confirms that 600 is a large sample, which does nothing to fix a biased one. (A) and (D) concern cost and votes, not residents' opinions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most Ludlow County residents favor building the arena.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 78 percent of 600-plus fair attendees surveyed favor it; the sample is large.

breakdown.analysis: Who answered this survey? People at a county fair, which already leans toward people who care about fairs. A big sample doesn't help if it's the wrong people. It's like polling a golf club about whether to build a golf course and calling the result "public opinion." We need an answer that shows the people questioned weren't like county residents in general on this issue.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The cost might make it a bad idea, but the question is whether most residents favor it.
So? A few undecided respondents don't change the fact that 78 percent were in favor.
Tempting, because it seems to be about the survey's quality. But it only confirms the sample is big. Size was never the problem; who was asked is the problem.
Irrelevant. How commissioners vote doesn't tell us what residents think.
CORRECT. The people surveyed were mostly exhibitors who would use the arena. Of course they want it. That's a biased sample, so it tells us little about residents as a whole.

questions.stimulus: If Marta finishes the draft of her thesis by March, her advisor will be able to review it in April. And if her advisor reviews the draft in April, Marta will be able to defend her thesis in June. Marta is certain to finish the draft by March. So Marta will be able to defend her thesis in June.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: If the county approves the road budget this spring, Elm Road will be repaved in the summer. If it is repaved then, the Route 4 bus will be detoured. The county will approve the budget, so the bus will be detoured.

If the bakery's new oven arrives this week, the bakery will start selling bagels. If it starts selling bagels, it will need another baker. The bakery has just hired another baker, so its new oven must have arrived this week.

Most graduate students who finish their thesis drafts early go on to defend their theses on schedule. Lena finished her draft two months early. So Lena will very likely defend her thesis on schedule, as she had planned.

If it rains on Saturday, the club's picnic will be moved indoors. If the picnic is moved indoors, there will be no room for games. It will not rain on Saturday, so there will be room for games at the picnic.

If the library extends its evening hours, it will need to hire more staff. Hiring more staff would strain the library's budget. So the library should not extend its evening hours, at least not during this year.
questions.explanation: The argument is a valid chain: if A then B, if B then C, A is true, so C. (A) follows exactly that chain with the road budget, the repaving and the detour. (B) runs the chain backward from the last result, (D) denies the first condition, (C) shares the thesis topic but reasons from a 'most' generalization, and (E) ends in a recommendation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Marta will be able to defend her thesis in June.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Draft by March → review in April; review in April → defense in June; she will finish by March.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A → B; B → C; A; so C.

breakdown.analysis: Strip out the topic and you get a plain chain: A → B → C, and A happens, so C happens. That's valid. Look for an answer with two linked if-thens, the first condition stated as true, and the last result as a certain conclusion. Ignore anything about theses or students; topic doesn't matter in parallel questions.

choices.note: CORRECT. Budget → repaving; repaving → detour; budget will be approved; so detour. A → B → C, A, so C. Same certainty, same shape.
This runs backward: it starts from the last result (hired a baker) and concludes the first condition (oven arrived). That's affirming the consequent, and it's invalid. Our argument goes forward.
Tempting, because it's about a thesis. But it reasons from "most students" to "very likely," a probability argument with no if-then chain. Same topic, different structure.
Looks like a chain, but it denies the first condition (no rain) and concludes the last result won't happen. That's a different (and invalid) move. Our argument affirms the first condition.
Ends with a recommendation ("should not") and has no stated fact triggering the chain. Different conclusion type.

questions.stimulus: Parks director: On weekday evenings our public tennis courts are so crowded that players often wait an hour for a court, yet the courts sit mostly empty before noon. So we plan to cut the court fee in half for morning play. This should reduce the evening crowding, since some players who now play in the evening will switch to the cheaper morning hours.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the parks director's argument?
choices: The lights that make evening play possible on the public courts are expensive for the parks department to operate.
In a survey, many evening players said they could switch to morning play and would if it cost less.
Players who already use the courts in the morning say that they would play more often if the court fee were reduced.
Several private tennis clubs in the area charge their members much more for court time than the public courts charge.
Morning players and evening players currently pay the same fee for each hour they use the public tennis courts.
questions.explanation: The plan works only if evening players are able and willing to move to the cheaper mornings. (B) supports exactly that assumption. (C) is the trap: it shows the discount would draw more morning play from people already playing in the morning, which does nothing to empty the evening courts. (E) restates what the plan already implies, and (A) and (D) are about costs and other clubs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Halving the morning fee will reduce evening crowding.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Evening courts are packed while morning courts are empty; some evening players will switch to cheaper mornings.

breakdown.analysis: The whole plan rests on one claim: evening players will actually move. Can they? Plenty of people work in the morning, and no discount helps someone who has to be at a desk at 9. We need an answer that shows evening players can and will switch for a lower price.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. This could be a reason to want less evening play, but it doesn't show the discount will move anyone.
CORRECT. Evening players say they could come in the morning and would for a lower price. That's the exact link the plan needs.
Tempting, because it shows the discount changes behavior. But it's the wrong group: people already playing in the morning. More morning play from them does nothing to free up evening courts.
Irrelevant comparison. Private clubs' prices don't tell us whether public evening players will shift to mornings.
Already implied: the plan creates a price difference that doesn't exist now. Saying so doesn't show anyone will respond to it.

questions.stimulus: Angler: On Tamber Lake, fishing lures painted bright chartreuse catch about twice as many bass as lures that are identical except that they are painted blue. Since the only difference between the lures is their color, it is clear that the lake's bass are more strongly attracted to chartreuse than to blue.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the angler's argument?
choices: Bass in Tamber Lake feed most actively in the early morning and during the hour or so just before sunset each day.
Chartreuse lures cost slightly more than blue lures at the bait shop nearest to Tamber Lake.
Many of the fish that live in Tamber Lake are able to distinguish colors that are invisible to the human eye.
Most chartreuse lures were used by guides fishing the coves where bass gather; most blue ones were cast from the pier.
Some anglers on Tamber Lake catch more bass with lures of other colors than they catch with either chartreuse or blue lures.
questions.explanation: The angler says color is the only difference between the lures, but that ignores who uses them and where. (D) shows the chartreuse lures were mostly used by skilled guides in the best spots, which could explain the extra catches without any color preference. (C) is the trap: it sounds scientific, but it neither shows nor rules out a preference for chartreuse. (E) concerns other colors and some anglers only.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Tamber Lake bass are more attracted to chartreuse than to blue.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Chartreuse lures catch about twice as many bass as otherwise identical blue lures.

breakdown.analysis: The lures differ only in color. Fine, but do the people and places using them differ? The angler ignores that. It's like saying a brand of running shoe makes people faster because its wearers win more races, when it turns out mostly pros wear it. We need an answer showing that something other than color separates the chartreuse catches from the blue ones.

choices.note: Irrelevant. When bass feed doesn't explain why one color catches more.
Price has nothing to do with what bass are attracted to.
Tempting, because it's about fish and color vision. But seeing extra colors doesn't tell us whether they prefer chartreuse to blue. It neither helps nor hurts.
CORRECT. Experts fishing where the bass are used the chartreuse lures; casual anglers on the pier used the blue ones. That could explain the difference in catches with no color preference at all.
So? Other colors doing even better for some people says nothing about chartreuse versus blue.

questions.stimulus: Every ride at the Marrick Point amusement park that turns riders upside down has a height requirement. No ride at the park that has a height requirement is open to children under the age of six. The Comet is a ride at Marrick Point that is open to children under the age of six.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Every ride at Marrick Point that is open to children under six moves more slowly than the park's other rides.
Every ride at Marrick Point that does not turn riders upside down is open to children under the age of six.
The Comet does not turn its riders upside down.
Some rides at Marrick Point that have a height requirement do not turn their riders upside down.
Most of the rides at the Marrick Point amusement park are closed to children under the age of six.
questions.explanation: The rules chain: upside down → height requirement → not open to children under six. The Comet is open to children under six, so by the contrapositive it has no height requirement and does not turn riders upside down, which is (C). (B) is the trap: it negates the first condition and its result, which the rules don't support. (D) and (E) could be true but aren't required, and (A) brings in speed.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Upside down → height requirement; 2. Height requirement → not open to under-sixes; 3. The Comet is open to under-sixes.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: upside down → height requirement → not open to under-sixes. Contrapositive: open to under-sixes → no height requirement → not upside down. The Comet is open to under-sixes, so it doesn't go upside down. That's the answer to look for. Watch for answers that flip or negate the chain.

choices.note: Speed is never mentioned. New information.
Tempting, because it uses the rule's terms. But it negates both sides: "not upside down → open to under-sixes." The rules never say that. A gentle ride could still have a height requirement.
CORRECT. Open to under-sixes → no height requirement → not upside down. Straight contrapositive of the chain.
Could be true, but nothing forces it. Maybe every height-requirement ride goes upside down.
We don't know how many rides there are or how many have height requirements. Could be false.

questions.stimulus: Inspector: This morning I selected thirty jars at random from the Fenley plant's production run of strawberry jam, and every one of them was properly sealed. Because the jars were chosen at random, it is likely that nearly all of the jars produced in this morning's run are properly sealed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: The Fenley plant has passed every one of its safety inspections over the past ten years. So this morning's run of jam at the plant was probably also produced in compliance with every applicable safety standard.

Every reader who wrote to the magazine about its redesign said that he or she disliked the new layout. So most of the magazine's readers probably dislike the new layout and would prefer to have the old one back.

Nearly all of the bottles of cider produced at the Ardmoor orchard last month were properly labeled. So the bottle of cider that Gareth bought from the orchard last month was very probably labeled properly.
Any jar that is not properly sealed will leak when it is turned upside down. None of the jars on this shelf leaked when they were turned over, so every jar on this shelf must be properly sealed.

A gardener chose forty tomato seedlings at random from the nursery's greenhouse, and none showed any sign of blight. Since they were chosen at random, very probably almost none of the greenhouse's seedlings have blight.
questions.explanation: The inspector generalizes from a random sample in which every item had a property to the probable conclusion that nearly all of the whole group has it. (E) does the same with randomly chosen seedlings. (B) is the near miss: it generalizes from letter writers, who chose themselves, not from a random sample. (C) reasons from the group to one member, (A) from a track record, and (D) uses a certain conditional rule.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Nearly all of this morning's jars are probably properly sealed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Thirty randomly selected jars were all properly sealed.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Every member of a random sample of group G has property P; so probably nearly all of G has P.

breakdown.analysis: This is a generalization from a random sample: test a random handful, find they all pass, conclude the whole batch probably passes. The key features are (1) a random sample, (2) all of it has the property, and (3) a probable conclusion about nearly all of the larger group. Find the answer with all three.

choices.note: Same plant, but a different kind of evidence: a ten-year track record, not a sample from this run. Past performance → this time. Topic match, structure miss.
Tempting, because it also goes from a group of respondents to "most." But letter writers pick themselves; they aren't a random sample. The original's key feature is the random selection.
This runs the other direction: from the whole group (nearly all bottles) to one member (Gareth's bottle). The original goes from a sample to the group.
A certain deduction from a conditional rule (not sealed → leaks; nothing leaked; so all sealed). No sampling and no "probably."

CORRECT. Random sample of forty seedlings, all free of blight, so probably almost none of the greenhouse's seedlings have blight. Random sample, all pass, probable conclusion about nearly all. Same pattern.

questions.stimulus: Public works director: Most of the litter on our downtown sidewalks consists of paper coffee cups. People tend to litter when no trash can is close at hand, so doubling the number of trash cans on downtown sidewalks will substantially reduce the amount of litter there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the public works director's argument?
choices: Emptying the additional trash cans will require the city to hire at least two more sanitation workers for the downtown area.
Most of the coffee cups found on downtown sidewalks were dropped within a few steps of an existing trash can.
Several downtown cafés plan to begin offering a discount to customers who bring their own reusable mugs.
In other cities that have added trash cans to their downtown sidewalks, the amount of litter there has declined somewhat.
Some downtown shop owners have complained that trash cans placed in front of their stores make their entrances look cluttered.
questions.explanation: The plan assumes downtown litter happens because trash cans are too far away. (B) undercuts that: most cups were dropped right next to an existing can, so adding more cans is unlikely to change behavior. (D) is the trap, but it supports the plan rather than weakening it. (A) and (E) raise costs and complaints, not whether litter will fall.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Doubling downtown trash cans will substantially reduce litter.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most downtown litter is coffee cups; people litter when no trash can is close at hand.

breakdown.analysis: More cans means less litter, but only if a missing can is why people are littering downtown. What if the cans are already right there and people toss their cups anyway? Then more cans won't help. We need an answer that shows the downtown litter isn't caused by cans being too far away.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Hiring costs might make the plan expensive, but they don't show it won't reduce litter.
CORRECT. The cups are being dropped a few steps from a can that's already there. Distance to a can isn't the problem, so doubling the cans probably won't fix it.
This might reduce cup litter on its own, but it doesn't show the director's plan won't work. Both could help.
Tempting, because it's about the same plan. But read the direction: litter declined elsewhere. That strengthens the plan.
Complaints about clutter are a cost, not evidence that litter won't fall.

questions.stimulus: In the Merran Valley, the dusky barn bat roosts almost exclusively in old timber barns; it does not roost in steel buildings. Over the past twenty years, most of the valley's timber barns have been torn down and replaced with steel buildings. During that same period, the valley's population of dusky barn bats has fallen by more than half.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The replacement of timber barns with steel buildings has reduced the number of places in the Merran Valley where dusky barn bats can roost.
Steel buildings give off something that is harmful to the dusky barn bats that live in the area around them.
If the valley's timber barns were rebuilt, the population of dusky barn bats would return to its former size.
Most of the dusky barn bats that once lived in the Merran Valley have moved to neighboring valleys that have more timber barns.
Dusky barn bats in the Merran Valley never roost anywhere other than in old timber barns.
questions.explanation: The bats roost almost only in timber barns, not in steel buildings, and most timber barns have been replaced by steel buildings, so roosting places have very likely shrunk, which is (A). (E) is the trap: 'almost exclusively' does not mean 'never anywhere else.' (C) and (D) predict or explain far more than the facts show, and (B) invents a harm.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Dusky barn bats roost almost exclusively in old timber barns, not steel buildings; 2. Most of the valley's timber barns were replaced with steel buildings over twenty years; 3. The bat population fell by more than half over the same period.

breakdown.analysis: The bats roost almost only in timber barns, and most timber barns are gone, replaced by buildings the bats won't use. What follows with almost no risk? The bats have fewer places to roost. That's modest and nearly guaranteed. Watch for answers that turn "almost exclusively" into "never," or that predict a recovery.

choices.note: CORRECT. Most of the barns the bats roost in have become steel buildings they don't roost in. That means fewer roosting places, which the facts support almost directly.
Nothing suggests steel buildings harm bats. The bats just don't use them. Invented cause.
Too strong. Rebuilding barns might help, but a full recovery depends on many things the facts don't cover.
We don't know where the missing bats went. They may have died. Unsupported.
Tempting, because it looks like a restatement. But "almost exclusively" leaves room for a few other roosts. "Never" is too strong.

questions.stimulus: Archivist: The water stains on the maps donated to our library were made either while the maps were being shipped or after they arrived here. But the shipping crate's seal was unbroken when it reached us, and its moisture indicator showed no exposure to water. So the stains must have been made after the maps arrived.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Lionel will spend his vacation either hiking in the mountains or visiting his sister in Calder. He has already bought new hiking boots for the trip. So he will not be visiting his sister in Calder during his vacation.

Maps stored in the library's basement have far more water stains than those stored upstairs, and the basement floods now and then. So flooding in the basement is probably what caused most of the stains on the library's maps.

Most packages that arrive at our warehouse damaged were damaged by the delivery company rather than by the sender. This package arrived damaged. So it was most likely damaged by the delivery company, not the sender.
Ilse's spare key is either in her desk at work or in her car. She searched her car thoroughly this morning, and the key was not there. So the spare key must be in her desk at work.

The concert will go ahead only if the stage is repaired and the permit is approved. The permit has now been approved. So, as long as the stage is repaired, the concert will certainly go ahead as scheduled.
questions.explanation: The archivist argues by elimination: either X or Y; evidence rules out X; so Y. (D) does the same with the key: desk or car, not the car, so the desk. (A) is the near miss: it starts with an either/or but concludes that one option is false because the other is true, which doesn't follow, since he could do both. (B) shares the map topic but reasons causally, and (C) reasons from a 'most' generalization.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The stains were made after the maps arrived.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The stains were made either during shipping or after arrival; the sealed, dry crate rules out shipping.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Either X or Y; not X; so Y.

breakdown.analysis: Process of elimination: two possibilities, one ruled out, so the other. Look for an answer that names two options, gives evidence that eliminates one, and concludes with certainty that the other is true. Be careful with answers that use "either/or" but then do something else with it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it opens with "either/or." But then it affirms one option (hiking) and denies the other. That doesn't follow: he could hike and also visit his sister. Our argument eliminates an option; this one uses one option to eliminate the other.
Same topic (stained maps), different reasoning: a correlation (basement maps are more stained) used to infer a probable cause. No either/or elimination.
Applies a "most" generalization to one case to reach a "most likely" conclusion. No elimination of an option.
CORRECT. Desk or car; not the car; so the desk. Either X or Y, not X, so Y.
This is about necessary conditions ("only if") and wrongly treats them as enough. No either/or elimination.

questions.stimulus: Engineer: We poured two test slabs from the same batch of concrete on the same day in the same yard. One slab was kept covered with wet burlap while it cured; the other was left uncovered. A month later, the covered slab was markedly stronger. Since the slabs differed only in whether they were covered, covering the concrete while it cured must have made it stronger.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Students who use flashcards when studying for the history final tend to score higher on it than students who do not. So using flashcards must improve the scores of students who take the history final.

After the Corlow bakery switched to a new brand of flour last month, its bread sales rose sharply. So the new flour must have made the bakery's bread taste better to its customers than the old flour did.

Two sections of a chemistry course had the same instructor, textbook, and schedule, but only one section took weekly practice quizzes. That section scored much higher on the final. Since the sections differed only in the quizzes, the quizzes must have raised the scores.

Concrete that is kept moist while it cures is generally stronger than concrete that is allowed to dry out. The foundation of the Garvey house was kept moist while it cured. So that foundation is probably stronger than most foundations.

Two orchards were treated identically except that one was pruned in winter and the other in spring, and the winter-pruned orchard produced more fruit. So the growers' association should require all of its members to prune their trees in winter.
questions.explanation: The engineer compares two cases that are alike except for one factor and concludes that the factor caused the difference in outcome. (C) does the same with two course sections that differ only in the quizzes. (E) is the near miss: it has the same controlled comparison but ends in a recommendation for everyone rather than a causal conclusion. (A) uses a bare correlation, (B) a before-and-after change, and (D) shares the concrete topic but applies a generalization to one case.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Covering the concrete while it cured made it stronger.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two slabs alike in every way except covering; the covered one ended up stronger.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Two cases alike except for factor F; the case with F had outcome O; so F caused O.

breakdown.analysis: This is a controlled comparison, the logic of an experiment: hold everything constant, change one thing, see a different result, and credit the one thing. Find the answer with (1) two cases, (2) explicitly alike except for one factor, (3) a different outcome, and (4) a causal conclusion about that factor.

choices.note: A plain correlation with no claim that the groups are otherwise alike. Maybe stronger students use flashcards. Not a controlled comparison.
One bakery before and after, with no claim that nothing else changed, and the conclusion jumps to taste. Not two matched cases.
CORRECT. Two sections alike in instructor, textbook and schedule; only one had quizzes; it scored higher; so the quizzes raised scores. Same skeleton.
Same topic (moist curing), different structure: a general rule applied to one foundation to reach a probable conclusion. No comparison of two matched cases.

Tempting, because the first half is a perfect controlled comparison. But the conclusion is a recommendation for every grower, not a claim about what caused the difference. Changing the conclusion type breaks the match.

questions.stimulus: Groundskeeper: Whenever the sky over the Bexley golf course stays clear all night in October, frost covers the greens by dawn. This morning, an October morning, there was no frost on the greens at all. So the sky over the course must not have stayed clear all last night.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Whenever the Halloway choir sings at the spring festival, Nadia performs a solo. Nadia performed a solo at last night's concert, so the choir must have been singing at the spring festival last night.
Whenever the Brenner Street bakery runs out of rye bread, it closes early for the day. The bakery did not run out of rye bread today, so it will not close early today.
Frost usually forms on the greens after a clear October night. Last night was clear and cold, so there was probably frost on the greens this morning, though no one has gone out yet to check.
The greens at the golf course were damaged last winter after several nights of hard frost. So the groundskeepers should cover the greens on any night this year when hard frost is expected.
Whenever Dr. Okafor's lab runs its large centrifuge, the circuit breaker in the basement trips. The breaker did not trip yesterday, so the lab must not have run its large centrifuge yesterday.
questions.explanation: The groundskeeper reasons: whenever X, Y; not Y; so not X, the valid contrapositive. (E) does the same with the centrifuge and the breaker. (A) affirms the result to conclude the condition, and (B) denies the condition to conclude the result is absent; both are invalid. (C) and (D) share the frost and golf-course topic but use a probability claim and a recommendation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The sky did not stay clear all last night.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Clear October night → frost on the greens; there was no frost this morning.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X → Y; not Y; so not X.

breakdown.analysis: Clear night → frost. No frost → so not a clear night. That's the contrapositive, and it's valid. The answer must have the same move: a "whenever" rule, the result fails to happen, so the condition didn't happen either. Two classic decoys: affirming the result (Y, so X) and denying the condition (not X, so not Y).

choices.note: Affirms the result (Nadia sang a solo) to conclude the condition (it was the spring festival). Invalid; she might solo at other concerts too. Our argument denies the result.
Denies the condition (didn't run out of rye) to conclude the result won't happen. Invalid; it could close early for other reasons. Different move.
Tempting, because it's frost on the greens again. But it's a "usually" probability argument that runs forward from the condition. Topic match, structure miss.
Same golf-course topic, but it ends in a recommendation drawn from one bad winter. No if-then rule.
CORRECT. Centrifuge → breaker trips; breaker didn't trip; so no centrifuge. X → Y, not Y, so not X.

questions.stimulus: Pantry coordinator: Most of the people who volunteer at the Delling food pantry are retired teachers. Moreover, every retired teacher who volunteers at the pantry works the Saturday morning shift. It follows that most of the people who volunteer at the pantry work the Saturday morning shift.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Most of the trees in the Harlow orchard are pear trees, and every pear tree in the orchard was planted before 1990. So most of the orchard's trees were planted before 1990.
Most of the members of the Ridley hiking club live in the city, and most of the city's residents own a car. It follows that most of the members of the Ridley hiking club own a car.

Every painting in the Varga collection was framed by the Lisle workshop, and most of the works framed by the Lisle workshop are oil paintings. It follows that most of the paintings in the Varga collection are oil paintings.

Most of the students in Ms. Dorn's class play an instrument, and every student in her class who plays an instrument is in the school band. It follows that every student in Ms. Dorn's class is in the school band.

Most of the volunteers at the city animal shelter are college students, and most college students in the city have flexible schedules. So Ana, who volunteers at the shelter, probably has a flexible schedule.
questions.explanation: The coordinator's argument is a valid quantifier chain: most A are B, all B (in A) are C, so most A are C. (A) matches it exactly with trees, pear trees and planting dates. (B) chains two 'most' statements, which is invalid, and (C) puts the 'all' and 'most' in the wrong places. (D) is the near miss: same premises, but it concludes 'every' instead of 'most'. (E) concludes about one person.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most pantry volunteers work the Saturday morning shift.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most volunteers are retired teachers; every retired-teacher volunteer works that shift.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; every B among the A is C; so most A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Check the quantifiers, not the topic. Most volunteers are retired teachers, and all of those work Saturday. So the Saturday group includes at least that majority, and most volunteers work Saturday. Valid. The match needs "most," then "every," then "most" in the conclusion. Watch for "most + most" (invalid), "all + most" in reverse order, and a conclusion that jumps to "every."

choices.note: CORRECT. Most trees are pear trees; every pear tree was planted before 1990; so most trees were planted before 1990. Most + all → most. Exact match.
Most + most. Invalid: the car-owning majority of city residents could exclude the hikers entirely. The original's second premise is "every," not "most."
The quantifiers are in the wrong slots: all A are B, most B are C. The Varga paintings could be among the framed works that aren't oils. Different (and invalid) structure.
Tempting, because the premises match perfectly (most, then every). But the conclusion says "every student," when the premises only support "most." One word breaks the parallel.
Uses two "most" premises and concludes about one person with "probably." Different quantifiers, different conclusion type, even though it shares the volunteer theme.

questions.stimulus: Harbor commission: We want the Port Sennet shipping channel to remain usable by the new, deeper cargo ships. The channel fills with silt every winter, and dredging it each spring is the only way to keep it deep enough for those ships. So we should arrange to have the channel dredged every spring.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: The town wants to reduce traffic on Mill Street, and adding a traffic light at the corner of Mill and Fifth is one of several ways it could do so. So the town should add a traffic light at that corner as soon as it can.

Most people who become fluent in a second language within a year take an intensive course. Ana wants to become fluent in Portuguese within a year. So Ana should sign up for an intensive Portuguese course.

Rosa wants to be able to read her grandmother's letters, which are written in Portuguese. Taking a year of Portuguese classes is the only way she could learn to read them. So she should enroll in a year of Portuguese classes.

The library wants to keep its rare-book room open on weekends. The only way to do that is to hire another archivist, and the budget cannot cover another salary. So the library should give up on opening the room on weekends.

Every winter, silt fills the Port Sennet channel, and in years when the channel is not dredged, fewer cargo ships call at the port. So the silt is probably the main reason fewer ships call at Port Sennet in those years.
questions.explanation: The commission reasons: we want goal G; action M is the only way to achieve G; so we should do M. (C) matches: Rosa wants to read the letters, classes are the only way, so she should take them. (A) is the near miss: the light is merely one of several ways, which is a weaker premise. (D) starts the same way but concludes the goal should be abandoned, (B) relies on what most people do, and (E) shares the harbor topic but draws a causal conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The commission should have the channel dredged every spring.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The goal is a channel usable by deeper ships; annual spring dredging is the only way to achieve it.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: We want G; M is the only way to get G; so we should do M.

breakdown.analysis: Goal plus only means equals do the means. The "only way" is what makes this argument tick: if the action were just one option among many, the conclusion wouldn't follow. Find an answer with a goal, a single necessary means, and a recommendation to take that means. Watch for "one of several ways" and for answers that flip the conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's goal → action → "should." But the light is "one of several ways," not the only way. That's a weaker premise, so it's a different (and weaker) argument.
Reasons from what most successful people did, not from an only means. A statistical recommendation.
CORRECT. Goal (read the letters); only means (a year of classes); so she should take them. Same skeleton.
Starts the same way, with a goal and an only means, but then adds a cost and concludes the goal should be dropped. Opposite kind of conclusion.
Same harbor and silt, but it's a causal inference (silt explains fewer ships), not a recommendation based on an only means.

questions.stimulus: Shipbuilder: The new trawler Gannet was built at the same yard, to the same design, and from the same timber as the trawler Petrel, which has needed no major hull repairs in its twenty-five years at sea. So the Gannet will probably also go many years without needing major hull repairs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every boat built at the Kessing yard has a hull strong enough to last for decades without major repairs. The Merlin was built at the Kessing yard. So the Merlin will last for decades without needing major hull repairs.

This year's trainee nurses at Corran Hospital were taught by the same instructor, using the same methods and simulators, as last year's trainees, nearly all of whom passed the licensing exam. So this year's will probably pass too.

The Heron was built at the same yard as the Osprey, which has needed few repairs. But the Heron was built from a different timber than the Osprey was. So the Heron will probably need more repairs than the Osprey has needed.

Of the twenty trawlers built at the Harrow yard that we inspected this year, none has ever needed major hull repairs. So probably few of the trawlers that the Harrow yard has built have ever needed such repairs.

The Petrel has needed no major hull repairs in twenty-five years, while trawlers of the same age built at other yards have needed many. So the timber used in the Petrel must be what has kept its hull sound.
questions.explanation: The shipbuilder argues by analogy: a new case shares several relevant features with an older case that had a good outcome, so the new case will probably have the same outcome. (B) does this with two classes of trainee nurses taught the same way. (A) is the trap: it reaches a similar conclusion but deduces it from a rule covering every boat, not from a comparison with one case. (C) draws a contrast from a difference, (D) generalizes from a sample, and (E) makes a causal claim.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Gannet will probably go many years without major hull repairs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Gannet matches the Petrel in yard, design and timber; the Petrel has needed no major hull repairs in twenty-five years.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: New case N shares features a, b, c with old case O; O had result R; so N will probably have R.

breakdown.analysis: This is an argument by analogy: same yard, same design, same wood as a boat that held up, so this one probably will too. The match needs a new case, an older case with several shared features, the old case's good result, and a "probably" prediction for the new one. A rule about every member of a group is a different argument, even if the conclusion sounds alike.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about boats from one yard lasting without repairs. But it deduces the result from a universal rule ("every boat built at the Kessing yard") with certainty. The original compares one boat to another and says "probably."
CORRECT. Same instructor, methods and simulators as last year's trainees, nearly all of whom passed; so this year's will probably pass. Shared features → same likely result. Same pattern.
Uses a difference between the cases to predict a different result. The original relies on similarities to predict the same result.
A generalization from an inspected sample to all of the yard's trawlers. No single comparison case.
A causal claim about why the Petrel lasted. The original never explains why; it just predicts that the Gannet will match.

questions.stimulus: Some residents blame vibration from the new highway for the cracks that have appeared in Varlow's old town hall. But if traffic vibration were the cause, the walls facing the highway would be the most badly cracked, and in fact the cracks are spread evenly over all four walls. So vibration from the highway is probably not what is causing the cracks.
