questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Some people say runoff from the new farm is killing the river's fish. If runoff were the cause, the fish nearest the farm would be dying first, and that is exactly what has happened. So runoff from the farm is surely the cause.

Some residents blame the new highway for the noise in their neighborhood. But the engineers who designed the highway insist that it is quieter than the old road it replaced. So the highway is probably not the cause of the noise.

The cracks in the town hall were caused either by vibration or by settling of the foundation. Inspectors found that the foundation has not settled at all. So the cracks in the town hall must have been caused by vibration.

Some blame the rising price of coffee for the café's falling sales. But even if the café lowered its prices, it would still face stiff competition from the new shop across the street. So the café should not lower its prices.

Some blame the bakery's new recipe for its falling bread sales. But if the recipe were the cause, sales of breads made with it would have fallen most, whereas all its breads fell equally. So the recipe is probably not the cause.
questions.explanation: The argument tests a proposed cause by its prediction: if H were true, we would see a certain pattern; we don't; so H is probably false. (E) does the same with the recipe and the pattern of bread sales. (A) is the reverse: the prediction comes true and the hypothesis is called certain. (B) relies on what experts say, (C) shares the town-hall topic but argues by elimination, and (D) ends in a recommendation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Highway vibration is probably not causing the cracks.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: If vibration were the cause, the walls facing the highway would be the most cracked; instead the cracks are spread evenly.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Some blame H for E; if H, we'd expect pattern P; P is absent; so H probably isn't the cause.

breakdown.analysis: This is how you test a suspect: if vibration did it, the damage would be worst on the highway side. It isn't, so vibration probably didn't do it. Find the answer that names a suspected cause, says what pattern that cause would produce, shows the pattern is missing, and rejects the cause with "probably." Expect a decoy where the predicted pattern does show up.

choices.note: Tempting, because it has the same "if H, we'd see P" setup. But here P shows up and the argument concludes the cause is certain. That runs the reasoning the other way and overstates it.
Same highway topic, but the rebuttal rests on what the designers say, not on a missing pattern. An appeal to authority.
Same town hall and cracks, but it's elimination (vibration or settling; not settling; so vibration), and it ends up blaming vibration.
Rejects lowering prices because of competition. No prediction tested against evidence, and it ends in a recommendation.
CORRECT. If the recipe were to blame, the new-recipe breads would have dropped most; all breads dropped equally; so probably not the recipe. Same test, same "probably not."

questions.stimulus: The robotics team at Wellsby High will compete in the national finals only if it wins the regional tournament, and it will win the regional tournament only if its robot is rebuilt before March. The team's coach has just learned that the robot cannot be rebuilt before March. So the team will not compete in the national finals.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Danica will be named head chef only if she completes the advanced pastry course, and she will complete that course only if the restaurant pays her tuition. The restaurant has agreed to pay her tuition. So Danica will be named head chef.

The orchestra will tour Europe only if it finds a corporate sponsor. The orchestra did not tour Europe this year. So it must not have found a corporate sponsor this year, despite all of the director's efforts to secure one.

The museum will open its new wing only if it raises the needed funds, and it will raise those funds only if the city provides a grant. So the museum should apply for the city's grant as soon as it possibly can.

The Hollis farm will qualify for the organic label only if it stops using synthetic fertilizer, and it will stop only if it can buy enough compost. It cannot buy enough compost. So it will not qualify for the organic label.

Robotics teams that win their regional tournament usually go on to compete in the national finals. The Wellsby team is favored to win its regional tournament this year. So the team will probably compete in the national finals.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two necessary conditions and then denies the last one: A only if B, B only if C, not C, so not A. (D) matches exactly. (A) is the trap: it has the same 'only if' chain but affirms the last condition and concludes the first, treating necessary conditions as sufficient. (B) uses one link and reasons backward, (C) ends in a recommendation, and (E) shares the robotics topic but reasons from 'usually.'

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The team will not compete in the national finals.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Finals → regional win → robot rebuilt before March; the robot can't be rebuilt in time.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A only if B; B only if C; not C; so not A.

breakdown.analysis: Translate "only if": finals → win regional → rebuilt by March. The robot won't be rebuilt, so no regional win, so no finals. Valid contrapositive chain. The match must have two "only if" links and must deny the last condition to deny the first. The classic decoy uses the same chain but affirms the last condition, which proves nothing.

choices.note: Tempting, because the "only if" chain looks identical. But it affirms the last condition (tuition paid) and concludes the first (head chef). Necessary isn't sufficient: paying tuition doesn't guarantee she finishes or gets the job.
Only one link, and it reasons from "didn't tour" to "no sponsor," which is backward: a sponsor is necessary for touring, not enough for it.
Same two-link chain, but no fact triggers it, and it ends with a recommendation. Different conclusion type.
CORRECT. Label → stop synthetic fertilizer → enough compost; not enough compost; so no label. A only if B, B only if C, not C, so not A.
Same robotics topic, but it reasons from "usually" and "favored" to "probably." No necessary conditions at all.

questions.stimulus: Last year, deliveries made by Pelling Couriers' bicycle couriers took 20 percent less time, on average, than they had the year before, while deliveries made by its van drivers took 5 percent more time, on average. Each group made about the same number of deliveries in both years. Yet the average time taken by all of the company's deliveries was greater last year than it had been the year before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: In each of the two years, Pelling Couriers' van drivers made more deliveries than its bicycle couriers did.
In the year before last, van deliveries accounted for far more of the company's total delivery time than bicycle deliveries did.
Most of the deliveries that the company's van drivers made last year took longer than such deliveries had taken the year before.
Pelling Couriers could reduce its average delivery time by assigning a larger share of its deliveries to bicycle couriers.
Traffic on the routes that Pelling Couriers' van drivers use became more congested last year than it had been the year before.
questions.explanation: With delivery counts steady, the overall average rises only if the vans' 5 percent increase adds more total time than the bicycles' 20 percent cut removes, so van deliveries must have accounted for more than four times as much total delivery time as bicycle deliveries; (B) states that. (A) is the dominant trap: it swaps total time for number of deliveries, but vans could make fewer deliveries that each take much longer. (C) treats an average as 'most,' and (D) and (E) add causes or predictions the facts don't support.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Bicycle deliveries got 20 percent faster on average; 2. Van deliveries got 5 percent slower on average; 3. Each group made about the same number of deliveries both years; 4. The company-wide average delivery time still rose.

breakdown.analysis: How can a 20 percent improvement lose to a 5 percent decline? Only if the van side is much bigger, measured in total minutes. Run numbers: say bikes used 100 total hours and vans 300. Bikes save 20 hours; vans add 15. Net change is down, so the average falls. To get a rise, vans' 5 percent must exceed bikes' 20 percent: van time has to be more than four times bike time. So van deliveries took up far more of the total time. Most students pick (A) because "bigger group" feels like "more deliveries." It fails because the weight here is total time, not count: a few long van runs can outweigh many quick bike trips.

choices.note: Tempting, and it's the trap most people take. It converts "more total time" into "more deliveries." But imagine 200 van deliveries at 60 minutes each and 400 bike deliveries at 5 minutes each: vans are fewer in number but have six times the total time. The facts force a time comparison, not a count comparison.

CORRECT. With counts steady, the overall average rises only if the vans' added time (5 percent of their total) beats the bikes' saved time (20 percent of their total). That needs van total time to be more than four times bike total time, which means far more of the total.
An average rising 5 percent doesn't mean most van deliveries got slower. A few very slow trips could pull the average up while most got faster. Average isn't "most."
Not supported. Bike and van deliveries may differ in distance or cargo; shifting work to bikes might not even be possible. A prediction the facts don't back.
Possible explanation for slower vans, but nothing in the facts points to traffic over other causes like longer routes.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: In the Tarsk Range, pikas whose winter dens lie beneath boulders thickly covered with moss are far more likely to survive the winter than pikas whose dens lie beneath bare boulders. A thick mat of moss traps a layer of air against the rock, so it probably insulates the dens beneath it from extreme cold, and this insulation is what improves those pikas' chances of surviving the winter.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the biologist's argument?
choices: During the long winter, pikas in the Tarsk Range often eat the moss that they scrape from the boulders above and around their dens.
Moss-covered boulders in the Tarsk Range tend to be larger than bare ones and so offer better protection from predators such as weasels.
Pikas cannot tolerate high temperatures, and they die quickly if they are exposed to the summer heat that is found at low elevations.
Moss grows very slowly in the Tarsk Range, so thick moss is found mainly on boulders that have not shifted for many decades.
On the range's lower slopes, where winters are mild, pikas under mossy boulders survive no more often than pikas under bare boulders.
questions.explanation: The biologist claims a specific mechanism: moss helps because it insulates against extreme cold. (E) supports that mechanism indirectly: the survival advantage disappears where the cold isn't extreme, which is exactly what insulation predicts and what rival explanations, such as food or predator protection, do not. (A) is the dominant trap: it ties moss to survival, but through eating, a different mechanism that competes with insulation. (B) and (D) also offer rival explanations, and (C) concerns heat, not winter cold.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The moss's insulation against extreme cold is what improves the pikas' winter survival.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pikas under mossy boulders survive winter far more often than those under bare boulders; moss traps air and so probably insulates.

breakdown.analysis: The correlation (moss, more survivors) is given. The argument's real claim is the mechanism: insulation against extreme cold. So what else could make mossy dens better? Food, cover from predators, steadier rocks. A strong strengthener shows the advantage tracks cold specifically. Think of a winter coat: if it's really the coat keeping you alive, the coat stops mattering on a mild day. Most students pick (A) because it links moss to survival. It fails because eating moss is a different way moss could help. It competes with the insulation story rather than supporting it.

choices.note: Tempting. It ties moss directly to winter survival. But the argument isn't just "moss helps"; it's "moss helps by insulating." Moss as food is a rival mechanism, so if anything it weakens the biologist's explanation.
A rival explanation: bigger boulders keep predators out. That would explain the survival gap without insulation. Weakens.
Irrelevant. Pikas' trouble with summer heat tells us nothing about why mossy dens help in winter cold.
Hints at another rival (stable boulders may make better dens). At best irrelevant; at worst it offers another cause besides insulation.

CORRECT. Where winters aren't extremely cold, the moss advantage vanishes. That's what insulation against extreme cold predicts. If moss helped through food or predator cover, the advantage should show up on the mild slopes too.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Critics claim that the congestion charge Ostley imposed on drivers entering its downtown has hurt downtown retailers, whose sales fell 8 percent in the year after the charge took effect. Admittedly, fewer shoppers now drive downtown. But retail sales fell by a similar percentage throughout the region, including at suburban malls the charge does not affect. So the charge is not what hurt downtown retailers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the economist's argument?
choices: In the years before the charge took effect, downtown retail sales had consistently grown much faster than retail sales elsewhere in the region.
Since the charge took effect, the number of cars entering downtown Ostley during business hours has fallen by about a third.
Revenue from the congestion charge has been used to expand bus service between Ostley's suburbs and its downtown shopping district.
A few downtown retailers, mostly those that sell groceries and other necessities, reported higher sales after the charge took effect.
Most suburban malls in the region provide free parking, whereas parking in downtown Ostley has long been expensive.
questions.explanation: The economist uses the region as a comparison group: since sales fell just as much where there is no charge, the charge can't be the cause. (A) undermines that comparison: downtown had been consistently outgrowing the region, so without the charge it would probably have done better, and merely matching the regional decline suggests a downtown-specific drag such as the charge. (B) is the dominant trap: it shows fewer drivers, but the economist already concedes that, and fewer drivers alone doesn't show lost sales. (C) tends to help the economist, and (D) and (E) don't touch the comparison.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The congestion charge is not what hurt downtown retailers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Downtown sales fell 8 percent, but sales fell by a similar percentage across the region, including where there is no charge (concession: fewer shoppers drive downtown).

breakdown.analysis: The whole rebuttal rests on one comparison: downtown fell about as much as everywhere else, so nothing special to downtown was at work. But is the region the right baseline? If downtown normally beats the region, then "falling the same" is actually doing worse than expected. It's like a straight-A student getting a B on a test where the class average dropped a grade: matching the class is still a slump for her. Most students pick (B) because it shows the charge kept cars out. It fails because the economist already admits fewer shoppers drive downtown; the question is whether that cost retailers sales, and (B) says nothing about sales.

choices.note: CORRECT. Downtown usually outgrew the region. If it had stayed on that path, it should have fallen less than the region or not at all. Falling just as much means downtown underperformed, and that points to something downtown-specific, like the charge.

Tempting. It makes the charge's effect vivid. But the economist already concedes that fewer shoppers drive downtown. Fewer cars doesn't show fewer sales: those shoppers may come by bus. It supports a point the argument already granted.
If anything, this helps the economist: better buses could bring back shoppers who stopped driving, softening any harm from the charge.
A few grocers doing well says little about retailers overall, and it doesn't touch the regional comparison.
This was true before the charge and stays true. It doesn't explain why the charge would or wouldn't change sales, and it doesn't touch the comparison.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: Since 2015, the forestry service has felled most of the old trees in Fenwold Wood, and over the same period the wood's population of marsh tits, which nest only in cavities in old trees, has fallen by half. Admittedly, the past several winters have been unusually harsh, and harsh winters can kill many small birds. Still, the loss of nesting sites, not the weather, is the main cause of the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ornithologist's argument?
choices: Marsh tits in Fenwold Wood have never once been observed nesting anywhere other than in cavities in the wood's old trees.
Winters in Fenwold Wood since 2015 have been colder, on average, than the winters of any comparable period on record there.
In several nearby woods where no old trees were felled, marsh tit populations have also fallen by about half since 2015.
Among banded adult marsh tits in Fenwold Wood, winter survival since 2015 has been no lower than in earlier years.
The forestry service has announced that it will stop felling old trees in Fenwold Wood once its current contracts expire.
questions.explanation: The ornithologist must show that the harsh winters, which are conceded, are not the main cause. (D) does that indirectly: if adult winter survival hasn't changed, the harsh winters aren't killing more birds, which leaves the loss of nest sites as the better explanation. (A) is the dominant trap: it sounds like support, but it only restates the premise that marsh tits nest only in old-tree cavities. (B) and (C) point toward the weather and so weaken, and (E) is about the future.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Loss of nesting sites, not the harsh weather, is the main cause of the marsh tit decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most old trees were felled since 2015; marsh tits nest only in old-tree cavities; the population halved (concession: winters were harsh, and harsh winters kill small birds).

breakdown.analysis: Two suspects: felling and winters. The ornithologist picks felling but never actually clears the winters. The best strengthener eliminates the rival. How? Show the winters aren't killing more birds than before. Think of a store whose sales dropped the year a rival opened and the year it rained a lot; you'd blame the rival more confidently if you learned foot traffic on rainy days was normal. Most students pick (A) because it's squarely about nesting in old trees. It fails because the stimulus already says they nest only there. Repeating a premise adds nothing.

choices.note: Tempting. It's on topic and sounds like evidence for the nest-site story. But the stimulus already tells us marsh tits nest only in cavities in old trees. Restating a premise doesn't strengthen the link between the felling and the decline, or rule out the winters.
This beefs up the rival suspect: the winters were record cold. That weakens the claim that weather isn't the main cause.
Opposite direction. Populations halved even where no trees were felled, which points to something shared, like the weather. Weakens.
CORRECT. If harsh winters were driving the decline, more adults would be dying each winter. They aren't. That removes the main rival and leaves the loss of nest sites as the better explanation.
Future plans don't tell us what caused the past decline. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Park ranger: Of the hikers who had to be rescued on Mount Tavel last year, 75 percent were carrying a GPS device at the time. Clearly, then, carrying a GPS device does little to keep hikers on the mountain from getting into the kind of trouble that requires a rescue.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the park ranger's argument?
choices: Hikers rescued on Mount Tavel who carried a GPS device were, on average, located by rescuers much more quickly than those who did not.
Most of last year's rescues on Mount Tavel involved hikers who had been injured in falls on steep or icy sections of trail.
Hikers without a GPS device make up only a small fraction of all those who hike on Mount Tavel.
The batteries in many GPS devices drain quickly in cold weather, which can leave hikers without a working device.
Many of the hikers on Mount Tavel who carry a GPS device also carry printed trail maps of the mountain.
questions.explanation: The ranger treats 75 percent of rescues as a high number without asking what share of all hikers carry GPS. (C) supplies that base rate: if hikers without GPS are only a small fraction of all hikers yet account for 25 percent of rescues, they are rescued at a far higher rate, which suggests GPS does help. (A) is the dominant trap: it shows a real benefit of GPS, but a benefit after the trouble starts (being found faster), not in avoiding the trouble the ranger is talking about. (B) and (D) tend to support the ranger, and (E) is irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Carrying a GPS device does little to keep hikers out of rescue-level trouble.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 75 percent of rescued hikers were carrying GPS.

breakdown.analysis: Is 75 percent a lot? That depends on how many hikers carry GPS in the first place. If 95 percent of hikers carry one, then GPS carriers are underrepresented among the rescued, and the 5 percent without GPS account for a quarter of rescues. That's a huge risk difference. It's like saying most drivers in accidents were wearing seatbelts, so seatbelts don't help; almost everyone wears one. Most students pick (A) because it shows GPS helps. It fails because it helps with a different thing: getting found faster. The ranger's claim is about getting into trouble, not about the rescue.

choices.note: Tempting. It's pro-GPS and about rescues. But it shows GPS helps rescuers find people faster, after they're already in trouble. The ranger's claim is that GPS doesn't keep hikers out of trouble. Wrong part of the argument.
If most rescues follow falls, and a GPS can't stop a fall, this tends to support the ranger.

CORRECT. If nearly every hiker carries GPS, 75 percent of rescues is actually low, and the few without GPS are rescued far out of proportion to their numbers. That suggests GPS does help keep hikers out of trouble.
Dead batteries would make GPS less useful, which fits the ranger's conclusion rather than weakening it.
Irrelevant. Carrying maps as well tells us nothing about whether carrying GPS lowers the chance of needing a rescue.

questions.stimulus: Cheesemaker: Cheeses aged in our dairy's old limestone caves develop a richer flavor than identical cheeses aged in our modern aging rooms, even though the rooms are kept at the same temperature and humidity as the caves. The difference must come from the molds that live naturally in the caves and settle on the cheeses' rinds as they age.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the cheesemaker's argument?
choices: In blind tastings, a panel of experienced judges consistently rated the cave-aged cheeses as having a richer flavor than the room-aged cheeses.
Air circulates much more slowly through the limestone caves than it does through the dairy's modern aging rooms.
The dairy's most experienced workers are the ones assigned to turn and brush the cheeses while they are aging in the caves.
Cheeses aged in the limestone caves sell for a higher price than cheeses aged in the dairy's modern aging rooms.
Cheeses aged in the modern rooms developed the richer flavor when placed on wooden shelves that had first spent a year in the caves.
questions.explanation: The cheesemaker credits the caves' molds rather than anything else about the caves. (E) supports this through an unstated mechanism: shelves that spent a year in the caves would carry the cave molds, and cheeses aged on them away from the caves developed the richer flavor, which rules out the rock, the air and the cave setting. (A) is the dominant trap: it confirms that the cave cheeses taste richer, which the argument already takes as given, but says nothing about why. (B) and (C) offer rival causes, and (D) is about price.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The caves' natural molds cause the richer flavor.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Cave-aged cheeses taste richer than identical room-aged cheeses; temperature and humidity are the same in both.

breakdown.analysis: The cheesemaker rules out temperature and humidity. But caves differ from rooms in lots of other ways: rock, airflow, who tends the cheese. We need evidence that points to the molds in particular. The neat way is to move the suspected cause and see if the effect moves with it. Shelves that sat in the caves for a year would pick up the cave molds; bring them into the modern rooms, and if the flavor follows, it's the molds, not the rock or the air. Most students pick (A) because it's strong evidence about flavor. It fails because the flavor difference is the premise. Proving the premise again doesn't explain the cause.

choices.note: Tempting. It's careful, expert evidence. But it only confirms that the cave cheeses taste richer, which the argument already assumes. It says nothing about whether molds are why.
A rival cause: slower air in the caves could produce the flavor. That weakens the mold explanation.
Another rival cause: better handling. Weakens.
Price tells us nothing about what causes the flavor.

CORRECT. Wood that spent a year in the caves carries the caves' molds but none of their rock or air. Cheeses aged on it in the modern rooms got the richer flavor. The effect followed the molds, which supports the cheesemaker's explanation.

questions.stimulus: Transit planner: The 8:00 a.m. express from Ashlow to the city is so crowded that many riders must stand for the whole trip, and most of them take it only because it is currently the sole morning express. So adding a second express that leaves Ashlow at 7:40 a.m. will substantially relieve crowding on the 8:00 train, since many of its riders will switch to the earlier one.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the transit planner's argument?
choices: Riders on the 8:00 a.m. express frequently complain to the transit authority that the train is too crowded for them to find a seat.
Some riders take the 8:00 a.m. express because it is the only train on the line with a quiet car in which phone calls are forbidden.
The transit authority will charge the same fare for a trip on the new 7:40 a.m. express as for a trip on the 8:00 a.m. express.
Most riders on the 8:00 a.m. express reach the Ashlow station on a connecting bus whose first morning arrival there is at 7:50.
Running the new 7:40 a.m. express will require the transit authority to hire two additional train crews at considerable expense.
questions.explanation: The plan depends on an unstated precondition: that the 8:00 riders can actually get to the station in time to catch a 7:40 train. (D) shows that most of them cannot, since their bus doesn't arrive until 7:50, so few will switch. (B) is the dominant trap: it seems to undercut the premise about why riders choose the 8:00 train, but 'some' riders is compatible with 'most' taking it only because it is the sole express. (A) restates the crowding, (C) removes a possible obstacle, and (E) is about cost.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Adding a 7:40 express will substantially relieve crowding on the 8:00 train.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The 8:00 is packed; most riders take it only because it's the sole express; many will switch to the 7:40.

breakdown.analysis: Will riders switch? The planner assumes they want to and can. Wanting is covered by the premise that most take the 8:00 only because it's the only express. But can they? An earlier train helps only people who can reach the station earlier. It's like adding an early class section for students who all ride a bus that arrives after it starts. We need an answer that blocks the switch. Most students pick (B) because it seems to attack why people ride the 8:00. It fails on the quantifier: "some" riders wanting the quiet car is perfectly consistent with "most" riding only because it's the sole express.

choices.note: Restates the crowding the planner already describes. Confirming a premise doesn't weaken anything.

Tempting. It looks like a reason riders won't leave the 8:00. But it's only "some" riders, and the planner says "most" take it only because it's the sole express. Those claims fit together, so the plan's logic survives.
Same fare removes a possible obstacle to switching. If anything it helps the plan.
CORRECT. Most 8:00 riders can't get to the station before 7:50, so they can't catch a 7:40 train. They'll stay on the 8:00, and the crowding won't ease much.
Wrong dimension. Expense might make the plan unwise, but it doesn't show the plan won't relieve crowding.

passages.title: Vera Linnaker’s self-translations
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
The poet Vera Linnaker wrote in Ostric, a language spoken by some two hundred thousand people on the Halse islands, and from 1952 until her death she translated most of her own poems into English. The English versions are anything but close. Lines are cut, images are replaced, and in several poems the closing stanza says nearly the opposite of what the original says. For decades her English-speaking readers knew her only through these versions, and when scholars who read Ostric began comparing the two, many concluded that the self-translations were simply inferior: hurried, compromised renderings by a poet working in a language she had learned as an adult.

The critic Tomas Hendry has argued that this judgment misunderstands what Linnaker was doing. A translator working on another writer’s poem, he observes, is bound by the original, because its author is the authority on what it means; but when author and translator are one person, that authority travels with the translation. On Hendry’s view, the English versions should therefore be read as revisions, later and so final statements of what the poems were meant to be, and the Ostric texts as drafts that the English versions superseded. Hendry notes, too, that Linnaker never called the English poems translations; their title pages describe them as “versions by the author.”

Hendry is right that Linnaker’s departures cannot be dismissed as the lapses of an unequal translator. Her letters show her laboring over the English versions for months and rejecting closer renderings that her editors proposed. But his conclusion does not follow from that premise. That the departures were deliberate shows that she meant the English poems to be as they are; it does not show that she meant them to replace the originals. Indeed, she continued to publish the Ostric texts, unchanged, in new editions at home, which is hard to reconcile with the claim that she regarded them as superseded. She once told an interviewer that the two texts of a poem were “twins, not parent and child.”

A more plausible view is that Linnaker produced pairs of related poems for two audiences. Her Ostric readers shared a stock of local reference—place-names, hymns, the vocabulary of the islands’ farming calendar—that her English readers lacked, and many of her changes replace such references with ones an outsider could follow, leaving the sense of the poem much as it was. Where the English closing stanzas reverse the originals, however, no such explanation is available, and there the two poems differ in more than idiom. In those cases, especially, neither version should be privileged over the other: each shows what the poem might have been, and each is best read alongside the other.

passages.title: Staggered market days in the Vellan lowlands
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
In the Vellan lowlands during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, some forty towns held weekly markets, and the towns’ charters reveal a striking pattern: towns lying within a day’s walk of one another almost never shared a market day. A town whose market met on Tuesday was typically ringed by neighbors meeting on Monday, Wednesday, or Thursday. Historians long attributed the pattern to rivalry among the lords who held the markets. Because a market brought its holder tolls, a lord who chartered a market on the same day as a nearby one could expect the holder of the older market to challenge it in court, and the staggered days were, on this view, the residue of such disputes.

The economic historian Clara Wendt has proposed instead that the pattern arose from the needs of itinerant traders: the peddlers, cattle dealers, and cloth merchants who carried goods from town to town. A trader who could attend a different market on each day of the week could sell to the customers of several towns rather than one, and towns whose market days fit into such circuits drew more traders and therefore more buyers. A peddler’s week, as Wendt reconstructs it from surviving account books, might take him through five or six towns in a loop that brought him home by Saturday. Staggering, on this account, was a coordination the towns arrived at because each of them gained from it, not a truce imposed by litigation.

Wendt’s strongest evidence is a set of charters recording changes of market day. Of the thirty-one changes recorded between 1550 and 1650, twenty-six moved a town’s market off a day it shared with a neighbor, and most were requested by the townspeople themselves rather than imposed after a lawsuit. A theory of lordly rivalry cannot easily explain why towns would abandon days that no court had forbidden them to keep, or why the pattern holds even among towns whose lords were allied by marriage and had no record of quarrels.

Still, Wendt’s account explains why the pattern was maintained better than it explains why it arose. The earliest Vellan markets were chartered in the thirteenth century, when the region’s itinerant trade was slight, and the surviving court records from that period show numerous disputes between lords over conflicting market days. It seems likely that litigation produced the first staggered days and that the advantages Wendt identifies, which grew along with the trade, later gave towns reason to keep the pattern and extend it to markets founded afterward. The arrangement, in other words, may owe its origin to one set of circumstances and its persistence to another, and an account built on evidence from the later period should not be expected to explain both.

passages.title: Child trespassers and artificial hazards
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Under the law of the province of Ardena, a landowner ordinarily owes a trespasser no duty except to refrain from injuring him deliberately. Since the 1880s, however, Ardenan courts have recognized an exception for children. A landowner who maintains an artificial hazard—an unfenced reservoir, a stack of loose timber, idle machinery—may be liable to a trespassing child injured by it if the owner knew that children were likely to enter, the child was too young to appreciate the danger, and the hazard could have been made safe at modest cost. The courts first justified the exception on the ground that such hazards “invite” children onto the land, so that the child is not truly a trespasser; for decades, accordingly, a child could recover only by showing that the hazard itself had drawn him there.

That requirement has since been abandoned, and the legal scholar Miriam Achterberg argues that its abandonment exposes the exception’s real basis. Once the child need not have been lured by the hazard, the fiction of invitation does no work. What remains, Achterberg contends, is a judgment that a child’s inability to recognize danger shifts responsibility to the adult best placed to prevent harm. The exception, on this view, is not really an exception at all but an application of the ordinary principle of negligence—that one must take reasonable care against foreseeable injury—to persons whose presence is foreseeable even though unwelcome.

Achterberg’s reconstruction makes good sense of the doctrine’s elements: the owner’s knowledge establishes foreseeability, the child’s youth explains why the danger was not obvious to the victim, and the modest cost of a remedy marks the precaution as reasonable. But it fits poorly with a limitation the courts have never relaxed: the exception covers only artificial hazards. An owner whose land contains a natural pond is not liable when a trespassing child drowns in it, however foreseeable the child’s presence and however cheaply the pond might have been fenced. If ordinary negligence were the doctrine’s whole basis, this line would be arbitrary.

Achterberg replies that natural features are so widespread that requiring owners to guard them all would be unreasonably burdensome. The reply has force for large tracts of open country, but not for a single pond beside a schoolyard. A better explanation may be that the courts have kept, without saying so, part of the logic of the invitation theory. That theory blamed the owner for something he had done—placing a lure on his land—and the artificial-hazard limit preserves its focus on the owner’s own conduct: one who builds a hazard has helped bring the danger about, whereas one who holds land as nature left it has not. If so, the doctrine rests on two foundations, foreseeability and the owner’s agency, and Achterberg’s account captures only the first.

passages.title: Persister cells in Marisella
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
When a culture of the soil bacterium Marisella fenni is exposed to the antibiotic cardomycin, nearly all of its cells die within hours, but a small fraction, typically about one cell in ten thousand, survives. If the survivors are allowed to multiply and the new culture is exposed in turn, the same small fraction survives again: the survivors’ descendants are no harder to kill than the original population was. The survivors, called persisters, are therefore not resistant mutants. They are cells that happened, at the moment of exposure, to be in a state in which the drug could not kill them. Because cardomycin attacks the machinery of cell growth, the leading explanation is that persisters are dormant: having stopped growing, they offer the drug nothing to act on.

Two accounts of how cells come to be dormant have been proposed. On the first, associated with the microbiologist Ruth Abernathy, dormancy is a response: cells enter it when they detect stresses such as starvation, so that the number of persisters in a culture should depend on the conditions the culture has experienced. On the second, defended by Lars Pettersen, dormancy arises by chance: every growing cell has a small, constant probability of switching into dormancy whatever its conditions, so that a population always contains a few dormant cells, a hedge against catastrophes it cannot anticipate. Either account explains why the survivors’ descendants are no harder to kill, since on both views dormancy is a passing state rather than an inherited trait.

Experiments with Marisella have been taken to favor chance switching. Pettersen’s group tracked individual cells in a microfluidic chamber supplied with a steady flow of abundant nutrients. Dormant cells appeared at a low but constant rate, and when cardomycin was added, these were the cells that survived. The observations were repeated in several hundred chambers, and the rate varied little among them. Because the chamber imposed no starvation, Pettersen argued, the dormancy could not have been a response to stress.

This inference is weaker than it looks. Conditions that are uniform at the scale of a chamber need not be uniform at the scale of a cell. A cell’s internal supply of a scarce metabolite fluctuates as the cell grows and divides, and a cell that happened to run short might sense a starvation the chamber never imposed. What the experiment shows, then, is that dormancy can arise without stress in the environment, not that it arises without stress the cell detects. It does establish a more modest point of some importance: persister formation does not require that a population have faced hardship. That finding is consistent with Pettersen’s hedging account, but it is not decisive against Abernathy’s.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Linnaker’s English versions are hurried and compromised renderings of her poems, produced by a poet writing in a language she had learned as an adult.
Because Linnaker’s departures from her originals were deliberate, her English versions should be read as her final statements of what the poems were meant to be.
Although Linnaker’s departures from her originals were deliberate, her English versions are better read as companions to the Ostric poems than as replacements for them.
Linnaker’s letters show that she labored over her English versions for months and rejected the closer renderings that her editors proposed to her.
The scholars who compared Linnaker’s English versions with her Ostric originals failed to notice how much her two audiences of readers differed.
questions.explanation: The author grants Hendry that the departures were deliberate (first sentence of the third paragraph) but denies that the English versions replace the originals, concluding that Linnaker produced 'pairs of related poems' and that 'neither version should be privileged' (fourth paragraph). C states that position. B is the most tempting trap: it is Hendry's conclusion, which the author says 'does not follow.' A is the earlier scholars' view, D is a supporting detail from the third paragraph, and E puts a claim about the scholars in the author's mouth that the passage never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall position on how Linnaker's English versions should be read.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentences of the third paragraph and the fourth paragraph, and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Three views: the scholars (inferior translations), Hendry (deliberate revisions that supersede the originals), and the author (deliberate, yes, but companions, not replacements). The author takes Hendry's premise and rejects his conclusion. We need both halves: deliberate, but not a replacement.

choices.note: This is the earlier scholars' view, and both Hendry and the author reject it: the departures were deliberate, not lapses.

Tempting, because the author agrees the departures were deliberate. But this is Hendry's conclusion, and the author says it 'does not follow from that premise.' Deliberate isn't the same as meant to replace.
CORRECT. The concession (deliberate departures) plus the author's own view (pairs of related poems, neither privileged).
True (third paragraph), but it's evidence for one step, not the point of the passage.
The author never says the scholars overlooked the two audiences. The audiences come up in the author's own account, not as a criticism of the scholars.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the scholars described in the last sentence of the first paragraph regarded
choices: Linnaker’s Ostric texts as the standard against which her English versions should be measured
Linnaker’s English versions as revisions that superseded the poems she had written in Ostric
the local place-names and hymns in the Ostric poems as impossible to translate
Linnaker’s command of English as equal to her command of the Ostric language
the reversed closing stanzas as the most successful of the changes Linnaker made
questions.explanation: These scholars compared the two texts and judged the English versions 'inferior…renderings' (first paragraph). Calling a version an inferior rendering means measuring it against the original, so A is correct. B is the trap: it is Hendry's view, which he offers against those scholars. D contradicts their remark about a language 'she had learned as an adult,' and C and E have no support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the scholars who compared the texts must have assumed.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What did they conclude? That the English versions were inferior renderings. Inferior to what? The originals. So they treated the Ostric poems as the yardstick. Prephrase: the originals are the standard.

choices.note: CORRECT. Judging the English versions as inferior renderings only makes sense if the Ostric texts are the benchmark.
Tempting, because the passage says it. But it's Hendry's view, offered against these scholars. They saw the English versions as failed copies, not as final revisions.
Local references appear in the author's account in the fourth paragraph, and nobody says they can't be translated.
Opposite. They put the problems down to a language 'she had learned as an adult,' which implies her English was weaker.
No support. They thought the versions inferior across the board, and the passage reports no ranking of changes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Hendry holds that
choices: the English versions are hurried renderings by a poet writing in a language learned in adulthood
in all of Linnaker’s English versions, the closing stanza reverses the sense of the original
neither the Ostric texts nor the English versions should be privileged over the other
Linnaker wrote her English versions as separate poems for readers who lacked local knowledge
a poet who translates her own poem keeps an authority over its meaning that other translators lack
questions.explanation: The second paragraph reports Hendry's claim that a translator of another's poem is bound by the original, but 'when author and translator are one person, that authority travels with the translation.' E paraphrases this. C and D are the strongest traps: both use the passage's own language, but they are the author's views from the fourth paragraph, offered against Hendry. A is the earlier scholars' view, and B turns 'several poems' into 'all' and is not attributed to Hendry anyway.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the statement the passage attributes to Hendry, not to the earlier scholars or the author.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph (Hendry). Compare the last sentence of the first paragraph (the scholars) and the fourth paragraph (the author).

breakdown.analysis: Keep the three voices apart. Scholars: inferior renderings. Hendry: self-translation carries the author's authority, so the English versions are final and the originals are drafts. Author: two related poems for two audiences, neither privileged. Expect traps that hand the author's words to Hendry, plus one with a quantifier stretched ('several' to 'all').

choices.note: Wrong person. This is the scholars' judgment, the one Hendry says 'misunderstands what Linnaker was doing.'
Too strong, and not Hendry's. The first paragraph says 'in several poems,' not all, and it's the passage's description of the texts.
Tempting, because it's nearly a quotation. But it's the author's conclusion. Hendry privileges the English versions as final.
Tempting for the same reason. The two-audience account is the author's 'more plausible view,' offered as an alternative to Hendry's.
CORRECT. 'When author and translator are one person, that authority travels with the translation.' Other translators are 'bound by the original.'

questions.stem: The author mentions that Linnaker continued to publish the Ostric texts unchanged (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that Linnaker’s Ostric readers preferred her originals to her English versions
offer evidence against the claim that Linnaker regarded her Ostric texts as superseded
support Hendry’s claim that Linnaker’s departures from her originals were deliberate
explain why Linnaker’s English-speaking readers knew her poems only through the versions she made herself
suggest that Linnaker’s editors had objected to the changes she made in translating
questions.explanation: The author says the unchanged reissues are 'hard to reconcile with the claim that she regarded them as superseded' (third paragraph), so they are evidence against Hendry's conclusion, as B says. C is the trap: the deliberateness of the departures is supported by the letters, not by the reissues, and the reissues are used against Hendry, not for him. A, D, and E bring in claims the passage never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up the unchanged Ostric editions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The author tells you the job right away: the reissues are 'hard to reconcile with the claim that she regarded them as superseded.' Who made that claim? Hendry. So the fact is evidence against Hendry's conclusion.

choices.note: Nothing about what Ostric readers preferred. The point is about what Linnaker herself thought of the originals.
CORRECT. If she thought the Ostric texts were superseded drafts, why keep reprinting them unchanged? It counts against Hendry's conclusion.
Tempting, because the author does accept that the departures were deliberate. But the evidence for that is the letters. The reissues are aimed at a different claim, and against Hendry.
English readers relied on her versions because they didn't read Ostric (first paragraph). That has nothing to do with the reissues.
The editors proposed closer renderings, and she rejected them. The reissues aren't about the editors.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A controversy about a poet’s translations is described, a critic’s resolution of that controversy is presented and defended against an objection, and the implications of that resolution are then drawn out.
Two opposing assessments of a poet’s translations are described, evidence bearing on each is weighed, and the earlier of the two assessments is ultimately shown to be correct.
The reception of a poet’s translations is traced through several stages, the reasons for each change are identified, and a prediction about their future standing is offered.
A judgment about a poet’s translations is described, a critic’s rejection of it is presented, the critic’s conclusion is shown not to follow from his evidence, and an alternative is proposed.
A view of translation in general is presented, a critic’s objections to that view are rejected, and an alternative theory of how translators should treat their originals is developed.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 gives the scholars' judgment, paragraph 2 gives Hendry's rejection of it, paragraph 3 argues that his 'conclusion does not follow from that premise,' and paragraph 4 offers 'a more plausible view.' D matches every step. A is the main trap: it has Hendry's view 'defended against an objection,' but the author raises the objection and never answers it. B wrongly vindicates the scholars, C invents a prediction, and E turns a passage about one poet into a general theory of translation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match each paragraph to a step in the answer choice. One wrong step kills a choice.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of each paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: 1. scholars' judgment (inferior); 2. Hendry rejects it (deliberate, final revisions); 3. author: his conclusion doesn't follow; 4. author's alternative (two related poems). Organization answers are long; check every clause.

choices.note: Tempting, because the first two steps fit. But the third step is backwards: the author objects to Hendry and doesn't defend him.
The scholars' view (inferior renderings) is rejected by both Hendry and the author, so nobody shows it correct.
There's a little reception history, but no stages with causes for each and no prediction.
CORRECT. Judgment (inferior), critic's rejection (Hendry), conclusion doesn't follow (deliberate ≠ meant to replace), alternative (pairs of poems).
The passage is about Linnaker's self-translations, not translation in general, and the author accepts part of Hendry's argument.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The reversed closing stanzas in Linnaker’s English versions resulted from her imperfect command of English.
Some of Linnaker’s changes reflect differences between what her two groups of readers already knew.
Hendry was wrong to claim that Linnaker’s departures from her originals were deliberate ones.
Linnaker regarded her English versions as better poems than those she wrote in Ostric.
English-speaking readers should read Linnaker’s poems in close translations made by others.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says that 'many of her changes replace such references with ones an outsider could follow,' references her Ostric readers shared and her English readers lacked. B restates this modestly. A contradicts the author's acceptance that the departures were deliberate, C reverses the author's agreement with Hendry on that point, D conflicts with the 'twins, not parent and child' remark, and E has no support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's views support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph, with the first two sentences of the third.

breakdown.analysis: The author explains many changes by audience: Ostric readers knew the local references, English readers didn't, so she swapped them. Look for an answer that says that, worded modestly ('some').

choices.note: Contradicted. The author agrees with Hendry that the departures 'cannot be dismissed as the lapses of an unequal translator.' The reversals are the case where the poems 'differ in more than idiom,' not mistakes.
CORRECT. Many changes replace local references that English readers wouldn't know. 'Some' is safely within 'many.'
Reversed. 'Hendry is right that Linnaker's departures cannot be dismissed' as lapses; the author accepts that they were deliberate.
No. Her 'twins, not parent and child' remark points the other way: neither version ranks above the other.
The author never recommends other translators. The fourth paragraph values her English versions as poems in their own right.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The staggered market days of the Vellan lowlands were maintained throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries by lords’ lawsuits against competing markets.
Wendt has shown that the staggering of market days in the Vellan lowlands arose from the needs of itinerant traders who traveled from town to town.
Most of the changes of market day recorded in Vellan charters between 1550 and 1650 moved a town’s market off a day it shared with a neighbor.
Wendt’s account of the staggered market days in the Vellan lowlands explains why the pattern persisted better than it explains how the pattern arose.
Vellan towns staggered their market days chiefly because their lords forbade them to compete with one another for the tolls paid by traders.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph's first sentence states the thesis: Wendt's account 'explains why the pattern was maintained better than it explains why it arose,' and the final sentence restates it. That is D. B is the main trap: it credits Wendt with explaining the pattern's origin, which is exactly what the author doubts. A contradicts the third paragraph's evidence that towns changed days voluntarily, C is a supporting detail, and E invents a prohibition the passage never mentions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall conclusion about Wendt's explanation of the staggered market days.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first and last sentences of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1–3 report others: the old lordly-rivalry view and Wendt's trader-circuit view with her evidence. Paragraph 4 opens with 'Still' and gives the verdict: Wendt explains persistence, but the origin probably lies in litigation. We need persistence-yes, origin-not-so-much.

choices.note: Contradicted for the later period. The third paragraph shows towns moving their days on their own, not because of lawsuits. The author ties litigation to the thirteenth-century origin only.
Tempting, because it's Wendt's thesis. But 'arose' is the problem: the author thinks litigation probably produced the first staggered days, when itinerant trade was slight.
True (third paragraph), but it's Wendt's evidence, not the passage's main point.
CORRECT. That's the first sentence of the fourth paragraph, restated in the passage's last sentence.
No one in the passage says lords forbade towns to compete. The rivalry view is about lawsuits between lords, not orders to towns.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the changes of market day recorded in Vellan charters between 1550 and 1650
choices: were for the most part imposed on towns as a result of lawsuits between lords
without exception moved a town’s market off a day it shared with a neighbor
occurred chiefly in towns lying more than a day’s walk from any other market town
were made at the request of itinerant traders who wished to attend more markets
were more often sought by the towns themselves than ordered after litigation
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says that 'most were requested by the townspeople themselves rather than imposed after a lawsuit,' which E paraphrases. B is the strongest trap: it echoes the passage but turns 'twenty-six' of thirty-one into 'without exception.' A reverses the statement, D gives the requests to the traders instead of the townspeople, and C has no support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the recorded changes of market day.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Two facts about the 31 changes: 26 moved a market off a shared day, and most were requested by townspeople, not imposed after a lawsuit. Expect a trap that rounds 26 of 31 up to all, and one that swaps who asked for the change.

choices.note: Reversed. Most were requested by the townspeople 'rather than imposed after a lawsuit.'
Tempting, because it's nearly the passage's wording. But it was 26 of 31, not all. Five changes didn't move a market off a shared day.
Nothing about distance. The pattern concerns towns within a day's walk of each other.
Wrong party. The townspeople requested the changes. Traders are the reason Wendt thinks towns wanted them, but the passage never says traders asked.
CORRECT. 'Most were requested by the townspeople themselves rather than imposed after a lawsuit.'

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that, according to the view historians long held, a lord who chartered a market on the same day as a nearby market
choices: risked a legal challenge from the holder of the nearby market
was usually made to move his market to another day by the townspeople
could expect to draw more itinerant traders than the nearby market drew
collected higher tolls than lords whose markets met on other days
was acting with the consent of the holder of the older market
questions.explanation: On the older view, such a lord 'could expect the holder of the older market to challenge it in court' (first paragraph), which A restates. C is the trap: it borrows Wendt's emphasis on traders, but on her account a shared day would draw fewer traders, not more. B confuses the old view with the later evidence about townspeople, and D and E have no support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the old rivalry view says happens to a lord who picks a nearby market's day.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The old view in one line: markets earn tolls, so a same-day rival gets challenged in court. Prephrase: he'd probably get sued.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Could expect the holder of the older market to challenge it in court.'
Townspeople requesting changes is Wendt's evidence from 1550–1650, not part of the old view.
Backwards, and from the wrong view. Wendt's point is that overlapping days fit trader circuits badly, so a shared day would draw fewer traders.
No support. Same-day competition would, if anything, cut into tolls, which is why lords sued.
The opposite. The old view assumes the older market's holder objected.

questions.stem: The author mentions “peddlers, cattle dealers, and cloth merchants” (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: explain why holding a market brought its holder tolls
suggest that livestock dominated the trade of the Vellan lowlands
identify the kinds of traders on whose travels Wendt’s account depends
give examples of the parties to lawsuits over conflicting market days
show that itinerant trade in the region was slight in the thirteenth century
questions.explanation: The list follows the colon after 'itinerant traders' and names who they were; the rest of the paragraph explains how their circuits made staggering valuable (second paragraph). C is correct. B overreads one item in the list, D confuses the traders with the lords who sued, and A and E draw on the first and fourth paragraphs instead.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the passage lists these three kinds of traders.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The list comes right after 'the needs of itinerant traders:' and spells out who those traders were. Wendt's whole account runs on their weekly circuits. So the list identifies the people her explanation is about.

choices.note: Tolls come up in the first paragraph as part of the old view. The list isn't about them.
Cattle dealers are one of three examples. Nothing says livestock dominated.
CORRECT. These are the itinerant traders whose circuits make staggered days worthwhile on Wendt's account.
The lawsuits were between lords, not traders.
The thirteenth century comes up in the fourth paragraph. The list doesn't say anything about how big the trade was then.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship of the fourth paragraph to the third paragraph?
choices: The fourth paragraph presents evidence that undermines the reliability of the evidence described in the third paragraph.
The fourth paragraph limits the scope of an explanation that the evidence described in the third paragraph supports.
The fourth paragraph offers an alternative interpretation of the changes of market day described in the third paragraph.
The fourth paragraph extends the explanation supported in the third paragraph to an earlier period in the region’s history.
The fourth paragraph shows that the evidence described in the third paragraph is better explained by the theory of lordly rivalry.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph gives Wendt's evidence from 1550–1650; the fourth accepts that her account explains why the pattern 'was maintained' but argues that litigation likely explains why it 'arose.' That is a limit on scope, as B says. D is the main trap: the fourth paragraph does turn to an earlier period, but to argue that Wendt's explanation does not fit it. E is also tempting because the author revives the rivalry theory, but only for the thirteenth century, not for the later changes. A and C wrongly have the author dispute or reinterpret the third paragraph's evidence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what the fourth paragraph does to the claims of the third.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The whole third paragraph and the first, third, and last sentences of the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Does the author fight Wendt's charter evidence? No. The author grants it explains why the pattern lasted, and says Wendt's advantages 'later gave towns reason to keep the pattern.' What the author denies is that the evidence reaches back to the pattern's start. That's a scope limit. Two traps to expect: one that has the author applying Wendt to the thirteenth century (the reverse), and one that hands the later evidence to the rivalry theory (too far).

choices.note: Too hostile. The author never questions the charters; the advantages Wendt identifies are accepted for the later period.
CORRECT. The third paragraph supports Wendt's account; the fourth confines it to the pattern's persistence, not its origin.
The fourth paragraph doesn't reinterpret the 1550–1650 changes. It talks about a different period, the thirteenth century.

Tempting, because the fourth paragraph does go back to an earlier period. But it argues Wendt's explanation does not fit there: trade was slight and lords were suing. This reverses the paragraph's point.
Tempting, because the author does revive the rivalry theory. But only for the origin. The later changes are still explained by Wendt's advantages, and the author says so.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Wendt’s account of the staggered market days is best described as
choices: skepticism about the evidence on which it chiefly relies, combined with sympathy for its general aims
qualified acceptance, tempered by doubt that the charters on which it relies are representative of the region as a whole
firm rejection, on the ground that thirteenth-century court records show numerous disputes between lords
general endorsement, with the reservation that it overstates the role that litigation played in producing the pattern of days
acceptance of it as an account of the pattern’s persistence, together with doubt that it explains the pattern’s origin
questions.explanation: The author calls the charters Wendt's 'strongest evidence,' accepts that 'the advantages Wendt identifies' gave towns reason to keep the pattern, and doubts only that her account explains why the pattern 'arose' (fourth paragraph). E states that mix. B is the strongest trap: it has the right tone but puts the reservation on the representativeness of the charters, which the author never questions. A has the same misplaced doubt, C overshoots to rejection, and D reverses the reservation, since the author thinks Wendt gives litigation too small a role, not too large.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author regards Wendt's account, including what the author accepts and what the author doubts.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the third paragraph and the whole fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Mostly for Wendt, with one reservation. Find what the reservation is about. Not her evidence (it's her 'strongest'). Not her mechanism (her advantages explain why towns kept the pattern). It's reach: she can't explain the start, when trade was slight and lords were suing. The right answer must name that reservation.

choices.note: The author doesn't doubt the evidence; the third paragraph presents it as Wendt's strongest, and the fourth builds on it.
Tempting: 'qualified acceptance' is the right tone. But the qualification is in the wrong place. The author never suggests the charters are unrepresentative; the doubt is about the pattern's origin.
Too strong. The court records limit Wendt's account to the later period; they don't sink it.
Reversed. Wendt calls staggering 'not a truce imposed by litigation'; the author thinks litigation probably started the pattern. If anything, she understates litigation's role.
CORRECT. Persistence explained (accepted), origin not explained (doubted). That's the first sentence of the fourth paragraph.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Although the children’s exception reflects ordinary negligence principles, as Achterberg argues, its limitation to artificial hazards suggests that it also rests on an owner’s responsibility for dangers the owner has created.

The children’s exception is best understood not as an exception at all but as an application of the ordinary principle of negligence to trespassers whose presence on the land is foreseeable though unwelcome.

Because the children’s exception covers only artificial hazards, the courts’ refusal to hold landowners liable for injuries that natural hazards cause to trespassing children is arbitrary and ought to be abandoned.
Despite the abandonment of the luring requirement, the children’s exception still depends on the fiction that artificial hazards invite children onto land that they enter.
Achterberg’s account of the children’s exception fails to make sense of the doctrine’s elements, since an owner’s knowledge that children may enter does not establish foreseeability.
questions.explanation: The author accepts that Achterberg's reconstruction 'makes good sense of the doctrine's elements' but argues that the artificial-hazard limit shows a second foundation, 'the owner's agency,' which her account misses (last sentence of the fourth paragraph). A captures both halves. B is the dominant trap: it is Achterberg's thesis, in the passage's own words, and the author's point is that it is incomplete. C turns the author's conditional ('If ordinary negligence were the doctrine's whole basis, this line would be arbitrary') into an outright verdict, D overstates keeping 'part of the logic' of the invitation theory as keeping the fiction itself, and E contradicts the third paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall position on Achterberg's account of the children's exception.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first two sentences of the third paragraph and the last sentence of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: This is a concede-and-correct passage. Concession: Achterberg is right that negligence ideas (foreseeability, reasonable precaution) explain the elements. Correction: the artificial-only limit doesn't fit pure negligence, so the doctrine must also rest on what the owner did. The last sentence says it outright: two foundations, and Achterberg captures only the first. A main-point answer here needs the concession and the 'also.' Be careful with the conditional 'If ordinary negligence were the whole basis, this line would be arbitrary.' The author uses it to show negligence isn't the whole basis, not to call the line arbitrary.

choices.note: CORRECT. Concession (negligence principles are really there) plus the author's addition (a second basis in the owner's responsibility for dangers the owner created). It's the 'two foundations' sentence in other words.

Tempting, because it's nearly a quotation of the second paragraph, and the author does agree with much of it. But this is Achterberg's whole thesis, and the author's point is that it's incomplete: the doctrine 'rests on two foundations' and she captures 'only the first.'

The author says the line would be arbitrary only if negligence were the whole basis, and then argues it isn't. The author never calls the line arbitrary or says it should go. This turns a conditional into a conclusion.
Too strong. The author says the courts kept 'part of the logic' of the invitation theory (its focus on the owner's conduct), not the fiction that children are invited. The luring requirement is gone.
Contradicted. The third paragraph says the owner's knowledge 'establishes foreseeability' and that Achterberg's reconstruction 'makes good sense of the doctrine's elements.'

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that, before the requirement described in the last sentence of the first paragraph was abandoned, a trespassing child injured by an artificial hazard could not recover if the child
choices: was injured on land whose owner knew that children were likely to enter
had been drawn onto the land by the hazard that caused the injury
was too young to appreciate the danger that the hazard posed
had entered the land for some reason unrelated to the hazard
was injured by a hazard that could have been made safe at little cost
questions.explanation: Under the old requirement 'a child could recover only by showing that the hazard itself had drawn him there' (last sentence of the first paragraph). A child who came for another reason could not show that, so D is correct. B states the condition for recovering, not for failing to recover. A, C, and E are elements that help a child's claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation in which a child could not recover under the old requirement.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: 'Recover only if the hazard drew him there.' Recover → drawn by the hazard. Contrapositive: not drawn by the hazard → no recovery. So a child who came for some other reason loses.

choices.note: The owner's knowledge is one of the elements that supports liability. It helps the child.
This is the reverse. Being drawn by the hazard was what let a child recover.
Youth is another element that supports the child's claim.
CORRECT. Recovery required that the hazard drew the child. A child who came for another reason fails that requirement.
Cheap safety measures make the owner's failure less reasonable, which helps the child.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Achterberg holds that
choices: the artificial-hazard limitation preserves the invitation theory’s focus on the owner’s own conduct
landowners should be required to guard natural features that lie close to places where children gather
the abandonment of the luring requirement revealed what had actually justified the children’s exception
the luring requirement was abandoned because courts came to regard invitation as a legal fiction
an owner who knows that children are likely to enter is liable for any injury that they suffer there
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says Achterberg 'argues that its abandonment exposes the exception's real basis,' which C paraphrases. A is the strongest trap: it uses the passage's language, but it is the author's 'better explanation' from the fourth paragraph, offered against Achterberg. D supplies a cause for the abandonment that the passage never gives; Achterberg says the abandonment shows the invitation idea was a fiction, not that courts dropped it for that reason. B and E are unsupported and too strong.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the view the passage attributes to Achterberg, not to the courts or the author.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph and the first sentence of the fourth paragraph (Achterberg's views). Compare with the rest of the fourth paragraph (the author's view).

breakdown.analysis: Keep the voices apart. Achterberg: dropping the luring requirement exposes the real basis, which is ordinary negligence; and natural features are too common to guard. The author: the artificial-only limit keeps part of the invitation logic. Expect a trap that hands the author's idea to Achterberg, and one that invents a reason the courts acted.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's in the passage nearly word for word. But it's the author's explanation ('A better explanation may be…'), offered to show what Achterberg's account misses.
Nobody in the passage proposes this. Achterberg actually argues the opposite direction: guarding natural features would be too burdensome.
CORRECT. 'Its abandonment exposes the exception's real basis.' The basis was there all along; dropping the requirement revealed it.
This reverses the direction of the claim. Achterberg says that once the requirement was abandoned, the invitation idea does no work. She says nothing about why courts abandoned it.
Too strong. Knowledge is one of several elements (youth, modest cost, artificial hazard). Achterberg never says knowledge alone creates liability for any injury.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of an Ardenan landowner whose land contains a natural pond?
choices: The owner owes no duty of any kind to a child who enters the land without the owner’s permission, whatever the child’s age.
The owner is shielded from liability because the courts have judged that guarding natural features would be unreasonably burdensome.
The owner can be held liable if the pond lies beside a schoolyard and could have been fenced at little cost.
The owner can be held liable to a trespassing child only if the pond itself drew the child onto the land in the first place.
Knowing that children are likely to enter does not make the owner liable to a trespassing child who drowns in the pond.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says such an owner 'is not liable when a trespassing child drowns in it, however foreseeable the child's presence,' which E restates. A is the trap with the passage's own wording: the first sentence says a landowner owes a trespasser 'no duty except to refrain from injuring him deliberately,' so 'no duty of any kind' is too strong. B attributes Achterberg's justification to the courts, C turns the author's criticism of that justification into a rule of law, and D applies the abandoned luring requirement to natural hazards, which were never covered.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage supports about an owner whose land has a natural pond.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the first paragraph (the general rule) and the second and third sentences of the third paragraph (natural ponds).

breakdown.analysis: Two rules apply. General rule: no duty to trespassers except not to injure them deliberately. Natural pond: no liability when a trespassing child drowns, however foreseeable the child's presence. Now watch the traps. 'No duty' drops the 'except.' A schoolyard pond appears in the fourth paragraph, but only in the author's argument about Achterberg, not as law. And the burden rationale is Achterberg's, not the courts'.

choices.note: Tempting, because the passage says owners owe trespassers 'no duty except to refrain from injuring him deliberately.' Drop the 'except' and you get this answer, which is wrong. Even a trespasser is owed something.
Wrong source. The courts' reason is never given; the burden point is Achterberg's reply, and the author thinks it fails for some ponds.
