The schoolyard pond is the author's example of a case where Achterberg's reply has no force. The author doesn't say the law makes such owners liable; the limit still applies to them.
The luring requirement was abandoned, and it applied to artificial hazards anyway. Natural ponds fall outside the exception completely.
CORRECT. 'Not liable…however foreseeable the child's presence.' Knowing children are likely to come is foreseeability, and it isn't enough.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: argue that a doctrine’s restriction to one class of hazards is arbitrary and should therefore be eliminated by the courts
acknowledge how well an account fits several features of a doctrine before identifying one it seems unable to explain
present evidence that the courts of Ardena have adopted the account of the doctrine described in the second paragraph
explain why the requirement described at the end of the first paragraph was eventually abandoned
answer an objection that has been raised to the account of the doctrine presented in the second paragraph of the passage
questions.explanation: The third paragraph first shows how Achterberg's reconstruction 'makes good sense of the doctrine's elements' and then turns ('But') to the artificial-hazard limit it 'fits poorly with.' B describes that move. A is the main trap: the paragraph's final sentence says the line 'would be arbitrary' only if negligence were the doctrine's whole basis, a conditional the author uses against Achterberg rather than a call to drop the line. C, D, and E misdescribe the paragraph; the objection in it is raised, not answered.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what the third paragraph does in the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The whole third paragraph, especially its first two sentences and its last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Structure of the paragraph: 1. praise (the account explains knowledge, youth, and cost); 2. 'But' (it fits poorly with the artificial-only limit); 3. if negligence were everything, that limit would be arbitrary. So the paragraph credits an account and then finds a problem for it. The last sentence is a conditional: the author isn't saying the line is arbitrary, but that Achterberg's view would make it so.

choices.note: Tempting, because the paragraph ends with 'arbitrary.' But it's conditional: 'If ordinary negligence were the doctrine's whole basis.' The author is pressing Achterberg, and in the next paragraph defends the line with another explanation. Nobody calls for eliminating it.
CORRECT. Credit (fits the elements), then the problem (the artificial-hazard limit it can't explain).
The paragraph doesn't claim the courts adopted Achterberg's account. It tests her account against what the courts do.
The abandonment comes up in the second paragraph, and its cause is never explained.
The paragraph raises an objection to Achterberg; it doesn't answer one. Her answer comes in the fourth paragraph.

questions.stem: The author’s reference to “a single pond beside a schoolyard” (fourth paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: provide an example of a natural feature that the Ardenan courts have required landowners to guard against trespassing children who enter
illustrate the kind of natural feature whose guarding would impose the burden that Achterberg describes
suggest that the courts should extend the children’s exception to cover natural hazards located near places where children gather
point to a case in which the artificial-hazard limitation still applies although the reason Achterberg offers for it does not
show that Achterberg’s account cannot explain why the doctrine requires that the injured child have been too young to see the danger
questions.explanation: Achterberg defends the artificial-hazard limit by saying that guarding all natural features would be too burdensome; the author replies that this 'has force for large tracts of open country, but not for a single pond beside a schoolyard.' Yet such a pond still falls outside the exception, so the limit applies where her reason does not, as D says. C is the dominant trap: it gives the author a reform proposal the passage never makes; the author uses the case to find a better explanation of the existing rule. B reverses the example's role, A contradicts the third paragraph, and E concerns an element the third paragraph says her account explains well.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the schoolyard pond does in the author's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first three sentences of the fourth paragraph, with the third and fourth sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Achterberg's defense: natural features are everywhere, so guarding them all is too much to ask. The author's reply: true for big tracts of open country, not for one pond next to a school, which would be cheap and easy to guard. Yet the law still says no liability for that pond. So the rule reaches a case her reason doesn't cover, and the author goes looking for a different reason (the owner's agency). The pond is a test case, not a reform proposal.

choices.note: Opposite. The courts have never required guarding natural features; that's the point of the limit.
Backwards. The schoolyard pond is the case where guarding would not be burdensome. It's contrasted with large tracts of open country.

Tempting, because it sounds like what someone bothered by the schoolyard case would want. But the author never recommends changing the law. The author uses the case to find a better explanation of the rule as it stands (the owner's agency).
CORRECT. The limit still bars liability for the schoolyard pond, but Achterberg's burden reason doesn't apply there. That gap is why the author looks for a different explanation.

The third paragraph says Achterberg's account explains the youth element ('the child's youth explains why the danger was not obvious'). The schoolyard pond is aimed at her burden reply, not at the elements.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Experiments with Marisella have shown that cells become dormant by chance rather than in response to stresses that they detect in their surroundings.
The Marisella experiment shows that persisters can form without hardship in the environment, but it leaves open whether dormancy responds to stress that individual cells detect.
Persister cells in Marisella become dormant in response to internal shortages of scarce metabolites rather than in response to stress in their environment.
Persisters in Marisella survive cardomycin not because they are resistant mutants but because they happen to be dormant at the moment they are exposed.
Neither of the two accounts of dormancy in Marisella can explain why the descendants of persisters are no harder to kill than the original population.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph argues that the experiment 'shows…that dormancy can arise without stress in the environment, not that it arises without stress the cell detects,' and that it is 'not decisive against Abernathy's' view. B states this qualified position. A is the dominant trap: it is the conclusion Pettersen drew, which the author argues is too strong. C turns the author's possibility ('might sense a starvation') into a finding, D is the first paragraph's background, and E contradicts the second paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall conclusion about what the Marisella experiment shows.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph, especially its fourth through last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1–3 set up the puzzle and report Pettersen's experiment and conclusion. Paragraph 4 is the author: 'This inference is weaker than it looks.' The experiment shows dormancy can happen without environmental stress; it doesn't show the cell wasn't sensing a stress of its own. So the chance account is consistent with the data, but the response account isn't ruled out. Main point = shows X, doesn't show Y. The trap will be Pettersen's stronger claim, and maybe the author's 'might' upgraded to 'does.'

choices.note: Tempting, because it's what the experiments 'have been taken to' show and what Pettersen argued. But the author's whole point is that this inference is 'weaker than it looks.'
CORRECT. What the experiment establishes (no environmental hardship needed) and what it leaves open (stress detected by the cell). That's the author's qualified position.
Too strong. The author says a cell 'might sense a starvation the chamber never imposed,' a possibility that keeps Abernathy's view alive. The author doesn't claim it's what happens.
True, but it's the first paragraph's background: the accepted explanation that both accounts build on. The passage's argument is about how dormancy arises.
Contradicted. The second paragraph says 'Either account explains why the survivors' descendants are no harder to kill.'

questions.stem: The author mentions that cardomycin “attacks the machinery of cell growth” (first paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: explain why cells that have stopped growing would be able to survive exposure to the drug
support the claim that the cells surviving a first exposure to the drug are not resistant mutants
explain why most descendants of persisters are killed by a later exposure to the drug
distinguish cardomycin from the many antibiotics against which bacteria develop inherited resistance over time
suggest that starvation and exposure to cardomycin affect bacterial cells in similar ways
questions.explanation: The clause sets up the leading explanation in the first paragraph's last sentence: because the drug attacks growth, dormant cells, 'having stopped growing,' offer it 'nothing to act on.' That is A. B is the strongest trap: the not-a-mutant claim comes just before, but it rests on the regrowth result, not on how the drug works. C also borrows the regrowth result, and D and E bring in comparisons the passage never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author mentions what cardomycin attacks.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read the full sentence: 'Because cardomycin attacks the machinery of cell growth, the leading explanation is that persisters are dormant.' It's a 'because' clause supporting the dormancy explanation: a drug that hits growing cells can't hurt a cell that isn't growing. Don't confuse it with the evidence for 'not mutants,' which is the regrowth experiment a few sentences earlier.

choices.note: CORRECT. The drug targets growth; dormant cells aren't growing; so they survive. The clause is the 'because' behind the dormancy explanation.
Tempting, because it's right next door. But the not-mutant claim comes from the regrowth experiment: descendants are 'no harder to kill.' How the drug works has nothing to do with that.
That's also from the regrowth result, not from the drug's mechanism. The clause explains survival, not later deaths.
No other antibiotics are discussed. Invented comparison.
Starvation comes up later, as a stress that might trigger dormancy. The passage never compares its effects to the drug's.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following about the cells that survive a first exposure of a Marisella culture to cardomycin?
choices: They carry an inherited trait that makes them harder to kill than other cells in the culture.
They had been subjected to starvation shortly before the drug was added to the culture.
Most of their descendants would be killed by a later exposure to the drug.
They would survive a second exposure to the drug if it followed the first one immediately.
They form a larger share of the population in cultures supplied with abundant nutrients.
questions.explanation: When the survivors' descendants are exposed, 'the same small fraction survives again,' about one in ten thousand (first paragraph), so most of the descendants die, as C says. A contradicts the statement that persisters are 'not resistant mutants.' B is Abernathy's hypothesis, which the passage presents as unsettled. D and E go beyond anything the passage reports.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage supports about the survivors of a first exposure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first three sentences of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Regrow the survivors, expose the new culture, and 'the same small fraction survives again.' The fraction was about one in ten thousand. So nearly all of the descendants die. Prephrase: their offspring are as easy to kill as anyone.

choices.note: Contradicted. Persisters are 'not resistant mutants,' and their descendants are 'no harder to kill.'
That's one hypothesis (Abernathy's) about why cells go dormant, and the passage leaves it open. Pettersen's experiment even had survivors with no starvation in the chamber.
CORRECT. Only about one in ten thousand descendants survives the next exposure, so most are killed.
We don't know. The passage never describes an immediate second exposure of the same cells. Dormancy is 'a passing state,' but nothing says how long it lasts.
Nothing compares persister rates across nutrient conditions. Pettersen found persisters forming with abundant nutrients, but not more of them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the experiment conducted by Pettersen’s group showed that
choices: the cells that became dormant in the chamber were not responding to any stress
dormant cells appeared more often in chambers in which nutrients ran short
the rate at which cells became dormant rose once cardomycin had been added
a cell’s internal supply of a scarce metabolite fluctuates as it grows and divides
cells that became dormant while nutrients were abundant survived the drug
questions.explanation: The third paragraph reports that, with nutrients abundant, 'dormant cells appeared at a low but constant rate, and when cardomycin was added, these were the cells that survived.' E restates that observation. A is the dominant trap: it is the conclusion Pettersen drew, which the author argues the experiment does not show. D is the author's own claim in the fourth paragraph, not a result of the experiment. B and C contradict the reported steady, abundant conditions and constant rate.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the experiment itself showed, as opposed to what anyone concluded from it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second and third sentences of the third paragraph. Compare with its last sentence (Pettersen's conclusion) and the fourth paragraph (the author's reply).

breakdown.analysis: This question turns on the difference between observation and interpretation. Observation: with steady, abundant nutrients, some cells went dormant at a constant rate, and those were the survivors. Pettersen's interpretation: so dormancy wasn't a stress response. The author's reply: cells might sense internal shortages. Only the observation is something 'the experiment showed.'

choices.note: Tempting, because it's what Pettersen said the experiment showed. But the author argues that the experiment shows only that the chamber imposed no stress, not that the cell sensed none. The passage never presents it as a result.
Contradicted. The chamber had 'a steady flow of abundant nutrients,' and the passage never mentions any chamber where nutrients ran short.
The rate was 'low but constant.' Nothing says it rose when the drug was added.
Wrong source. This is the author's point in the fourth paragraph, offered against Pettersen's inference. It's not something the experiment measured.
CORRECT. Abundant nutrients, some cells went dormant, 'these were the cells that survived.' Pure observation.

questions.stem: The author’s statement that conditions “uniform at the scale of a chamber need not be uniform at the scale of a cell” (fourth paragraph) functions primarily to
choices: challenge the accuracy of the report that the chamber was supplied with a steady flow of abundant nutrients
establish that dormancy in Marisella is triggered by shortages of scarce metabolites inside individual cells
explain why the dormant cells observed in the chamber appeared at a low but constant rate
indicate how an observation taken to count against one account of dormancy might be compatible with it
show that the chance-switching account cannot explain why persisters survive their exposure to the drug
questions.explanation: Pettersen took dormancy in an unstressed chamber to count against Abernathy's response account; the author's statement opens the possibility that individual cells sensed a stress the chamber did not impose, so the observation is compatible with her account (fourth paragraph). That is D. A is the dominant trap: the author accepts that the chamber was steady and abundant and questions only what follows from it. B upgrades 'might' to 'established,' C answers a question the passage does not raise, and E contradicts the author's remark that the finding is 'consistent with Pettersen's hedging account.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the 'scale of a chamber… scale of a cell' statement does in the author's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first three sentences of the fourth paragraph and the last sentence of the third.

breakdown.analysis: Pettersen: the chamber had no starvation, so dormancy wasn't a response to stress. The author doesn't deny the chamber was well fed. The author says a single cell can still run short inside, so it might sense stress after all. The statement opens a gap between 'no stress in the chamber' and 'no stress the cell detects.' That makes the observation compatible with Abernathy's view. The answer will be abstract; don't pick the one that attacks the experiment's setup.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the author is questioning the experiment. But the author grants that the chamber was uniform and well supplied. The point is that uniformity at the chamber level doesn't settle what each cell experienced.
Too strong. The author says a cell 'might sense a starvation'; it's a possibility that keeps a hypothesis alive, not an established trigger.
The passage never explains the constant rate, and this statement isn't aimed at it.
CORRECT. The observation (dormancy without stress in the chamber) was taken to count against Abernathy. The statement shows how it could fit her account after all: the stress may be inside the cell.
Contradicted. The author says the finding is 'consistent with Pettersen's hedging account.' And both accounts accept that dormant cells survive the drug.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A phenomenon is explained, two accounts of a process on which the explanation depends are presented, and an experiment taken to favor one account is shown to establish less than was claimed.
A phenomenon is described, two accounts of its cause are presented, and an experiment thought to undermine one of them is then reinterpreted as providing positive support for that account instead.
A finding is described, two hypotheses about it are outlined, and evidence is presented showing that the two hypotheses can be combined into a single, more complete account.
A phenomenon is described, a widely accepted explanation of it is called into question, and two alternative explanations are then evaluated in light of a recent experiment on individual cells.
An experiment is described, the conclusion drawn from it is criticized on methodological grounds, and a revised version of the experiment is proposed to settle the question.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes persistence and explains it by dormancy; paragraph 2 presents two accounts of how cells become dormant; paragraph 3 describes the experiment 'taken to favor chance switching'; paragraph 4 argues that it shows only a 'more modest point.' A fits every step. B is the dominant trap: it has the experiment reinterpreted as supporting Abernathy's account, but the author says only that the experiment is 'not decisive against' it. C invents a synthesis, D has the dormancy explanation questioned when the passage accepts it, and E invents a methodological criticism and a proposed new experiment.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match each paragraph to a step in the answer choice; one wrong step kills a choice.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first and last sentences of each paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: 1. phenomenon (persisters) + accepted explanation (dormancy); 2. two accounts of how cells become dormant; 3. an experiment said to favor chance; 4. the author: it shows less than claimed (consistent with chance, not decisive against response). The key distinction for the hardest trap: 'not decisive against' Abernathy is not the same as 'supports' Abernathy.

choices.note: CORRECT. Explanation (dormancy), two accounts of the process it depends on (how cells become dormant), an experiment said to favor one, and the narrower reading of what it proves.

Tempting, because the author does rescue Abernathy's account from the experiment. But rescuing isn't the same as supporting: the author says the result is 'consistent with Pettersen's hedging account' and merely 'not decisive against Abernathy's.' 'Reinterpreted as providing support' overshoots.
No synthesis. The two accounts stay separate; the passage only narrows what the experiment settles between them.
The dormancy explanation is never questioned; it's 'the leading explanation,' and both accounts take it for granted.
The author criticizes the inference, not the method, and proposes no new experiment.

passages.title: Staging in Ilse Doreth’s Salt and Net
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In the late 1930s the photographer Ilse Doreth spent four winters in the herring villages of the Seland coast, and the pictures she brought back, published in 1941 as Salt and Net, were for a generation taken as the definitive record of a way of life that mechanized trawling was about to end. Then, in 1968, the journalist Paul Ostern interviewed surviving villagers and learned that many of the book’s best-known images had been arranged. Doreth had asked men to repeat the hauling of a net until the light was right, had given the women in a mending scene wooden needles of a kind they had long since replaced with steel ones, and in at least one case had paid a family to wear clothes it no longer wore except to church. Ostern’s conclusion was blunt: Salt and Net was not documentary at all but “a kind of costume drama,” and the book’s reputation collapsed accordingly.

The critic Rhea Valcourt has recently argued that this verdict rests on a mistaken idea of what documentary photography could be in Doreth’s time. The cameras Doreth used required long exposures and heavy tripods; a net hauled at full speed would have registered as a blur. To photograph work at all, Valcourt points out, a photographer had to ask workers to pause, to repeat, or to hold still, and the villagers’ letters show that they understood and often directed these arrangements, choosing which tasks deserved to be recorded. On Valcourt’s account the staging is evidence not of deception but of collaboration.

Valcourt’s argument succeeds against the cruder form of Ostern’s charge. That a scene was repeated for the camera does not make it false, any more than a transcript is false because the speaker was asked to slow down. But her defense covers less than it seems to. Technical limits explain why a haul might be repeated; they do not explain why the women were handed obsolete needles, still less why a family was dressed in clothes it had set aside. These choices served a picture of village life that was older, poorer, and more picturesque than the one the villagers were then living, and nothing in the letters suggests that the villagers asked for them. Collaboration was real, but collaboration and invention are not exclusive; a subject may help arrange a photograph whose overall meaning he or she would not endorse.

What Salt and Net requires, then, is neither Ostern’s dismissal nor Valcourt’s vindication but a sorting of its images by the kind of intervention each involved. Some are records shaped by the limits of the medium; others are illustrations of an idea Doreth brought with her. Both kinds have value, but only the first can bear the documentary weight the book once carried.

passages.title: The lay in the Port Quillan whaling fleet
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Through much of the nineteenth century, the whaling ships that sailed from Port Quillan paid their crews no wages. Each man signed on for a “lay,” a fixed fraction of the net proceeds of the voyage, payable only when the ship returned, often three or four years later. A captain might receive a fifteenth, a skilled harpooner an eightieth, and an inexperienced hand as little as a two-hundredth. Labor historians long treated the lay simply as an instrument of exploitation: by paying in shares, owners passed the risk of a poor voyage to the men least able to bear it, and by charging the crew for clothing and tobacco advanced at sea, they often reduced a novice’s earnings to almost nothing.

The economic historian Mira Rousset has proposed a different account. A whaling voyage, she observes, presented its owners with an extreme problem of supervision, one that few employers ashore faced in anything like the same form. Once a ship left port, no owner could see whether the crew pursued whales vigorously or merely waited out the voyage, and the decisions that most affected the catch—when to lower the boats, how long to chase a pod in rising seas—were made thousands of miles from any office. A share of the proceeds, Rousset argues, gave every man aboard a direct stake in the catch, enlisting his self-interest where no owner’s oversight could reach. The lay persisted, on this view, not because owners were unusually rapacious but because no wage contract could have drawn comparable effort from a crew beyond the reach of supervision.

Rousset’s account is persuasive for the officers and harpooners, whose shares were large enough to make a full hold worth striving for and whose judgment in the boats did much to determine the catch. It is far less persuasive for the ordinary hands, who made up most of every crew. A two-hundredth of a successful voyage’s proceeds, after deductions, might amount to less than a laborer ashore earned in a single season; the difference between a good catch and a mediocre one could hardly have moved such a man to greater exertion. Moreover, the ordinary hand’s chief tasks—rowing, hauling, and boiling down blubber—were performed under the officers’ direct eyes, so they required little of the self-direction that shares were supposedly needed to supply.

The two accounts are therefore better seen as describing different parts of the crew than as rivals. For the men who commanded the boats, the lay was an incentive; for the men at the oars, it functioned much as the earlier historians said, as a means of deferring and reducing pay. That a single contract could serve both purposes at once, rewarding the few while economizing on the many, goes far toward explaining its durability.

passages.title: The nightly glow of Lucidella vesperis
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Bioluminescence is costly. The light emitted by glowing fungi is produced by an enzyme-driven reaction that consumes oxygen and energy-rich compounds, and in a few species the glow is bright enough to read by. For decades, nonetheless, most mycologists doubted that fungal light served any purpose at all. Many luminous fungi glow not only in their mushrooms but also in the threadlike mycelium buried in soil and rotting wood, where no animal could see it, and the dominant view held that the light was a by-product of a reaction whose real function was chemical: neutralizing reactive forms of oxygen generated as the fungus breaks down wood.

The case of Lucidella vesperis, a small mushroom of the wet forests of the Kessrin highlands, has unsettled that consensus. In 2011 a team led by the mycologist Clara Weyl found that the mushroom’s glow is not constant: it rises sharply after dusk and fades before dawn, and it continues to follow this cycle when mushrooms are kept in constant darkness, indicating that it is governed by an internal clock rather than by outside conditions such as temperature or light. A by-product, Weyl reasoned, would be expected to track the fungus’s overall metabolic activity, which in Lucidella peaks during the warm afternoon; a glow timed to the hours when nocturnal insects are active suggests that the light is regulated for an audience.

To identify that audience, Weyl’s team placed sticky-coated plastic replicas of the mushroom on the forest floor, some fitted with small green lights matching the glow’s color and intensity and some left dark. Over three weeks the lit replicas captured roughly five times as many beetles, flies, and springtails as the dark ones, and many of the insects later collected from real Lucidella mushrooms carried spores on their bodies. Weyl concluded that the glow attracts insects that disperse the fungus’s spores, an advantage that would be considerable on a forest floor where the still air carries spores only short distances.

Weyl’s findings establish more than her critics have granted and less than her conclusion requires. That the glow is clock-driven and draws insects is now difficult to dispute, and a light that attracts animals at the hours they forage is unlikely to be wholly accidental. But to show that the glow exists for spore dispersal, one would need to show that insects actually carry viable spores to sites where new colonies take hold, and that glowing mushrooms leave more descendants than dark ones would. Nor does Weyl’s account explain why the buried mycelium glows; it remains possible that the light originated as the by-product the older view described and that the timing of its brightest phase was later adjusted to recruit insects.

passages.title: The lost-chance doctrine
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

In a negligence suit, a plaintiff must ordinarily prove that the defendant’s carelessness more likely than not caused the harm complained of. Some courts have relaxed this requirement in medical cases through the doctrine of lost chance. Suppose a physician negligently fails to diagnose a tumor, and the patient, who would have had a 40 percent chance of survival with timely treatment, dies. Under the traditional rule the estate recovers nothing, since the patient probably would have died anyway. Under the lost-chance doctrine the estate may recover a fraction of the damages for the death, proportional to the chance of survival the negligence destroyed.

The doctrine is usually defended as a matter of fairness, but it achieves fairness only by redefining the injury. What the patient lost, it says, was not life but a chance at life. Yet a chance is not something a person possesses in the way he or she possesses health. The estate is compensated for a statistic about patients like the decedent, and the court never determines whether this patient was among those who would have lived.

The redefinition also has no natural boundary. If a diminished chance is itself a compensable injury, then a patient whose chance of survival was negligently reduced but who in fact survived would seem to have a claim, and so would anyone exposed to a risk by a careless driver or manufacturer. Courts that have adopted the doctrine have confined it to medical malpractice and to patients who actually suffered the harm, but nothing in its logic supports either limit. The limits are better read as signs that these courts sense where the doctrine leads and decline to follow it.

Passage B

The traditional more-likely-than-not rule works well when uncertainty about causation arises because facts are missing; it lets a court decide what probably happened. It works poorly when the uncertainty is irreducible, as it often is in medicine. No evidence will ever reveal whether a particular patient with a poor prognosis would have been among the survivors, because the answer depends on biological variation that medicine cannot measure. Applied to such patients, the traditional rule does not resolve uncertainty; it simply declares that every patient whose chance was below one-half lost nothing, however careless the treatment.

The result is a class of patients to whom physicians owe a duty that cannot be enforced. A physician who negligently reduces a 45 percent chance of survival to 10 percent faces no liability, while one who reduces a 55 percent chance to 50 percent is liable for the full value of the death. Proportional recovery corrects both errors at once: across many cases, it makes negligent physicians pay for the harm they actually cause, no more and no less.

Courts that award damages for a lost chance are thus not inventing a new kind of injury. They are measuring an old one, death, under conditions in which its cause can be known only as a probability.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Ostern’s discovery that many images in Salt and Net were arranged shows that the book cannot be regarded as a documentary record of the Seland villages.
Valcourt has shown that the staging in Salt and Net reflected both the technical limits of Doreth’s cameras and the wishes of the villagers she photographed.
Documentary photographers of the 1930s could not record people at work without asking them to pause, to repeat their actions, or to hold still.
Valcourt’s defense of Salt and Net answers part but not all of Ostern’s charge, and the book’s images should be sorted by the kind of staging each involved.
Doreth’s photographs are more valuable as illustrations of her own idea of village life than as records of the villages as they actually were in the 1930s.
questions.explanation: The author grants that Valcourt’s argument ‘succeeds against the cruder form of Ostern’s charge’ but says her defense ‘covers less than it seems to,’ and concludes that the images must be sorted by kind of intervention (last paragraph), so D is correct. A is Ostern’s verdict, which the author calls a ‘dismissal’ and rejects. B is Valcourt’s view without the author’s reservation, and C is a supporting detail from the second paragraph. E ranks the two kinds of image, but the author says both kinds have value.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall position on the dispute between Ostern and Valcourt.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (‘succeeds against the cruder form … covers less than it seems to’) and paragraph 4 (‘neither Ostern’s dismissal nor Valcourt’s vindication’).

breakdown.analysis: Three people have views here: Ostern (the book is fake), Valcourt (the staging was collaboration, so it’s fine), and the author. Whose side is the author on? Neither, fully. The last paragraph says it outright: neither dismissal nor vindication, but a sorting of the images. We need an answer that says “Valcourt is partly right, Ostern is partly right, so sort the pictures.” When a passage ends with “neither X nor Y but Z,” Z is almost always the main point.

choices.note: This is Ostern’s view. The author calls it a ‘dismissal’ and says some images are genuine records shaped by the medium. Wrong party’s view.

Tempting, because Valcourt’s argument gets a whole paragraph. But the author says the technical limits explain the repeated haul, not the needles or the church clothes, and nothing suggests the villagers asked for those. ‘Has shown’ ignores the author’s reservation.
True according to the second paragraph, but it’s one supporting fact in Valcourt’s argument. A main point has to cover the author’s verdict.
CORRECT. It has the concession (Valcourt answers part of the charge), the limit (not all of it), and the conclusion of the last paragraph (sort the images by kind of intervention).
The author never ranks the two kinds of image. ‘Both kinds have value’; the point is only that the illustrations can’t carry documentary weight. This invents a comparison.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the villagers’ letters indicate that the villagers
choices: took part in deciding which of their tasks would be photographed
asked Doreth to show them with the clothes and tools of an earlier time
objected to the picture of village life that Salt and Net presented
always chose for themselves how each scene in the book would be arranged
did not realize that Doreth had altered scenes before photographing them
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the letters show the villagers ‘understood and often directed these arrangements, choosing which tasks deserved to be recorded,’ which A paraphrases. B is the trap: it extends the collaboration to the needles and church clothes, but the third paragraph says ‘nothing in the letters suggests that the villagers asked for them.’ D turns ‘often’ into ‘always,’ C is never stated, and E contradicts ‘understood.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says the letters reveal about the villagers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third sentence (‘the villagers’ letters show …’), and paragraph 3, fifth sentence (‘nothing in the letters suggests …’).

breakdown.analysis: The letters come up twice. In paragraph 2 they show the villagers understood and often directed the arrangements and chose which tasks to record. In paragraph 3 the author adds a limit: nothing in them suggests the villagers asked for the obsolete needles or the old clothes. So the letters support collaboration on some things and are silent on others. We need an answer that stays inside the first claim. Watch the qualifiers: ‘often’ is not ‘always,’ and ‘these arrangements’ means the pauses and repetitions, not the props.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Choosing which tasks deserved to be recorded’ is exactly taking part in deciding which tasks would be photographed.

Tempting, because the letters show collaboration and this sounds like more collaboration. But the author says the opposite about these choices: ‘nothing in the letters suggests that the villagers asked for them.’ The clothes and needles are the interventions the letters don’t cover.
We don’t know this. The author says a subject may help arrange a photograph whose meaning he or she would not endorse, but never says the letters record any objection.
Too strong. The passage says the villagers ‘often directed’ the arrangements. ‘Always … each scene’ turns a frequent practice into a universal one.
This contradicts the passage. The letters show the villagers ‘understood’ the arrangements.

questions.stem: By calling Salt and Net “a kind of costume drama” (last sentence of the first paragraph), Ostern most probably means that the book
choices: shows the villagers in clothing suited to formal occasions such as church services
tells a story about the villages in the manner of a stage play with a plot
presents scenes arranged for the camera as though they were unposed records
was produced with the help of performers hired from outside the villages
gives more attention to the villagers’ dress than to the work they performed
questions.explanation: Ostern says the book ‘was not documentary at all but a kind of costume drama’ after learning that its scenes had been arranged, so he means it presents staged scenes as if they were real records: C. A takes the church-clothes detail literally; only one family is said to have worn such clothes. B, D, and E describe things the passage never attributes to the book.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decide what Ostern’s phrase means in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last two sentences (what Ostern learned, then his verdict).

breakdown.analysis: Read the phrase against what it’s contrasted with: ‘not documentary at all but a kind of costume drama.’ Documentary means a record of what really happened. So ‘costume drama’ means a performance: scenes set up and acted for the camera but passed off as real. We need an answer about staging presented as fact. Meaning-in-context questions love to offer the literal sense of the word as a trap.

choices.note: Too literal. One family was paid to wear its church clothes, but Ostern’s phrase covers the whole book: the repeated hauls, the needles, all of it. It’s about staging, not about formal dress.
There’s no plot in a book of photographs, and Ostern never says there is. ‘Drama’ here means performance, not storytelling.
CORRECT. The contrast with ‘documentary’ shows the point: the scenes were performed for the camera but offered as records of real life.
The passage says Doreth asked villagers to repeat their work and paid a local family. Nobody was hired from outside.
Nothing says the book focuses on dress. The repeated net hauls and the mending scene are about work.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that, before Ostern’s interviews in 1968, Salt and Net was generally regarded as
choices: a skillful work of art whose accuracy as a record was beside the point
an accurate record of life in the herring villages of the Seland coast
an example of the technical limits that the cameras of its time imposed
a collaboration between Doreth and the villagers whose work she recorded
an argument against the spread of mechanized trawling along the coast
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the pictures ‘were for a generation taken as the definitive record of a way of life’ and that after Ostern’s findings ‘the book’s reputation collapsed,’ so it was regarded as an accurate record: B. A reverses the point, since the reputation depended on accuracy. C and D are Valcourt’s later arguments, and E confuses the book’s subject (a way of life trawling would end) with an argument against trawling.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find how the book was viewed before Ostern’s discovery.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, first sentence (‘taken as the definitive record’) and last sentence (‘reputation collapsed’).

breakdown.analysis: Why would a reputation collapse when people learn the pictures were staged? Because the reputation rested on the pictures being real. The first sentence says so directly: for a generation the book was ‘the definitive record.’ We need ‘accurate record.’ Easy, but don’t grab the answers that describe later critics’ views.

choices.note: This reverses it. If accuracy were beside the point, learning about the staging wouldn’t have sunk the book’s reputation.
CORRECT. ‘The definitive record of a way of life,’ and the collapse after Ostern, both show it was valued as accurate.
This is part of Valcourt’s recent argument, not how the book was seen before 1968.
Valcourt argues this now. Before 1968 nobody knew the scenes were arranged at all, so nobody would have called them collaborations.
The passage says trawling was about to end that way of life. It never says the book argued against trawling.

questions.stem: The author mentions a transcript of a speaker who was asked to slow down (second sentence of the third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: support Valcourt’s claim that the villagers worked with Doreth in arranging the scenes that she photographed
suggest that written records are subject to distortions similar to those that affect documentary photographs
show that each part of Ostern’s charge against Salt and Net is unfounded once the medium’s limits are considered
indicate that the women’s use of obsolete needles did not make Doreth’s photograph of the mending scene false
illustrate the claim that a record is not made false merely because its subject adjusted his or her actions for it
questions.explanation: The transcript comparison follows the claim that ‘a scene was repeated for the camera does not make it false’: a speaker who slows down for a transcriber still produces a true transcript, so E is correct. A is the trap: the comparison sits inside the author’s concession to Valcourt, but it concerns whether a record is accurate, not who directed it. C overstates the concession, which covers only ‘the cruder form’ of the charge, and D applies the point to an intervention the author says the medium does not explain. B reverses the analogy’s purpose.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author brings up the transcript.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first two sentences (‘succeeds against the cruder form … any more than a transcript is false …’).

breakdown.analysis: What claim is the transcript attached to? The sentence reads: repeating a scene for the camera doesn’t make it false, any more than a transcript is false because the speaker slowed down. So the transcript is an everyday case of the same idea: the subject changed what he did for the record-maker, and the record is still true. We need an answer about accuracy surviving an adjustment. The trap is to read it as support for Valcourt’s collaboration point just because it sits in the paragraph that opens by praising her.

choices.note: Tempting. The comparison comes right after the author grants that Valcourt’s argument succeeds, so it feels like support for her. But the transcript says nothing about who directed the change. It’s about whether the result is false, which is a different point from collaboration.
The author isn’t warning about transcripts. The transcript is offered as an obvious example of a record that is still accurate.
Too strong. The author says Valcourt succeeds only against ‘the cruder form’ of the charge and then argues that the needles and clothes are not explained by the medium.
Wrong intervention. The author says technical limits do NOT explain the obsolete needles; those served an invented picture of the past. The transcript point covers the repeated haul, not the props.
CORRECT. The speaker adjusts for the transcriber, as the fishermen repeated the haul for the camera, and in neither case is the record false.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Now that the staging of its images is known, Salt and Net no longer has any value as a work of photography.
The family photographed in its church clothes would have refused to wear them had Doreth not paid it to do so.
A photograph in Salt and Net showing a net haul repeated for the camera can still serve as a record of the work.
The technical limits of Doreth’s cameras explain most of the interventions that Ostern discovered in his interviews.
Valcourt’s reading of the villagers’ letters is mistaken about the part that the villagers played in the staging.
questions.explanation: The author says repeating a scene does not make it false and that some images ‘are records shaped by the limits of the medium’ that can still bear documentary weight (third and fourth paragraphs), so C follows. D is the main trap: the author says the limits explain the repeated haul but not the needles or the clothes, and never says how many interventions fall on each side. A contradicts ‘both kinds have value,’ B is unsupported, and E contradicts ‘collaboration was real.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a statement the author’s views support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (what technical limits do and do not explain) and paragraph 4 (‘records shaped by the limits of the medium’).

breakdown.analysis: The author splits the images into two kinds: records shaped by the camera’s limits (like the repeated haul) and illustrations of Doreth’s idea (like the needles and church clothes). The first kind keeps its documentary weight. Hard to prephrase exactly, so look for an answer that puts the repeated haul on the record side, and reject anything that sinks the whole book or saves the whole book.

choices.note: This contradicts the last paragraph: ‘Both kinds have value.’ The author rejects Ostern’s blanket dismissal.
We don’t know this. The passage says Doreth paid the family, not what the family would have done otherwise.
CORRECT. A repeated haul is the author’s own example of staging that doesn’t make a picture false, and such images are ‘records shaped by the limits of the medium.’
Tempting, because the author does grant that technical limits explain some staging. But the passage lists three interventions and says the limits explain only one of them. ‘Most’ is never supported.
The author accepts Valcourt’s reading of the letters (‘Collaboration was real’) and objects only that it doesn’t reach the props and clothes.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The lay persisted in the Port Quillan fleet because it allowed owners to shift the risk of a poor voyage onto the men least able to bear it.
Rousset’s account of the lay as a solution to the difficulty of supervising a crew fits the officers and harpooners, while the older account fits the ordinary hands.
Rousset has shown that the lay gave every member of a whaling crew a direct stake in the catch and so drew more effort from crews than wages could have.
The shares paid to ordinary hands on Port Quillan whaling ships were too small to have moved them to work harder for a larger catch.
Historians of whaling have exaggerated how far owners used charges for goods advanced at sea to reduce the earnings of their crews.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the author’s conclusion: the two accounts describe ‘different parts of the crew’ rather than being rivals, with the lay an incentive for the men commanding the boats and a means of reducing pay for the men at the oars, so B is correct. A is the older historians’ view and C is Rousset’s, each without the author’s division. D is a supporting point from the third paragraph, and E is never claimed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall conclusion about the two accounts of the lay.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first two sentences (‘better seen as describing different parts of the crew than as rivals’).

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 gives the old view (exploitation), paragraph 2 gives Rousset’s view (incentive under no supervision), paragraph 3 says Rousset fits the officers but not the ordinary hands, and paragraph 4 puts it together. So who wins? Both, for different men. We need an answer that splits the crew: Rousset for the officers, the old view for the hands.

choices.note: This is the earlier labor historians’ view. The author says it fits only the men at the oars.
CORRECT. It matches the last paragraph: incentive for the men who commanded the boats, deferred and reduced pay for the ordinary hands.
This is Rousset’s view, and the author rejects the ‘every member’ part. The ordinary hands’ shares were too small to motivate them.
True according to the third paragraph, but it’s one supporting point. It leaves out Rousset’s account entirely.
The author never says the deductions were exaggerated; in fact the last paragraph endorses the older view for the ordinary hands.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Rousset holds that
choices: the lay served as an effective incentive chiefly for those members of a crew whose decisions most affected the catch
the lay gave the ordinary hands little reason for greater effort, since their tasks were performed under direct supervision
owners charged their crews for clothing and tobacco advanced at sea as a way of reducing what they paid out at a voyage’s end
a whaling crew paid fixed wages would probably have worked less vigorously than a crew paid in shares of the catch
the lay was adopted because owners could not afford to pay wages before the proceeds of a voyage’s catch were sold
questions.explanation: Rousset argues that the lay persisted ‘because no wage contract could have drawn comparable effort from a crew beyond the reach of supervision’ (end of the second paragraph), which D restates. A is the trap: it is the author’s refinement in the third and fourth paragraphs, while Rousset says the lay gave ‘every man aboard’ a stake. B is also the author’s view, C belongs to the earlier labor historians, and E gives a reason no one in the passage offers.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim that belongs to Rousset, not to the author or the earlier historians.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (Rousset’s account). Compare with paragraph 1 (earlier historians) and paragraphs 3–4 (the author).

breakdown.analysis: This passage has three voices, and every wrong answer here is something someone in the passage says, just not Rousset. Before you pick, ask: whose sentence is this? Rousset: no owner could supervise; shares gave every man a stake; no wage contract could have drawn comparable effort. The author: that works for officers, not for ordinary hands. The earlier historians: the lay shifted risk, and deductions cut pay. We need Rousset’s claim, probably in different words. ‘No wage contract could have drawn comparable effort’ means wage-paid crews would have worked less hard.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds like a careful version of Rousset, and Rousset does mention the decisions that most affect the catch. But restricting the incentive to those men is the author’s move in the third paragraph. Rousset says the lay gave ‘every man aboard’ a direct stake.
This is the author’s objection to Rousset, from the third paragraph. Rousset claims the opposite: everyone, the hands included, had a stake.
This is the earlier labor historians’ point in the first paragraph. Rousset offers a different account and never discusses the deductions.
CORRECT. Rousset says no wage contract could have drawn comparable effort. So a crew on fixed wages would have worked less hard. The answer’s ‘probably’ is weaker than her claim, which is fine.
Nobody in the passage says this. Rousset explains why the lay persisted, by its effect on effort, not by the owners’ cash.

questions.stem: The author mentions what a laborer ashore might earn in a single season (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: indicate how small an ordinary hand’s share of even a successful voyage might be
explain why most ordinary hands eventually left whaling for work ashore
support Rousset’s claim that the lay drew more effort than a wage contract could
show that the earlier historians overstated the deductions from crews’ pay
contrast the risks borne by ordinary hands with the risks borne by the ship’s officers
questions.explanation: The comparison shows that an ordinary hand’s two-hundredth share might amount to less than a laborer ashore earned in one season, so the share was too small to motivate him (third paragraph): A. B is never stated. C reverses the point, since the comparison is used against Rousset’s account for the ordinary hands. D and E are not what the comparison does.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author compares the share to a laborer’s pay ashore.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: What is the author arguing in this paragraph? That Rousset’s incentive story fails for the ordinary hands. How does the laborer’s pay help? It shows just how tiny a two-hundredth share was: less than one season ashore for years at sea. Tiny share, no incentive. We need an answer about the share’s smallness.

choices.note: CORRECT. The comparison makes the two-hundredth share concrete: even a good voyage paid a hand less than a season’s work ashore.
We don’t know this. The passage never says what ordinary hands did afterward.
This reverses the point. The comparison is used against Rousset’s account as applied to the ordinary hands.
The author never says the deductions were overstated. The comparison even includes them (‘after deductions’).
The paragraph contrasts the size of shares, not the risks borne by each group.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the lay as the author describes it in the last paragraph?
choices: a bonus plan that rewards every employee of a firm equally whenever the firm meets its annual sales target
a commission plan that motivates a firm’s sales staff but that the firm’s owners abandon once sales decline
a pay scale that was introduced to reduce a firm’s labor costs but that later came to motivate its employees as well
a profit-sharing plan that the senior managers of a firm regard as unfair to the firm’s junior clerks
a profit-sharing plan that motivates a firm’s senior managers but chiefly defers and reduces its junior clerks’ pay
questions.explanation: In the last paragraph the lay is one contract that does two things at once: it is an incentive for the men commanding the boats and a means of deferring and reducing pay for the men at the oars. E has the same structure. C is the trap: it has both functions, but in sequence rather than at once for different groups. A gives everyone the same effect, B adds abandonment, and D is about how one group judges the plan.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation with the same structure as the lay in the author’s final account.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Strip the lay down: a single pay arrangement; for the top group it works as an incentive; for the larger bottom group it mainly delays and cuts pay; both at the same time. We need an answer with one arrangement, two groups, and two simultaneous functions. Analogy traps usually match some of the elements, so check each one.

choices.note: Same effect for everyone. The lay works differently for different parts of the crew.
Abandonment has no parallel. The author stresses the lay’s durability.
Tempting, because it has both functions. But they come one after the other, for the same employees. In the lay the two functions run at once, for different groups.
This is about one group’s opinion of the plan. The author describes what the lay did, not what the officers thought of it.
CORRECT. One plan; incentive for the senior group; deferred and reduced pay for the junior group. That’s the lay.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward the view of the lay held by the earlier labor historians mentioned in the first paragraph can most accurately be described as
choices: rejection, on the grounds that Rousset has shown that it rests on a misunderstanding of the problem owners faced
qualified acceptance, since it describes the lay’s effect on officers and harpooners but not its effect on ordinary hands
qualified acceptance, since it describes the lay’s effect on most crew members but misses a function served for some
full acceptance, since it explains the durability of the lay better than Rousset’s account of the lay is able to
skepticism, on the grounds that it exaggerates how far deductions reduced the earnings of the ordinary hands
questions.explanation: The author says the lay functioned for the men at the oars ‘much as the earlier historians said,’ and the ordinary hands ‘made up most of every crew’; the view misses the incentive the lay supplied to the men commanding the boats (third and fourth paragraphs). So C is correct. B is the trap: it has the right attitude but swaps the groups. A and D overshoot in opposite directions, since the author credits both accounts and ties the lay’s durability to its doing both jobs, and E is never suggested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find how the author judges the older exploitation view, and why.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence (‘most of every crew’), and paragraph 4 (‘much as the earlier historians said’).

breakdown.analysis: The author doesn’t reject the old view and doesn’t fully accept it. For the ordinary hands, it’s right: the lay deferred and cut their pay. For the officers and harpooners, it misses something: the lay really was an incentive for them. And the ordinary hands were most of the crew. So: qualified acceptance; right about most of the crew; misses a function for a few. Two answers say ‘qualified acceptance.’ The difference is which group is which. Read the groups word by word.

choices.note: Too strong, and Rousset never addresses the old view’s claims about the hands. The author endorses the old view for the men at the oars.
Tempting, because the attitude word is right and it names both groups. But it swaps them. The old view fits the ordinary hands, not the officers; the officers are where Rousset is right.
CORRECT. The old view fits the ordinary hands, who were ‘most of every crew,’ and misses the incentive the lay gave the officers and harpooners.
Too strong. The author says the lay lasted because one contract could serve both purposes, which gives Rousset’s account a share of the credit.
The author never questions the deductions. ‘After deductions’ in the third paragraph treats them as real.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: describe a discovery that has overturned a long-standing explanation of a biological phenomenon
argue that the glow of luminous fungi is a by-product of a chemical reaction rather than an adaptation
show that two rival explanations of a trait are each correct for a different part of the same organism
explain how an experiment was designed to identify which insects are drawn to a fungus’s glow
assess how far a researcher’s findings support her hypothesis about the function of a trait
questions.explanation: The passage sets out the older view, presents Weyl’s findings and her conclusion that the glow recruits spore-dispersing insects, and then judges that the findings ‘establish more than her critics have granted and less than her conclusion requires’ (fourth paragraph), so E is correct. A is the main trap: the case ‘unsettled’ the consensus, but the author says Weyl’s conclusion is not established and the older view may be partly right. C hardens the closing possibility into a claim, D covers only the third paragraph, and B misstates the author’s position.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage as a whole is trying to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, first sentence (‘unsettled that consensus’), and paragraph 4, first sentence (‘more than her critics have granted and less than her conclusion requires’).

breakdown.analysis: Does the author announce a breakthrough? No. The key sentence is the first of paragraph 4: Weyl proved more than critics admit and less than she claims. Everything before it sets up what she found; everything after spells out what’s missing. So the passage is an evaluation of how much Weyl’s evidence proves. We need an abstract ‘assess/evaluate’ answer. Purpose traps often invent a stronger frame (‘overturned’) or stretch one sentence into the whole point.

choices.note: Tempting, because Weyl’s work is the passage’s centerpiece and it did shake the old view. But ‘unsettled’ is not ‘overturned,’ and the author says her conclusion goes beyond her evidence and that the by-product view may explain the glow’s origin. Too strong.
The author doesn’t argue this. The light ‘is unlikely to be wholly accidental,’ which tells against a pure by-product view.
This takes the last sentence’s ‘it remains possible’ and turns it into a finding. And the possibility there is about origin and later timing, not about the mushroom versus the mycelium.
This describes the third paragraph only. The passage also covers the older view, the clock finding, and the author’s verdict.
CORRECT. The passage weighs Weyl’s evidence against her conclusion: the clock and the insect attraction are established, spore dispersal is not.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Weyl’s team found that the glow of Lucidella vesperis
choices: is in some of the mushrooms bright enough to read by
keeps to its daily cycle even when the mushrooms are kept dark
is brightest during the hours when the fungus’s metabolism peaks
drew more spore-carrying insects to lit replicas than to dark ones
is produced by a reaction that neutralizes reactive forms of oxygen
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the glow ‘continues to follow this cycle when mushrooms are kept in constant darkness,’ which B restates. D is the trap: the lit replicas caught more insects, but the spores were found on insects ‘collected from real Lucidella mushrooms,’ not on insects from the replicas. A is said of ‘a few species’ of luminous fungi, not of Lucidella; C reverses the finding, since metabolism peaks in the afternoon and the glow at night; and E is the older view’s claim about fungal light in general.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Weyl’s team actually found about Lucidella’s glow.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, second sentence, and paragraph 3, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Weyl’s team found two things: the glow cycles on an internal clock, even in constant darkness; and lit replicas caught about five times as many insects as dark ones. Separately, insects collected from real mushrooms carried spores. Keep those apart. We need an answer that matches one finding exactly. Detail traps here borrow a word from the right sentence (‘spores,’ ‘bright enough to read by’) and attach it to the wrong thing.

choices.note: The passage says ‘in a few species the glow is bright enough to read by.’ Nothing says Lucidella is one of them. Wrong scope.
CORRECT. ‘Continues to follow this cycle when mushrooms are kept in constant darkness.’
This reverses it. Metabolism peaks in the warm afternoon; the glow rises after dusk. That mismatch is the whole point of Weyl’s argument.

Tempting, because the replica result and the spores sit in the same sentence. But the spores were found on insects from real mushrooms. The passage never says the replica insects carried spores; the replicas just caught more insects.
This is the older view’s account of fungal light in general, from the first paragraph. It isn’t something Weyl’s team found.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that those who held the view described in the first paragraph regarded the glow of the buried mycelium as
choices: evidence that the light of luminous fungi is too faint for animals to see
a sign that the mycelium is more active metabolically than the mushroom
an adaptation that protects the mycelium from animals that feed on wood
evidence that fungal light does not serve to communicate with animals
a trait found only in those species whose mushrooms do not themselves glow
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the mycelium glows ‘where no animal could see it’ and that this fed the view that the light was a by-product, so its holders took the buried glow as evidence that the light is not meant for animals: D. A confuses being out of sight with being too faint. B and E are never suggested, and C gives the light a purpose the older view denied.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find why the older view pointed to the glowing mycelium.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, fourth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Why mention that the mycelium glows underground? Because a signal nobody can see isn’t a signal. If the light were for animals, why would it shine where no animal can see it? So the buried glow supported the idea that the light has no audience: it’s a by-product. We need ‘not for animals.’

choices.note: The problem is location, not brightness. The mycelium is buried; the passage says some fungal light is bright enough to read by.
Nothing in the passage compares the metabolism of the mycelium and the mushroom.
The older view denied that the light served any purpose. An adaptation is a purpose.
CORRECT. A light shining ‘where no animal could see it’ can’t be a message to animals, which is why the older view treated it as a by-product.
The passage says many fungi glow in both mushroom and mycelium. It never limits mycelium glow to species with dark mushrooms.

questions.stem: In the second sentence of the fourth paragraph, the author’s claim that a light that attracts animals at the hours they forage “is unlikely to be wholly accidental” functions primarily to
choices: acknowledge one respect in which Weyl’s findings tell against the view that fungal light serves no purpose
show that Weyl’s findings establish that the glow of Lucidella evolved to promote the dispersal of spores
concede that the view described in the first paragraph correctly explains why the buried mycelium glows
raise a possibility about the origin of the glow that the final sentence of the passage then rules out
cast doubt on Weyl’s claim that the glow of Lucidella is governed by an internal clock and not by light
questions.explanation: The claim belongs to the first half of the author’s verdict, the part saying Weyl’s findings ‘establish more than her critics have granted’: a timed, attracting light probably has some purpose, contrary to the older view that fungal light served none. So A is correct. B is the trap: it treats this concession as proof of Weyl’s spore-dispersal conclusion, which the next sentence says requires evidence not yet in hand. C and D misdescribe the final sentence, which leaves the by-product origin open, and E contradicts ‘difficult to dispute.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what the ‘unlikely to be wholly accidental’ claim does in the author’s argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first three sentences (‘more than … less than …’, the claim itself, then ‘But to show …’).

breakdown.analysis: The fourth paragraph has a two-part verdict: more than critics grant, less than Weyl’s conclusion needs. The second sentence is the ‘more than’ half: the glow is clock-driven, it draws insects, and that’s not likely to be pure accident. The ‘But’ sentence starts the ‘less than’ half. So this claim gives Weyl something against the old no-purpose view, without giving her spore dispersal. We need an answer that says ‘concedes a point against the old view’ and stops there.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Not wholly accidental’ cuts against the older view that the light served no purpose at all. It’s the ‘more than her critics have granted’ half of the verdict.

Tempting, because the claim does favor Weyl. But ‘not accidental’ isn’t ‘for spore dispersal.’ The very next sentence says that would take evidence about viable spores and descendants that nobody has yet. Too strong.
The final sentence says only that the by-product origin ‘remains possible.’ It doesn’t say the older view is correct, and this claim isn’t about the mycelium at all.
The final sentence doesn’t rule anything out. It leaves open that the light began as a by-product.
This is backward. The author says the clock-driven glow is ‘now difficult to dispute.’

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A long-standing explanation of a trait is presented; evidence against it drawn from one species is described; the explanation is rejected outright; and a new hypothesis is then put forward by the author to replace the rejected one.
Two rival explanations of a trait are presented; an experiment designed to decide between them is described; and the experiment is judged to favor one of them without ruling out the other.

A long-standing explanation of a trait is presented; a finding that casts doubt on it is reported, followed by a test it prompted; and the evidence is judged to fall short of the conclusion drawn from it.

A long-standing explanation of a trait is presented; a finding that casts doubt on it is reported, followed by a test it prompted; and the evidence is judged to establish the conclusion drawn from it.

A finding about one species is reported; a long-standing explanation is offered to account for that finding; a test of that explanation is described; and further research is proposed to settle the matter.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives the by-product view, the second reports the clock finding and Weyl’s ‘audience’ hypothesis, the third the replica test and her conclusion, and the fourth judges that the findings establish ‘less than her conclusion requires.’ That is C. D is identical until its last clause, which reverses the verdict: the author grants that the glow is clock-driven and attracts insects but says the spore-dispersal conclusion is not shown. A has the author reject the older view, which the last sentence keeps open. B and E misorder or misdescribe the parts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the description that fits every paragraph, in order.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All four paragraphs; the decisive part is paragraph 4, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: P1, the old explanation (by-product). P2, a finding that doesn’t fit (the clock) plus Weyl’s idea that the light has an audience. P3, the test (lit replicas) and Weyl’s conclusion (spore dispersal). P4, the verdict: more than critics grant, less than her conclusion needs. Organization answers die on a single wrong element, so read every clause. Here two answers agree word for word until the final clause; the verdict decides it.

choices.note: The author never rejects the older view. The last sentence says the light may have begun as that very by-product. And the new hypothesis comes from Weyl, not as a replacement offered by the author.
The first paragraph presents one explanation, not two rivals, and the replica experiment was designed to identify the glow’s audience, not to decide between explanations.

CORRECT. Every clause matches: the clock finding prompted the replica test, and the last clause is the author’s verdict that the evidence establishes less than Weyl’s spore-dispersal conclusion requires.

Tempting. It matches the correct answer up to the last clause, and the author does grant Weyl a lot. But ‘establish the conclusion’ contradicts ‘less than her conclusion requires’: viable spores and more descendants are still unshown.
Wrong order and wrong roles. The long-standing view comes first, and it is the explanation the finding challenges, not one offered to account for it.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with answering which one of the following questions?
choices: Why have the courts that allow recovery for a lost chance limited such recovery to cases of medical malpractice?
Is it justifiable to compensate a patient’s estate in proportion to the chance of survival that negligence destroyed?
Under what circumstances does the more-likely-than-not rule let a court decide what probably happened in a case?
Should a patient who survives despite negligent treatment be permitted to recover for a reduced chance of survival?
Does the traditional rule of causation give physicians too little reason to take care with patients whose prognoses are poor?
questions.explanation: Passage A argues against the lost-chance doctrine and passage B defends proportional recovery, so both address whether compensation proportional to the lost chance is justified: B. E is the main trap: it is the heart of passage B’s argument, but passage A never discusses the traditional rule’s effect on physicians’ care. A and D come only from passage A’s third paragraph, and C is a passing remark at the start of passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question both passages are mainly trying to answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph (‘achieves fairness only by redefining the injury’); passage B, second and third paragraphs (‘Proportional recovery corrects both errors’).

breakdown.analysis: A says the lost-chance doctrine is a bad idea. B says proportional recovery is a good one. Same doctrine, opposite verdicts. So the shared question is ‘should courts do this?’ For a ‘both passages’ question, check every choice against BOTH passages; the trap is usually one passage’s central concern.

choices.note: Only passage A raises this, and only in its last paragraph. Passage B never mentions the limits.
CORRECT. A says no (it redefines the injury and has no natural boundary); B says yes (it charges negligent physicians for the harm they actually cause).
Passage B mentions this in its first sentence on the way to its real point. Passage A doesn’t address it.
Only passage A raises the surviving patient, and only as a consequence of the doctrine’s logic. Passage B is silent.
Tempting, because it’s the core of passage B (‘a duty that cannot be enforced’). But passage A never discusses how the traditional rule affects physicians’ care. One passage’s concern, not both.

questions.stem: According to passage A, courts that have adopted the lost-chance doctrine
choices: have openly acknowledged that its logic would extend to risks created by careless drivers and manufacturers
have confined it to cases in which the patient’s chance of survival was below one-half before the negligence
have defended the doctrine chiefly on the ground that it deters physicians from careless treatment
have recognized that a chance is not something a person possesses in the way a person possesses health
have restricted it in ways for which the doctrine’s own reasoning provides no support
questions.explanation: Passage A says these courts ‘have confined it to medical malpractice and to patients who actually suffered the harm, but nothing in its logic supports either limit’ (third paragraph), which E restates. A is the trap: the author says only that the limits are ‘signs that these courts sense where the doctrine leads,’ not that the courts have openly acknowledged it. B names a limit the passage never mentions, C replaces the ‘fairness’ defense with deterrence and does not attribute it to courts, and D is the author’s own objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says about the courts that use the doctrine.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A says three things about these courts: they limited the doctrine to medical malpractice and to patients who were actually harmed; nothing in the doctrine’s logic supports those limits; and the limits suggest the courts ‘sense’ where the doctrine leads. Watch the qualifiers. ‘Sense’ is an interpretation the author reads into what the courts did, not something the courts said. We need an answer that sticks to what the passage attributes to the courts.

choices.note: Tempting, because the passage does link the courts to the doctrine’s wider reach. But it says the courts ‘sense’ where it leads, and that is the author’s reading of their limits. ‘Openly acknowledged’ claims they said so. Wrong strength.
The limits named are medical malpractice and actual harm. A below-one-half limit is never mentioned; the 40 percent figure is just the example.
The passage says the doctrine is ‘usually defended as a matter of fairness,’ and doesn’t say by whom. Deterrence is passage B’s kind of argument.
This is passage A’s author’s objection to the doctrine. The courts adopted the doctrine, so they would hardly accept it.
CORRECT. The courts confined the doctrine, and ‘nothing in its logic supports either limit.’

questions.stem: By saying that physicians owe some patients “a duty that cannot be enforced” (first sentence of the second paragraph of passage B), the author of passage B most probably means that
choices: physicians have no legal obligation to treat those patients whose chance of survival is below one-half
