courts usually lack the evidence they need to determine whether a physician’s treatment was careless
patients with poor prognoses seldom bring negligence suits against the physicians who treated them
under the traditional rule, careless treatment of certain patients carries no legal consequence for physicians
the standard of care owed to patients with poor prognoses is too vague for courts to apply it consistently
questions.explanation: The phrase sums up the first paragraph of passage B: under the traditional rule every patient whose chance was below one-half ‘lost nothing, however careless the treatment,’ so negligence toward those patients brings no liability. D says this. B is the trap: passage B’s uncertainty concerns causation, whether the patient would have survived, not whether the treatment was careless, which its examples take as given (‘negligently reduces’). A denies that the duty exists, which the phrase presupposes, and C and E are never suggested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decide what passage B means by a duty that can’t be enforced.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph, last sentence, and second paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: A duty that ‘cannot be enforced’ still exists; the problem is that breaking it costs nothing. Why does it cost nothing? Paragraph 1 says: under the traditional rule, a patient below one-half ‘lost nothing, however careless the treatment.’ The 45-to-10 example makes it concrete: clearly negligent, no liability. So the phrase means ‘physicians can be careless with these patients and face no legal consequence.’ Note what is uncertain here: whether this patient would have lived, not whether the doctor was careless.

choices.note: The phrase assumes the duty exists (physicians ‘owe’ it). The problem is enforcement, not the absence of an obligation.

Tempting, because passage B is all about uncertainty and evidence that ‘will never reveal’ something. But what can’t be revealed is whether the patient would have survived: causation. Its examples stipulate the negligence (‘negligently reduces’). Wrong kind of uncertainty.
Passage B says nothing about how often such patients sue. The point is that suing would get them nothing.
CORRECT. Below one-half, the traditional rule says the patient ‘lost nothing, however careless the treatment,’ so breaching the duty carries no liability.
Passage B never says the standard of care is unclear. Its examples treat the negligence as clear; the obstacle is the causation rule.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?
choices: a case in which negligence that only slightly reduced a patient’s chance of survival results in liability for an entire death
a requirement that a plaintiff show that the defendant’s negligence more likely than not caused the harm that he or she complains of
a patient whose chance of survival was negligently reduced but who nonetheless went on to survive
damages reduced in proportion to the chance of survival that a physician’s negligence destroyed
a defense of the doctrine of lost chance on grounds of fairness to patients and their estates
questions.explanation: Passage B’s physician who ‘reduces a 55 percent chance to 50 percent is liable for the full value of the death,’ and passage A has no such case, so A is correct. D is the main trap: passage B calls it ‘proportional recovery’ without spelling it out, but passage A describes it in its first paragraph, so it appears in both. B is also in both; C and E appear only in passage A (its third and second paragraphs).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find something passage B mentions that passage A does not.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, second sentence. Check each choice against all of passage A.

breakdown.analysis: Go choice by choice and check both passages; don’t trust memory. The 55-to-50 physician is in B only: a five-point drop and full liability. Proportional damages look like B’s idea because B names ‘proportional recovery,’ but A describes the same thing in detail (‘a fraction of the damages … proportional to the chance … destroyed’). Fairness looks like B’s theme, but the word appears only in A. ‘B but not A’ questions punish answers that are in both, or only in the other one.

choices.note: CORRECT. Passage B’s 55-to-50 physician: a small drop in the chance of survival, full liability for the death. Passage A gives only the 40 percent example, where the estate recovers nothing.
This is in both. Passage A opens with it, and passage B’s ‘more-likely-than-not rule’ is the same requirement.
Only passage A mentions this, in its third paragraph, as a consequence of the doctrine’s logic.

Tempting, because ‘proportional recovery’ is passage B’s phrase. But passage A describes exactly this in its first paragraph: ‘a fraction of the damages for the death, proportional to the chance of survival the negligence destroyed.’ It’s in both.
Passage A says the doctrine ‘is usually defended as a matter of fairness.’ Passage B’s defense rests on making physicians pay for the harm they cause, and it never uses the word. Only in A.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A raises two objections to a legal doctrine, and passage B defends the doctrine by answering each of those objections in turn.
Passage A criticizes a traditional legal rule, and passage B defends that rule against a proposed alternative to it.
Passage A raises objections to a legal doctrine, and passage B concedes those objections but argues that the doctrine’s benefits outweigh them.
Passage A argues that a legal doctrine depends on a dubious conception of injury; passage B defends the doctrine and denies that it does.
Passage A argues that a legal doctrine should be extended beyond medical cases, and passage B argues that it should be confined to medical cases.
questions.explanation: Passage A says the doctrine ‘achieves fairness only by redefining the injury’ as a chance, and passage B defends proportional recovery and ends by saying such courts ‘are not inventing a new kind of injury’ but measuring an old one, so D is correct. A is the trap: passage B answers the redefinition objection but never addresses passage A’s second objection, that the doctrine has no natural boundary. C misses that passage B denies rather than concedes, B reverses which rule each passage targets, and E misreads passage A, which treats extension as an unwelcome implication.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B stands in relation to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second and third paragraphs (the two objections); passage B, third paragraph (‘not inventing a new kind of injury’).

breakdown.analysis: Passage A makes two objections: (1) the doctrine redefines the injury as a chance; (2) the redefinition has no natural boundary. Passage B defends the doctrine and, in its last paragraph, flatly denies (1). Does it say anything about (2)? No: no surviving patients, no careless drivers. So B answers one objection, not both. We need an answer with A’s injury objection and B’s denial of it. Relationship traps often say ‘answers each objection’ when the second passage only answers one.

choices.note: Tempting, because passage B does read like a reply to passage A, and its last paragraph answers the injury objection directly. But passage B never touches the boundary objection. ‘Each of those objections’ is one too many.
Reversed. Passage A criticizes the lost-chance doctrine, and passage B criticizes the traditional rule.
Passage B doesn’t concede anything. It says courts ‘are not inventing a new kind of injury,’ which denies passage A’s central objection.
CORRECT. Passage A: the doctrine treats a chance as the injury. Passage B: the injury is still death, measured as a probability. Defense plus denial.
Passage A doesn’t want the doctrine extended. It uses the extension as a sign that the doctrine’s logic is bad.

questions.stem: The attitude of the author of passage B toward the traditional more-likely-than-not rule is most accurately described as
choices: approval of the rule in general, together with the view that it should not be used in cases of medical malpractice at all
approval of the rule for one kind of uncertainty about causation, together with the view that it is unsuited to another
disapproval of the rule, on the grounds that it can make physicians liable for deaths that they did not in fact cause
approval of the rule, provided that it is applied only to patients whose chance of survival exceeded one-half
indifference to the rule, since it yields the same total liability as proportional recovery across many cases
questions.explanation: Passage B says the rule ‘works well when uncertainty about causation arises because facts are missing’ but ‘works poorly when the uncertainty is irreducible’ (first paragraph), which B describes. A is the trap: passage B says irreducible uncertainty arises ‘often’ in medicine, not always, so it does not reject the rule for medical cases as a class. C overstates one example into a total rejection, D ignores passage B’s complaint about the 55-to-50 case, and E contradicts ‘corrects both errors.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find how the author of passage B judges the traditional rule.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph (‘works well when … works poorly when …’) and second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B grades the rule by the kind of uncertainty. Facts missing: the rule works; it lets a court decide what probably happened. Uncertainty irreducible: the rule fails; it says the patient lost nothing. Where does medicine fit? ‘Often’ in the second group. Not always. So the author’s line is drawn by type of uncertainty, not by type of case. We need ‘good for one kind of uncertainty, bad for the other.’ Watch the qualifier ‘often.’

choices.note: Tempting, because passage B’s examples are all medical and proportional recovery is offered for physicians. But it says irreducible uncertainty arises ‘often’ in medicine, and the rule fails where uncertainty is irreducible, not in medical cases as such. A malpractice case with missing facts would still suit the rule. Wrong line.
CORRECT. Works well when facts are missing; works poorly when uncertainty is irreducible. One kind of uncertainty versus another.
Too strong. Passage B approves of the rule where facts are missing. The 55-to-50 example is one of two errors, not the whole verdict.
Passage B calls full liability in the 55-to-50 case an error too. Restricting the rule to patients above one-half keeps that error.
Passage B isn’t indifferent; it says proportional recovery ‘corrects both errors.’ It never says the totals match.
